t.nanxun section of jiangnan canal@30.9,12:
Nanxun is one of the water towns of the Yangtze delta, south of Lake Tai, where life has revolved around canals for more than a thousand years. In the nineteenth century, it became immensely rich through the silk trade, and its merchant families, known by nicknames like the four elephants and the eight bulls, built mansions that mixed Chinese courtyards with European columns, stained glass and Western-style furniture, an unusual blend you will not find in many other water towns. The canal running through the town is part of the Grand Canal, the immense waterway linking Beijing with Hangzhou, which UNESCO listed in 2014.

Walking along the canals, under arched stone bridges, past whitewashed houses with black-tiled roofs reflected in the water, is the essence of a visit. The Little Lotus Villa, a garden estate with a lotus pond, and the Jiaye Hall library, a private book collection housed in a beautiful building, are highlights, as is the Zhang Shiming residence, with its Western-influenced interiors. Nanxun is less crowded than better-known towns like Wuzhen or Zhouzhuang, especially early in the morning, when locals do tai chi by the water and the mist hangs over the canals.

Now the practical side for riders. Foreigners in China generally need a Chinese driving licence to ride, motorcycles are banned from expressways, and many cities restrict or prohibit them entirely, so independent motorcycle travel requires serious planning, often through a specialised tour operator. The roads in the delta are flat, straight and busy, crossing an endless network of canals, fish ponds and mulberry fields, with heavy traffic of trucks, cars and electric scooters. The old town of Nanxun itself is pedestrianised, so you will explore on foot or by boat.

Huzhou, about thirty kilometres away, and Wuzhen, about sixteen, have full services, and Nanxun has plenty of restaurants and guesthouses in and around the old town. Local specialities include freshwater fish and shrimp, braised pork and sweet rice cakes. The climate is humid, with hot summers, a rainy season in June and July, and cool winters. Spring and autumn are the most pleasant times to visit, with mild temperatures and clear skies.
t.classical gardens of suzhou@31.3,120.5:
A classical Chinese garden is a whole landscape squeezed into a courtyard: rocks stand in for mountains, ponds for lakes, and a winding covered walkway reveals one framed view after another, each window cut in a different shape. Suzhou, a canal city west of Shanghai, perfected the art over centuries, as scholars, officials and merchants built private retreats behind high white walls. Nine of its gardens are listed by UNESCO as the Classical Gardens of Suzhou, among them the Humble Administrator's Garden, the Lingering Garden and the tiny, exquisite Master-of-Nets Garden, and the Retreat and Reflection Garden in the water town of Tongli.

The point given here lies near Mudu, an old town on the western edge of Suzhou, close to the hills that rise towards Lake Tai. Mudu has its own historic gardens and canals, and the hills behind, such as Lingyan Shan, have temples and walks with views over the lake. Lake Tai is the source of the strange, eroded limestone rocks prized in Chinese gardens, and you will see them everywhere, full of holes and twisted shapes.

Suzhou is also famous for silk, embroidery so fine it looks painted, Biluochun green tea grown on the hills by the lake, and, in autumn, hairy crabs from the nearby Yangcheng Lake, a delicacy people travel across the country to eat.

Riding here requires preparation and realism. Foreign visitors generally cannot ride in China on a home licence, and arranging a temporary licence and permits for a motorbike is complex and often requires an organised tour. Many Chinese cities restrict or ban motorcycles in their centres, and expressways are generally closed to them. Electric scooters fill the streets, often silently and without lights, and traffic rules are interpreted creatively. If you do ride, the roads around Lake Tai and onto its peninsulas and islands are the most rewarding, with water views, tea terraces and orchards of loquat and bayberry.

The gardens are best visited early, as soon as they open, before tour groups arrive. Fuel, food and every service are easy to find in Suzhou. Try a bowl of Suzhou noodles in the morning, light and delicate, and a cup of Biluochun tea in a garden teahouse while rain falls on the pond.
t.wuxi city section of jiangnan canal@31.6:
The Grand Canal is the longest artificial waterway in the world, stretching from Beijing to Hangzhou, and some of its sections have been in use for more than two thousand years. In the Jiangnan region, south of the Yangtze, it flows through a landscape of rice paddies, lakes and old towns, and in Wuxi it runs right through the city. The canal was listed by UNESCO in 2014, and the Wuxi section includes historic streets, bridges and warehouses along its banks.

The most charming stretch is around the Qingming Bridge, an old stone arch over the canal, with narrow streets of whitewashed houses with black-tiled roofs, small shops and teahouses. Barges still chug along the water, heavily loaded with sand, gravel and coal, a reminder that the canal remains a working route. At night, red lanterns reflect in the water.

Wuxi lies on the northern shore of Lake Tai, one of China's largest freshwater lakes, and the lakeside is its main attraction. Yuantouzhu, a peninsula shaped like a turtle's head, has gardens, pavilions and cherry blossoms in spring. Further west, the Lingshan scenic area has one of the tallest bronze Buddhas in the world, overlooking the lake. Wuxi is also known for clay figurines from Huishan, colourful little dolls with chubby faces, and for its cuisine, which is famously sweet: try the spare ribs braised in soy and sugar, or soup dumplings that are sweeter than those of Shanghai.

If you are thinking of riding, be realistic. Getting a licence to ride as a foreigner in China involves bureaucracy, motorbikes are not allowed on expressways, and urban areas may have restrictions on motorcycles. Electric scooters and bicycles fill the streets, and traffic rules are loosely observed. For most visitors, the canal and the lake are best explored on foot, by boat or by bicycle.

The roads around Lake Tai, however, can be lovely, with water views, tea plantations and fruit orchards, and the islands in the lake, linked by bridges, offer quieter riding if you can arrange it. Wuxi is a large city with fuel, food and every service. Take a boat trip along the canal in the evening, and sit in a teahouse with a pot of green tea and a plate of sweet pastries while the barges pass.
t.jiaxing hangzhou section of jiangnan can:
The Grand Canal of China is the longest artificial waterway in the world, a chain of canals and rivers linking Beijing with Hangzhou that was begun in sections well over two thousand years ago and unified under the Sui dynasty in the seventh century. Its southernmost stretch, the Jiangnan Canal, crosses the flat, watery plain between Jiaxing and Hangzhou, and this section is part of the UNESCO World Heritage site. Grain, silk and salt moved north along it for centuries, and the towns that line its banks grew rich on that traffic.

The landscape is the classic Jiangnan picture: canals with stone humpback bridges, whitewashed houses with black tiled roofs, mulberry fields that once fed the silk industry, and fish ponds stretching to the horizon. It is completely flat and intensely farmed, with factories and new housing pressing in from every side, so the old beauty comes in pockets rather than wide vistas. Water towns such as Wuzhen to the north and Tangqi near Linping keep stretches of the old canal townscape, though they can be very crowded at weekends.

Riding here takes preparation. Foreign riders need a Chinese driving licence and properly registered bikes; temporary permits for overland travellers usually require an organised tour with a guide. Hangzhou restricts motorcycles in its urban areas, and motorcycles are generally not allowed on expressways in much of China, so you will use the older national and provincial roads, which are often busy with trucks, scooters and electric bikes. Stay alert at junctions, where right of way is a matter of interpretation.

Food makes up for a lot. Jiaxing is famous for zongzi, sticky rice dumplings wrapped in leaves, and Hangzhou's cuisine, from Dongpo pork to Longjing tea shrimp, is among the most refined in China. Fuel stations are plentiful along major roads. Spring, with mild weather and blossoming trees, and autumn are the best times; summer is hot and very humid, and the plum rains of June can be relentless.
t.hangzhou xiaoshan shaoxing section of zh:
Shaoxing is a city built on water. Its canals, bridges and narrow stone-paved lanes have made it one of the most photogenic towns in eastern China, and the Zhedong Canal, which links Hangzhou, Shaoxing and Ningbo, is its great artery. The canal belongs to the Grand Canal system, the longest artificial waterway in the world, which UNESCO listed in 2014. The Zhedong section carried grain, silk, tea and travellers for more than a thousand years, and in Shaoxing you can still see black-awninged boats, arched stone bridges and old warehouses along the banks.

The town has a literary history too. The writer Lu Xun grew up here, and his stories of village life and Shaoxing's odd characters are set in places that visitors can walk through. The city is famous for its rice wine, called huangjiu, a golden, mellow drink made from glutinous rice and the clear water of Jian Lake, which is served warm in small bowls with dried plums or with the local stinky tofu. Pottery jars of aged wine line the shelves in shops across the old town.

For a motorcyclist, the area is flat and heavily built-up, with expressways, bridges and dense urban traffic, and the pleasure is more about the culture than the riding. Foreign riders in China need a Chinese licence and registration, and in many cities motorcycles are restricted or banned from central districts, so a visit here is usually made by other means. Where riding is allowed, expect fast electric scooters, delivery vans and constant horn use, and watch out for slippery stone bridges in the rain. Spring and autumn are comfortable, and summer is hot and humid.

Shaoxing has abundant fuel, food and accommodation, and the canal-side districts offer tea houses, restaurants and guesthouses in restored buildings. Walk along the old canals at dusk, when lanterns are lit and the water reflects the bridges, and order a plate of drunken shrimp and a bowl of warmed wine. The pace is slow, the air smells of water and rice wine, and the city is a pleasure to explore at walking speed.
t.paris@48.9,2.3:
These coordinates land on the Place de la Concorde, the great octagonal square at the foot of the Champs-Élysées, where the Luxor obelisk stands in the middle. It is a gift from the ruler of Egypt, about three thousand years old, and it was set up here in 1836 on the spot where the guillotine stood during the Revolution. Louis XVI was executed on this square in 1793, and so, in the Terror that followed, were over a thousand others. Now the square is a roundabout with fountains, ringed by traffic and framed by the Tuileries gardens on one side and the Madeleine church on the other. The banks of the Seine in this part of the city are UNESCO listed.

The honest advice for a rider is to treat Paris as a city to park in. The Périphérique ring road is fast, dense and unforgiving, and central Paris is a web of one-way streets, bus lanes, cobbles and tram lines. Paris also has a low-emission zone, so find out if your bike needs the Crit'Air sticker before you ride in, and look up the latest rules on parking. Motorcycle bays are common at the edges of the centre, and a garage near a metro line is the sanest option. Petrol stations are rare in the middle of the city, so fill up on the outskirts, in Levallois-Perret or Clichy, which are only a few kilometres away.

On foot, the area is easy. You can walk the Tuileries to the Louvre, cross the Pont de la Concorde to the Assemblée nationale, or head up the Rue Royale to the Madeleine and the smart shops of the Faubourg Saint-Honoré. The Champs-Élysées begins at the square's northwest corner and runs gently uphill to the Arc de Triomphe. Early morning, before the coaches arrive, gives you the best light on the stone and the fewest crowds.

If you want a break, take a coffee at a pavement cafe and watch the traffic rotate around the obelisk. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with soft light and fewer tourists. The metro station at Concorde is a good way to move around if the bike stays in the garage.
t.le havre@49.5,0.1:
Le Havre was flattened. Allied bombing in September 1944 destroyed the old centre, and the French state hired the architect Auguste Perret to rebuild it, which he did in reinforced concrete, with straight boulevards, uniform apartment blocks and a grid of open squares. At first the town seemed grim. Today UNESCO calls it a masterpiece of postwar reconstruction, listed in 2005, and in the right light the concrete takes on a warm, pale-gold tone. The tower of the church of Saint-Joseph, over a hundred metres high, is the landmark, and inside, the light through its coloured glass is dazzling, a thing worth ten minutes of anyone's time.

The city has an older story as France's Atlantic port. It was founded in the early sixteenth century by King Francis I because the nearby harbours were silting up, and it later became the departure point for ocean liners. Monet painted the harbour at sunrise in 1872, in the picture that gave Impressionism its name, and the town still holds a museum with a fine collection of his circle. Sainte-Adresse, along the cliffs, was his subject in another painting, and its pebble beach and old villas have kept a seaside feel.

For riding, Le Havre is a gateway more than a destination. The Pont de Normandie, a long cable-stayed bridge opened in 1995, carries you across the Seine estuary to Honfleur and the Normandy coast, and on a clear day it is a thrilling bridge to cross, though the wind can be strong. To the north, the Pays de Caux plateau offers quiet farm roads, flint-walled villages and the white chalk cliffs of Étretat, around thirty kilometres away. Weather can change in minutes, with sea fog and sudden rain, and wet painted lines on the city's roads are slippery.

Fuel is easy in a city of nearly two hundred thousand, and ferries to England leave from the port. Parking for a bike near the centre is simple. Eat moules-frites near the harbour, and in summer look out for sea-salt caramel from local bakeries. Early morning, when the sun picks out the concrete and the harbour is grey and gold, is the time to be on the front.
t.the lingering garden@31.3,120.6:
The Lingering Garden, called Liu Yuan, is one of the four most famous gardens in China, and a masterpiece of the Suzhou school. It began in the sixteenth century as the private garden of an official of the Ming dynasty, and was later rebuilt by a Qing dynasty owner, whose family name, Liu, gave it its present name, which also means lingering or staying on, and that is exactly what visitors want to do. It belongs to the UNESCO listing of the classical gardens of Suzhou, from 1997, and it covers a couple of hectares, with halls, pavilions, corridors, ponds and rockeries arranged in a design that seems to turn a small space into a landscape.

The art of the Chinese scholar's garden is in the surprise. Covered walkways wind and turn, with windows of different shapes that frame a view, such as a bamboo, a rock or a bit of water, like a painting. The Cloud Capped Peak, a tall, perforated rock from Lake Tai, is considered one of the finest garden stones in China. Water, rock, plants and architecture are balanced, and the white walls with their grey tiles form a backdrop. Visit in the early morning or late afternoon, when the light is soft and the crowds are thin, and in rain, when the roofs drip and the pond ripples, the garden is at its most poetic.

Suzhou, an hour from Shanghai by fast train, is a canal city, often called the Venice of the East, though its waterways are quieter and more domestic than that comparison suggests. Silk has been woven here for centuries, and the city has a very good museum designed by the architect I. M. Pei, whose family came from Suzhou. The Retreat and Reflection Garden at Tongli, a water town nearby, is another listed garden, and the old street of Pingjiang Road is a pleasant place to walk.

Riding in China as a foreigner is highly restricted, so most visitors come by train and use taxis or hired bicycles. Suzhou has fuel and services everywhere, and the local food is sweet and delicate, with freshwater fish, river shrimp and noodles in broth. Spring, with the flowers, and autumn are the best seasons, and the summer heat can be heavy.
t.the mountain villa with embracing beauty:
Suzhou has been famous for its gardens for centuries, and the Mountain Villa with Embracing Beauty, known in Chinese as Huanxiu Shanzhuang, is one of the nine that UNESCO lists among the classical gardens of the city. It lies in the western part of town, a short way from the old centre, and it is quieter than the more famous gardens on the tourist trail. The name suggests a mountain retreat that holds beauty within it, and the design delivers on that: a pond at the centre, pavilions around it and a large rockery of weathered limestone that is the best-known feature.

The idea behind such gardens is to build a world in miniature. A wall hides the street, a doorway frames a view, a zigzag bridge slows your steps and a window with a pattern of tiles turns a bamboo grove into a picture. The rocks are taken from Lake Tai, nearby, and are chosen for their holes and twists, which suggest mountains and caves. The gardens were built by officials, scholars and merchants who had retired from public life or made their fortunes in silk, and they were places for tea, poetry and conversation with friends.

Suzhou itself is a canal city of more than five million people, with white walls and grey tile roofs, stone bridges and willows. The old moats and canals are still part of daily life. Be aware that riding conditions are quite different from Europe. Motorcycle regulations in Chinese cities are strict, many centres restrict petrol bikes, and traffic includes dense flows of electric scooters, buses and cars, so look into local rules and paperwork well in advance. In practice, visitors usually see the city on foot, by bike or by taxi.

The best times to visit are spring and autumn, when the air is mild, while summers are hot and humid. Early morning is quietest, before the tour groups arrive. Suzhou cuisine leans toward the sweet and light, with dishes such as sweet-and-sour mandarin fish and noodles with a clear broth, and tea houses offer a place to sit with a pot of green tea. Pingjiang Road, a restored canal street, is a nice place for a stroll and a snack in the evening.
t.area of yaoshan site@30.4,120.0:
Five thousand years ago, on the plain north of Hangzhou, people built a city with a water system so sophisticated that archaeologists still marvel at it. This is the Liangzhu culture, and the Yaoshan site is one of its most intriguing pieces, thought to be a ritual platform where elites took part in ceremonies and where beautifully worked jades were buried. The Liangzhu people carved jade into discs called bi and tubes known as cong, with delicate, mask-like faces, and these objects were symbols of status and belief. The whole Liangzhu complex has been a UNESCO site since 2019.

The scale is the astonishing thing. A walled city, a network of canals and a series of dams in the hills to the northwest that controlled flooding show that this was a well-organised society, built on rice farming, with no written records. Much of what we know comes from decades of patient excavation, and the Liangzhu museum on the plain tells the story with finds that are hard to forget. At Yaoshan itself there is less to see on the ground, and the value is in understanding what lies under the fields and the low hills.

The country around is soft and green, the sort of landscape for which this region, south of the Yangtze, is known: rice paddies, bamboo, tea bushes on the hills and small canals threading the plains. Deqing is a town of about 88,000 people 14 km away, and Hangzhou, with its West Lake and its tea plantations, is only about 20 km away. Roads are flat and well surfaced, though busy, and traffic includes many trucks and scooters. Spring brings blossom and green tea, while summer is humid and often rainy.

Practicalities for a motorcycle rider need care. Foreign riders can find it hard to ride in China, as local licensing and plate rules apply, and motorbikes are barred or restricted in many urban areas. If you are on the ground here, hire a car and driver or a bicycle, and use the time to see the jade and the museum. Hangzhou's Longjing tea, grown on the hills near the lake, is the thing to try, and a pot of it in a quiet tea house is a calm way to end the day.
t.cistercian abbey of fontenay@47.6,4.4:
The Abbey of Fontenay lies in a narrow, wooded valley in northern Burgundy, a few kilometres from the small town of Montbard. It was founded in 1118 by Bernard of Clairvaux's circle and became one of the earliest and best-preserved Cistercian houses in Europe. The Cistercians wanted a life of simplicity, work and silence, and they built accordingly: plain stone, no carvings of saints, no coloured glass, and a site chosen for water and seclusion. The result is a place of extraordinary calm.

What survives is remarkable because much of it is original twelfth-century work. The abbey church is long and austere, with a pointed barrel vault and light that falls in clean, plain shafts. The cloister is a quiet square of arches and the dormitory has a vast timber roof. There is even a forge, built by the monks beside the stream, where iron was worked using water power, which reminds you that these were farmers and engineers as much as contemplatives. After the Revolution the abbey became a paper mill, and was later bought and restored by a private family, which is partly why it was saved.

The ride in from Montbard is gentle, along small roads through oak and beech woods, with farmland on the plateau above. This is not high or dramatic country; it is soft and rolling, the sort of road that is a pleasure at moderate speed with a bit of dappled light. Cars and coaches arrive in summer, so mornings and weekdays are best. The car park is a short distance from the gate, and there is ample room for motorbikes.

Montbard, with about five and a half thousand people, has fuel, supermarkets and cafes, and it also has a handsome park laid out by the naturalist Buffon, who lived there in the eighteenth century. Bring a jacket because the stone buildings stay cool even in August, and allow at least an hour to walk around inside. The countryside nearby produces good cheese, notably Époisses to the south-east, and the bakeries do sound business all day.
t.the climats@47.1,4.9:
The Climats of Burgundy are, in plain terms, the vineyard plots of the Côte d'Or, each one with its own name and character, worked and described by monks and growers for nearly a thousand years. The word means little parcels of land with a specific soil, slope and exposure, and the idea is that two vines a few metres apart can yield wines that taste different. Near Ladoix-Serrigny and Beaune the slope faces east and south-east, and the great hill of Corton rises above the villages, covered in vines and crowned with woods.

History is soaked into these slopes. The Cistercians at Cîteaux and the Benedictines at Cluny began mapping the best ground in the Middle Ages, and the dukes of Burgundy later regulated and protected the wines. In Beaune the Hospices, a hospital with a brightly tiled roof founded in 1443, still owns vineyards and holds a famous charity auction every November. The patterns on the roof are glazed tiles in green, red, yellow and black.

For a rider, this is gentle, civilised country. The Route des Grands Crus, which runs along the foot of the slope from Dijon to Santenay, is a fine road for an easy day: smooth, lightly curved and lined with stone walls, village after village with famous names on the signs. Speeds are modest, the villages have speed bumps and cameras, and in the autumn harvest tractors and grape-laden trailers share the road, so patience is part of the deal. Wet leaves and mud from the vineyards can make the surface slick.

Beaune, four kilometres away and a town of about twenty-four thousand, has fuel, restaurants and a lively centre inside its old walls. Burgundy cooking is rich: beef bourguignon, eggs in red wine sauce, gougères and, in the season, fresh snails. Late September brings the colours; May has the vines in fresh green. A tasting is pleasant, but remember that you are riding.
t.archaeological ruins of liangzhu city@30:
Liangzhu is a city that existed before writing. About five thousand years ago, on a marshy plain south of the Yangtze, a Neolithic people built a walled capital with a palace platform, canals, workshops and cemeteries, and they carved jade into ritual objects of astonishing skill. The city covered several square kilometres, and its walls, built of rammed earth on a base of stone, were up to sixty metres wide at the base. UNESCO listed the archaeological ruins in 2019 as evidence of an early regional state.

The most famous objects are jade discs, called bi, and jade tubes with square outer shapes, called cong, many carved with a stylised face that combines a human and an animal. The jade came from a distance, and the workmanship shows specialised craftsmen working under strict control. Burials of elite people contained dozens of jade pieces, while ordinary graves held little. It is evidence of a society with strong social ranks and a shared religion.

Today the site is an archaeological park on the edge of Hangzhou, with a museum designed by the British architect David Chipperfield, which holds many of the finds. The ruins themselves are low mounds and ditches that have been landscaped and marked, and visitors can walk or cycle through the park. It is easy to confuse a field with a city, so the museum is a good place to start. The excavations are still going on, and new finds come out regularly.

Hangzhou has more than six million people, with every kind of service, and Deqing is smaller but also has facilities. The area has rice fields, tea gardens and bamboo forest, and local food includes fish from West Lake and the tea called Longjing. The climate is humid, with a rainy season in early summer and typhoons in late summer. Autumn is best. Foreign riders usually face restrictions in China, so check the rules before you go, and take the museum and the park at an easy pace.
t.immeuble locatif a la porte molitor@48.8:
Le Corbusier lived at the top of this building for more than thirty years and, in the end, swam away from it for the last time. The block at the Porte Molitor, on the edge of Paris where the sixteenth arrondissement meets Boulogne-Billancourt, was designed in the early 1930s as a set of apartments, and the architect kept the two top floors for his own flat and studio. It has a glass-and-steel facade, an open plan and a curved roof, and it was one of the first buildings to show that the white geometric language of modernism could work in a Parisian street. UNESCO listed it in 2016 as part of his body of work, and the apartment can be visited on guided tours, so check the opening hours before turning up.

He died in 1965 while swimming off the coast of the south of France, and the studio remains much as he left it, with the rough-cast walls, painted canvases and rooftop views. Next door stands the Piscine Molitor, an art deco swimming pool of the 1920s that fell into ruin and has since been restored as part of a hotel. Roland Garros and the Parc des Princes, the great tennis and football grounds, are only a short ride along the avenue.

Riding in this part of Paris means urban habits: patience, awareness of buses and cyclists, and a firm grip on the clutch. The périphérique runs close by, and the traffic on the boulevards of the sixteenth is dense in the morning and evening. The tarmac is generally good, apart from tram tracks and the occasional metal plate. Parking for motorbikes is available in designated bays, but it is not free everywhere, so check the signs. Paris and its suburbs have low-emission zones that can affect older bikes, so look into the rules before you arrive.

Fuel is available in Boulogne-Billancourt, which has more than a hundred thousand inhabitants and filling stations on the main roads. Cafes and bakeries are everywhere. If you want a break from the traffic, the Bois de Boulogne lies a few minutes west, and its quiet lanes are a pleasant place to unwind. Early morning on a Sunday is the best time to ride here, when the streets are empty and the light hits the glass.
t.the canglang pavilion@31.3,120.6:
The Canglang Pavilion is the oldest of Suzhou's classical gardens, and in a city famous for them, that gives it a certain quiet authority. Its origins go back to the Song dynasty in the eleventh century, when a scholar and poet named Su Shunqin, disgraced and out of office, bought a piece of land and built a retreat beside a pond. He named it Canglang, meaning blue waves, after an old poem about washing one's cap strings in clear water, and the garden has been associated with scholars in exile ever since.

What makes it different from most Suzhou gardens is its openness. Instead of being enclosed entirely by walls, the Canglang Pavilion borrows the view of the water outside, with a long covered corridor running beside the canal, and its walls are pierced with carved lattice windows, each a different pattern, framing little scenes of bamboo, rock and water. Artificial hills of rock and old trees give a feeling of a mountain landscape in miniature. UNESCO lists the classical gardens of Suzhou as a group, with an addition made in 2000.

Suzhou is a city of canals, stone bridges and whitewashed houses with dark roofs, often called the Venice of the East, and a saying goes that there is paradise in heaven and Suzhou and Hangzhou on earth. Silk and embroidery have been made here for centuries, and the local noodle soups and sweet-savoury dishes, often with a hint of sugar, are well known. Come early on a weekday to have the garden almost to yourself, and spring brings blossom and autumn gives clear skies.

Roads in and around Suzhou are busy, with electric scooters, buses and a heavy flow of traffic, so exploring the old city is easier on foot or by bicycle. Fuel, food and lodging are plentiful, and Mudu, a smaller town about eleven kilometres away, has a famous classical garden of its own. Check the rules for foreign motorcyclists in China before bringing a bike.
t.ruteng@-8.6,120.5:
Ruteng sits on a cool plateau in the middle of Flores, about twelve hundred metres above the sea, in country that feels more like the Alps in a heat wave than the tropics. Mornings here are cold enough for a jacket, mist hangs over the rice fields, and the hills are green with coffee, vanilla and clove plantations. About thirty-five thousand people live in the town, the main centre of the Manggarai region, and the majority are Catholic, a legacy of Portuguese traders and later Dutch missionaries that makes Flores unusual in mostly Muslim Indonesia. The cathedral is a large and busy landmark.

The Manggarai have their own distinctive culture, and the most striking evidence of it is in the fields. Around villages such as Cancar, a short ride from Ruteng, the rice paddies are laid out in great circular patterns called lingko, with the plots radiating from a central point like a spider web. The design reflects traditional land allocation by the village elders, and viewed from a nearby hill it is among the most unusual agricultural landscapes in the world. The old whip-fighting ritual called caci, in which men in buffalo-hide costumes duel with whips and shields, is still performed at festivals.

Ruteng has a place in science as well. In 2003, in the limestone cave of Liang Bua, a short distance north of town, archaeologists found the skeleton of a tiny human relative, nicknamed the hobbit, and named Homo floresiensis. It lived on Flores as recently as about fifty thousand years ago and stood only about a metre tall. The find changed ideas about human evolution, and the cave can be visited with a local guide.

The road here is a joy. The Trans-Flores Highway climbs from the coast through forest and farmland, with long curves and views of terraced fields and volcanic cones. Take care with the weather, since rain falls heavily in the wet season, from about November to March, and landslides can block the route. Fuel is available in town, and warm food, such as noodles and rice with chilli, is welcome on a damp evening. A cup of the local coffee, strong and slightly earthy, is the right way to warm up before the next stretch.
t.moni@-8.7,121.8:
Moni is a small village on the lower slopes of a volcano, and it exists largely because of what lies above it. About thirteen kilometres up a winding road is Kelimutu, a peak of around 1,640 metres whose summit holds three crater lakes in different colours, one of them often turquoise, another green and the third dark red or brown. The colours change over the years, depending on gases and minerals, and no one has fully explained why. Local belief holds that the souls of the dead go to the lakes, the young to one, the old to another and those who lived evil lives to the third.

Visitors usually leave Moni in the dark, around four in the morning, to reach the top for sunrise. The road is narrow and steep, and mist often fills the crater, so it can feel like a gamble. When the cloud lifts and the light strikes the water, the colours glow in a way that seems unreal, and the effect is worth the cold. By mid-morning the mist usually comes back. The climb from the car park to the viewpoint takes a few minutes on a paved path, and the air at that height is thin and chilly.

The village itself is simple, with a few guesthouses, small restaurants and shops, and weavers who sell ikat cloth, woven from dyed threads in traditional patterns, in the nearby market. Women in nearby villages still dye and weave by hand. Rice, vegetables and strong coffee are the staples of a Moni breakfast. The nights are cold, and many travellers are surprised by the need for a blanket in the tropics.

Moni lies on the Trans-Flores Highway, a winding road that links the island's towns, between Ruteng in the west and Maumere in the east. The nearest large town is Ende, about twenty-three kilometres to the south, where fuel and supplies are plentiful, and where Indonesia's first president, Sukarno, spent four years in exile in the 1930s, developing ideas that would shape the republic. Moni itself has little fuel, so fill the tank in Ende first. The dry season, from roughly May to October, offers the best chance of a clear dawn, though the volcano makes its own weather. Allow extra time for the winding road, and take warm clothes for the early start.
t.fontainebleau forest photo pull off@48.5:
Ablis and Sonchamp are small villages on the south-western fringe of the Paris basin, where the Beauce plain meets the forest of Rambouillet, and the contrast between the two landscapes is the most interesting thing about the area. To the south the land opens into the huge wheat fields of the Beauce, the granary of France, flat and vast, with church spires and wind turbines marking the horizon. To the north the ground rises into woods of oak, beech and pine, with ponds and clearings, the royal hunting forest of Rambouillet.

Rambouillet, a town of about twenty-six thousand, has a château, once a hunting residence of French kings and now a retreat for the president, with a park and a farm built for Marie-Antoinette, and a good selection of cafés and fuel stations. The forest around it covers over twenty thousand hectares and is crossed by quiet roads, with deer, wild boar and, in spring, bluebells beneath the trees. Fontainebleau, the forest and palace named in the ride, is about sixty kilometres to the east, a different forest with its own rocks and sandy soil.

For a rider, this is the most relaxed part of the Île-de-France. The roads here run in long, gentle curves through forest, with alternating light and shadow, and across open farmland with long views, and the surface is mostly good, though agricultural traffic can leave mud and the roads are narrow in places. Weekends bring many cyclists and Parisians seeking the countryside, and speed cameras are used at the entrance to villages. Dawn rides are rewarded with mist over the fields and animals crossing the road.

Autumn is a good season, when the forest turns russet and the air smells of damp earth and leaf mould, and you can stop for a coffee in one of the village cafés. Winter fog and frost are common, and the shaded forest roads can stay icy. Fuel is not difficult to find in the larger villages around, but the smallest places have none, so top up in Rambouillet or Dourdan before wandering into the woods.
t.seine loops and roche guyon scenic road@:
Élancourt and Maurepas are not villages in the sense that most riders imagine: they are part of Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines, a new town built in the 1970s on the plateau west of Versailles, a place of roundabouts, housing estates, a big shopping centre and business parks. It lies on the edge of the Paris conurbation, and this is where Parisian riders start or finish a day, wanting to leave the city behind and arrive at the Seine valley and La Roche-Guyon, an hour or so to the north-west.

It has a few curiosities. Élancourt has a hill, the Colline d'Élancourt, built up from decades of rubbish dumped here and now landscaped as a park with views over the plateau toward the Paris towers on a clear day, popular with mountain bikers and kite flyers. Nearby, the lake of Saint-Quentin, with its nature reserve, attracts waterbirds and walkers. For fuel and food the area is well served, with supermarkets and petrol stations at every turn, and a decent breakfast is easy to find.

The real attraction is what lies beyond. From here you can take quiet country roads north-west across the Mantois plateau to the Seine, which twists in great loops between chalk cliffs and orchards. La Roche-Guyon, a village of under five hundred people on the river, lies below a medieval castle with a keep and a long tunnel carved into the cliff, and was Field Marshal Rommel's headquarters in 1944. Monet's garden at Giverny is only a few kilometres away across the river. The road along the Seine, with the water on one side and white cliffs on the other, is an easy, scenic ride.

Weekend traffic around Saint-Quentin is heavy, and the nearby N12 and the A12 clog at peak hours, so leave early or late. The Yvelines countryside is surprisingly green, with forest, farmland and stately houses, and in spring the orchards blossom in the Seine valley. Be careful with farm machinery on narrow lanes and mud on the road after rain, and expect speed cameras in the built-up areas.
t.seine loops and roche guyon photo pull o:
Cerny is a village best known for its sky. Every year at Pentecost the airfield beside it, at La Ferté-Alais in the Essonne, hosts one of the biggest vintage aircraft displays in Europe, run by enthusiasts who restore and fly old fighters, bombers and biplanes, and on other weekends gliders and light aircraft use the strip. Boissy-le-Cutté, next door, is smaller still, with a handful of houses and a church, and the whole area is part of the valley of the Juine, a small river that winds through meadows and reedbeds south of Paris towards Étampes.

The ride that gives the point its name follows the Seine and the cliffs of La Roche-Guyon, far to the north-west, so this stop is the southern start of a long day or the unwinding end of it. The Essonne countryside is a patchwork of wheat fields, small woods and sandstone outcrops, with stone villages and an occasional château or mill beside the river. La Ferté-Alais, a short ride away, is a small town with a market and a few cafés, and Étampes, a larger town to the south with a medieval centre and a fine church tower, has the fuel and shops.

Roads here are quiet and rural, with long views over open fields and sudden dips into the river valleys, where the surface can be damp and the bends tighter. The Juine valley is attractive in spring when the water meadows are green and the poplars are fresh, and in autumn when mist lies in the hollows. There are few big climbs, and the riding is relaxed rather than demanding, with light traffic outside the weekends. When the air show is on, the roads for miles around are jammed, so avoid that weekend unless you want to be part of it.

Watch for farm vehicles, particularly in harvest season, and for mud and straw on the road. Early mornings bring mist and cool air, and the fields are often busy with pheasants and hares. The local restaurants serve classic French country dishes, and a stop at a village bakery for a warm baguette is a pleasure. Speed limits drop to fifty in the villages and cameras are not unknown.
t.route napoleon weekend@45.5,3.8:
Ambert is a market town of about eight thousand in the Livradois-Forez, a regional park of wooded mountains and high pastures in the eastern Auvergne, and it is known for two things above all: cheese and paper. The cheese is Fourme d'Ambert, a mild, creamy blue made in the hills since the Middle Ages, with its own protected name and a cylindrical shape, and you will find it on every menu and in every shop. The paper is the story of the Richard-de-Bas mill, a working museum in the valley where sheets are still made by hand in the manner of the fifteenth century, from rags and spring water.

The town centre is distinctive for its round town hall, a circular building in the middle of the main square, ringed by arcades, with a bustling café life around it. Marsac-en-Livradois, a village of fourteen hundred people a few kilometres away, is typical of the high farming country: steep meadows, stone farmhouses and lines of fir trees. Fuel and supplies are easily found in Ambert, which makes it a natural base or lunch stop.

The Route Napoléon of the ride's title is a long way to the south-east, so treat this as the food stop on the western side of a weekend that crosses the Rhône. The roads in the Livradois are calm and winding, climbing over passes at around a thousand metres, such as the Col du Béal and the Col des Pradeaux, through spruce and beech forest, past small lakes and between meadows full of wildflowers in June. The surface is mostly good, with the occasional patch of gravel, and traffic is very light, so you can go at your own pace.

Winters here are cold and snowy, with roads sometimes closed or slippery, and it is a quiet country in summer, with the sound of cowbells and the smell of cut grass. The local specialities include sausage, pork stews, lentils and potato dishes as well as the cheese, which is sometimes served with walnut bread. Plan to spend an extra half hour at the paper mill if you have a taste for old crafts, and note that opening hours can vary by season.
t.isere valley and belledonne scenic road@:
Beaujeu is the old capital of the Beaujolais, a small town of two thousand with a church, a market square and a name that gave the whole region its own. The Sires of Beaujeu ruled the area from the Middle Ages, and the town has a modest museum, narrow streets and an annual festival in November, the Sarmentelles, which marks the arrival of the new wine. It sits in the green, rolling hills north-west of Villefranche, with vines on almost every slope.

Villié-Morgon, a few kilometres on, is one of the great names of the region: Morgon is one of the ten crus of Beaujolais, producing deeper, more structured wines from the gamay grape on granite soils, and the roads nearby are lined with signs for domaines offering tastings. Fleurie, Brouilly and Moulin-à-Vent are also close, with their own colours and characters. The famous Beaujolais Nouveau, released on the third Thursday of November, is only one expression of a region that also produces serious, long-lived wines.

The Isère valley and the Belledonne range lie far to the south-east, so this is a warm-up leg on a long day. The riding in the Beaujolais is a pleasure of a different kind: narrow roads that wind between the vines, up and down short hills, with villages of golden stone on the crests, and views to the Alps on very clear days. The surfaces are generally good, but there is tractor mud in harvest time, and the corners are short and sometimes blind, so do not be in a hurry. Weekend traffic includes cyclists and wine tourists.

Fuel is available in larger places such as Belleville and Villefranche-sur-Saône, but not necessarily in the hill villages, so check the tank. Lunch in a small bouchon or village restaurant will bring charcuterie, andouillette, and chicken in wine sauce, and the beaujolais is served cool. The best time to ride is in September and October, with the harvest, the golden leaves and the smell of crushed grapes, but the roads can be busy. Please keep within the limits, since the roads are a living landscape.
t.isere valley and belledonne photo pull o:
Saint-Romain-le-Puy is easy to recognise from far away, because the village is built around a steep volcanic hill, a puy, rising sharply from the flat plain of the Forez, topped with a Romanesque priory church of the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The hill is a plug of old volcanic rock, one of several that stand like islands in the plain, and from the top you look across the flat basin, once a marsh and now farmland, towards the wooded hills that rise on both sides. It is a quiet place, a village of under three thousand people, with a few houses and a view.

Saint-Georges-Haute-Ville, next door on the list, is a hill village of about a thousand people at the foot of the Monts du Forez, and the region around has much to see. Montbrison, a small, elegant town a short way away and the historic capital of the Forez, has a good market and fuel, and the nearby town of Saint-Étienne, with its mining and manufacturing past, is a short drive east. The Forez plain is dotted with small lakes, called étangs, and in summer the roads are lined with fields of sunflowers and maize.

The Isère valley and Belledonne lie some way to the east, beyond Lyon and Grenoble, so this point serves as an early stage of the day. The riding in the Forez is a quiet blend of plain and hill: long straight roads across the flat, then twisting climbs into the Monts du Forez, past pine forests and high pastures, where the road becomes narrow and the surface variable. The Col de la Loge and the Col des Supeyres cross the range, with wide views over the plain, and are often almost empty of traffic.

Fill the tank in Montbrison or Boën, and check the weather before heading up into the hills, as the Monts du Forez are exposed and fog can come down quickly. The area produces fine cheeses, including Fourme de Montbrison, similar to the Ambert blue, and the farm shops sell sausages and honey. Summer is hot on the plain and cool on the heights, and winter brings snow to the hills, with the passes often closed.
t.beaujolais dawn sweep@45.8,4.2:
Balbigny sits on the Loire river in the northern part of the Forez plain, a market town of about two and a half thousand people that most traffic bypasses on its way between Lyon and Roanne. The young Loire, still narrow and fast here, runs through the town and then cuts a series of gorges to the north, between granite walls, on its way toward Roanne, a pattern that makes the area quietly attractive for riding, particularly early in the day. Pouilly-lès-Feurs, next door, is a smaller village near Feurs, a town founded by the Romans as Forum Segusiavorum, whose history is explained in a small museum.

The Beaujolais region, the focus of this ride, begins east of here beyond the Monts du Tarare, and a dawn sweep through the vineyards makes a natural plan: leave Lyon before first light and watch the sun rise over the vines. The land around Balbigny is more modest: meadows of Charolais cattle, apple orchards and a few vines, with the river and its willows and poplars winding through. It is good country for slow roads, small bridges, and half-timbered farmhouses, with a surface that is mostly decent but narrow, and bends hidden behind hedges.

Roanne, a short way north, is a city of thirty-five thousand people with a well-known restaurant tradition and a good range of services, which makes it the place to fill up and have a proper breakfast. Local cooking includes charcuterie, sausage in brioche, cheese from the Forez, and river fish such as pike-perch. Further along the river, the Loire gorges are a delight, with a section called the Gorges de la Loire where the road follows the water between wooded slopes, and the lake of Villerest, an artificial reservoir with fishing and boating, is a pleasant stop.

For fuel in the smaller places, check the hours, since stations may be unmanned or closed on Sundays. Early morning mist rises from the river, and the light on the Loire is soft and golden, so a sunrise start is rewarded. Summer afternoons can be hot, and thunderstorms roll across the plain, while autumn brings fog, and winter brings frost and the occasional icy stretch. Watch for herds of cattle on the road in some places.
t.annecy bauges loop@45.2,4.3:
Dunières is a small industrial town of three thousand in the Haute-Loire, tucked between the valley of the Dunières stream and the wooded hills of the Velay, and Montfaucon-en-Velay, a village of a little over a thousand on the plateau, is nearby. The area is a quiet corner of the eastern Massif Central, volcanic and high, with basalt outcrops, pine woods and open pastures, and it feels very far from Annecy and the Bauges, the Savoie lakes and mountains named in the ride, which lie a long way to the east.

The Velay is the land of the lentil, the small green lentille verte du Puy, which has its own protected name and is grown on the volcanic soils of the plateau. The harvest takes place in late summer, and the lentils turn up on every local menu, often with sausage or salted pork. Le Puy-en-Velay, a city of twenty thousand some forty kilometres to the south-west, is one of the most striking in France, with volcanic needles topped by a chapel and a statue, and it is the starting point of the pilgrim route to Santiago de Compostela. Yssingeaux, nearer, has services.

The mountains above, the Mézenc and the Meygal, are rounded volcanic massifs, with the Mézenc reaching about 1,750 metres, covered with meadows in summer and snow in winter. The roads in this district are narrow and winding, lined with stone walls and old farmhouses with their steep roofs, and the traffic is light. Surfaces vary, and in the higher stretches winter damage can leave potholes and loose gravel, so keep a sensible pace. The corners are tight but rhythmic, and the climbs are short but steep.

Fuel is available in Dunières and Montfaucon, but hours are limited, and the high villages have none. The weather changes quickly, with morning fog in the valleys and a cold wind on the heights, even in summer. The area is known for wind and for early snows, so a warm layer is sensible. Autumn brings clear days and golden light on the beeches, and the farm shops sell cheese, honey and cured meats.
t.provins medieval ridge loop photo pull o:
The Forêt de Lyons is one of the finest beech forests in France, a huge old woodland in the Eure department of Normandy, with tall, straight trees whose grey trunks rise to a green roof, and in autumn the canopy turns gold and copper and the forest floor is a carpet of leaves. La Feuillie and Charleval lie on its edge, small villages of about a thousand to two thousand people, with brick and half-timbered houses and a mixture of farmland and woodland around them, in the valley of the little Andelle river.

Lyons-la-Forêt, a village in the heart of the forest, is the place to visit: a ring of half-timbered houses around a covered market hall, built of oak, with flower boxes and cobbled lanes, a place so pretty that it has been used as a film set, notably for an adaptation of Madame Bovary. The composer Maurice Ravel is also remembered here, having spent time in the village during the First World War. It is a popular weekend destination for Parisians, but the forest roads are quiet in the week.

Provins, the medieval town named in the ride, lies far to the south-east in Seine-et-Marne, and this point is some way from it, so treat it as a first or last stop in the day. The roads through the forest are among the best in the region for relaxed riding: they run in long, smooth curves under the trees, with dappled light and the smell of damp earth, and the surface is generally good. The bends are easy and the climbs are gentle, but wet leaves, mud and logging lorries can be hazardous, and deer and wild boar cross at dawn and dusk.

Fuel is available in Gisors, Étrépagny and the larger towns around, but not in the small villages, so check the tank. The area is known for its cider and Neufchâtel cheese, shaped like a heart, and for apple dishes. The best time to ride is in spring, when the beech leaves are fresh and bright, or in October, when the colours are at their peak, though the forest is a pleasure in any season except deep winter, when ice can linger in the shade.
t.vallee de l eure easy scenic high point@:
The Brie is the plateau east of Paris, a wide, gently rolling country of wheat, sugar beet and rapeseed, divided into long fields by lines of poplars and punctuated by village church towers and silos, and La Houssaye-en-Brie and Neufmoutiers-en-Brie sit right in the middle of it. They are small villages of about a thousand people each, with brick and stone houses, a church and a bakery, and a pace of life that feels a long way from the commuter belt of Paris, though the capital is only an hour away.

The cheese that gives the region its name is Brie, a soft, bloomy-rind cheese made from cow's milk, which has been famous since the Middle Ages and was named king of cheeses at the Congress of Vienna in 1815. Brie de Meaux and Brie de Melun are the two protected varieties, and Coulommiers, a smaller cheese, is made nearby. A farm shop or a market stall is the best place to buy one, and the cheese is at its best when it is ripe, creamy and slightly runny, with a flavour that tastes of mushrooms and cellar.

The Vallée de l'Eure, which gives the ride its name, is a long way to the west, so this place is merely the high point of an easy loop, as the flat plain here offers views across a wide horizon. Riding is relaxed: long straight roads, gentle undulations, and roundabouts at every village entrance, with a surface that is mostly good but marked by agricultural traffic. The wind can be a nuisance, since there is little shelter, and the summer sun makes it feel hot. Beet lorries in autumn leave mud on the roads, which can be slippery.

Tournan-en-Brie and Rozay-en-Brie, both small towns nearby, have fuel and shops, and a village café will give you a coffee and a croissant. The market at Rozay on certain days is a good place for local produce. Spring and early summer bring bright green and yellow fields, and in September, the harvest brings combine harvesters and dust. Speed limits are strictly enforced in the villages, with cameras at some of the entrances. A slow day here, with lunch and a cheese, is an unhurried pleasure.
t.ardeche gorge long day@46.4,4.7:
Cluny is a small town of about four and a half thousand in southern Burgundy, and for several centuries it was the centre of the Christian world's most powerful monastic order. The abbey, founded in 910, grew into a great network of daughter houses across Europe, and its third church, begun in the eleventh century, was the largest in Christendom until St Peter's in Rome was built. The French Revolution turned the abbey into a quarry and most of it was demolished, but a surviving transept and tower give a sense of the size, and the town's streets still hold Romanesque houses and a fine medieval character.

La Roche-Vineuse, the village on the list, sits among the vines of the Mâconnais, a region of rolling hills and limestone outcrops south of Burgundy's better-known Côte d'Or, producing white wines from chardonnay, including the well-known Pouilly-Fuissé. Nearby rises the Roche de Solutré, a great cliff of pale limestone that sticks up from the vineyards like a ship's prow, and beneath it archaeologists found thousands of horse bones from prehistoric hunters. The French president François Mitterrand used to climb it each Pentecost, and it is a good viewpoint over the Saône valley.

The Ardèche Gorge, named in the ride, is far to the south, beyond Lyon, and this is a day's distance away, so the point is the northern end of a long haul. The roads around Cluny are a pleasure in their own right: quiet lanes that climb through woods and vineyards, with views of the Saône plain, and little hamlets of golden stone. The surface is generally good, with some patches, and the bends are gentle. The Voie Verte, a cycle track on the old railway line, runs close by, so expect cyclists.

For fuel and food, Cluny is the natural stop, with bakeries, restaurants and supermarkets, and plenty of cafés around the abbey. Local specialities include Burgundy dishes such as coq au vin, boeuf bourguignon, and goat cheese from Mâcon, with a glass of local white. The best time is spring or autumn, when the vines are green or golden, though summer is warm, and winter can be foggy. If you have an hour, the abbey's museum and its model of the great church are worth the visit.
t.chartreuse forest passes photo pull off@:
This corner of the Loire department sits on the western flank of the Monts de la Madeleine, a range of low, wooded hills between the Loire valley and the Allier, in a country of forest and meadow that few outsiders visit. Saint-Just-en-Chevalet, a village of about thirteen hundred people on the edge of the hills, is a quiet place, a mix of old stone houses and modest shops, and Lentigny, near the Loire, is a smaller village on the other side. Chartreuse, the limestone massif named in the ride, lies a good deal to the east, behind Lyon and Grenoble, so this is a gentle prelude.

The Monts de la Madeleine are a neglected delight: ridges covered with fir, beech and heather, cut by streams and scattered with small farms, rising to about 1,100 metres, with long views toward the Forez and the Auvergne mountains. The Loire runs to the east, flowing north to Roanne through a broad valley, and the lake of Villerest, an artificial reservoir, is a good place for a swim or a picnic. Roanne, the city on the Loire with thirty-five thousand people, has fuel stations, supermarkets and a good selection of restaurants, and it is the sensible place to prepare.

The riding is entirely local and unhurried, with small roads climbing over passes of between 600 and 1,000 metres, and taking you through forest and moorland, down to river valleys with old stone bridges. The surfaces vary from fine to patchy, and the road marking is minimal, so look for gravel and wet leaves. Traffic is very light, and you may go for half an hour without seeing another vehicle, which is part of the charm but means you should carry what you need.

The cuisine is that of the Loire and the Forez, with charcuterie, sausage, pork dishes, local cheeses and cakes, and the farms sell honey and walnut products. In spring the broom flowers yellow on the hillsides, and in autumn the beeches turn copper. Winter brings snow and fog to the hills, and the high roads may be icy for weeks. The weather can change quickly, so carry waterproofs, and fill the tank when you can, as the villages have few stations.
t.lac du bourget balcony ride photo pull o:
The village of Saint-Didier-sur-Chalaronne, and its neighbour Saint-Étienne-sur-Chalaronne, are in the Ain department, on the edge of the Bresse and the Dombes, a flat, green country of ponds, hedges and farms, a short distance east of the Saône. The Chalaronne is a small river that wanders through meadows and under old bridges, and the villages are quiet, with brick and half-timbered buildings and the occasional stork's nest on a rooftop.

Bresse is famous for its chickens, the poulet de Bresse, the only poultry in the world with its own appellation, raised free-range in the fields, with white feathers, blue feet and red combs, matching the colours of the French flag. They are served in restaurants across the region, often with cream and morels, and the farmhouses have the distinctive tall chimneys with pointed tops, called Saracen chimneys. The nearby Dombes plateau has more than a thousand fish ponds, and the area is a paradise for birdwatchers.

Lac du Bourget, named in the ride, lies in Savoie, a long way to the east, so this point is a gentle way into the day, far from the mountains. The riding on the Bresse is flat and easy, with straight roads between fields of maize and meadows, the surface generally good, and little traffic. The corners are few, and the ride's pleasure comes from the slow pace and the changing light over the plain. In summer the fields of maize are tall enough to block the view, while in spring the hedges are in blossom.

Châtillon-sur-Chalaronne is not far, and has a medieval market hall and a decent choice of restaurants and fuel stations, as does Villars-les-Dombes, with its bird park. Fog is common on autumn mornings, lying thick over the ponds and fields, and in winter the plain can be cold and damp. Be careful of tractors and harvesting machinery, and of mud on the road. The best season for riding is late spring or early autumn, when the light is soft and the air is clear.
Septeuil and Guerville are small places in the Yvelines, west of Paris, on the plateau of the Mantois, between the Mauldre and the Seine, with a landscape of fields, woods and small valleys that is often overlooked by those rushing past on the A13 motorway. Septeuil, a village of two thousand, has a château and a pleasant centre, and Guerville is close to Mantes-la-Jolie, a town of more than forty thousand on the Seine, with a fine Gothic collegiate church, Notre-Dame, whose façade resembles a small version of Notre-Dame de Paris.

The Seine below Mantes runs through great loops between steep white chalk cliffs, one of the most beautiful stretches of the river, and the Vexin plateau to the north has the same pale limestone in its villages and farms. Giverny, where Claude Monet lived and painted his water lilies, lies a few kilometres downstream on the right bank, and its garden is one of the most visited sights in the Île-de-France. The Vexin Français regional park, a protected landscape of villages, manors and stone walls, is nearby.

This is a gentle region, ideal for a relaxed ride. The roads cross the plateau in long, easy curves between wheat fields, then drop into the valleys through woods, with stone villages and church towers. The surface is usually good, though some of the lanes are narrow and rough, and farm vehicles are common. In spring, the rape fields blaze yellow, and in June the poppies colour the edges of the wheat. The traffic is light on weekdays, but weekends bring cyclists and walkers on the quiet roads.

For fuel and lunch, Mantes-la-Jolie or Houdan offer everything, and the villages have bakeries and small cafés. The cooking is classic, with cream, butter and cider, and Normandy is close enough to influence it. The limestone cliffs along the Seine can drop stones onto the road in some places after heavy rain, so watch the surface. Autumn mists and the smell of woodsmoke add to the charm, and winter can bring ice, so take care on shaded bends.
t.jura wine roads and cascades scenic road:
Aveize and Sainte-Foy-l'Argentière are two villages in the Monts du Lyonnais, a range of rounded hills west of Lyon that never quite reach a thousand metres, though the highest summits come close. The name Argentière suggests silver, and the region does have a mining past, with old lead and silver workings in the hills. Today it is farm country, with orchards, pastures and small woods, and a reputation for cherries, apples and raspberries, which are sold at roadside stalls in early summer, and for the goat cheeses that are made in the valleys.

The Jura, named in the ride, is a good hundred kilometres to the north-east, so the point is something like the western prelude of a day that finishes among the limestone gorges and wine villages of the Jura. The Monts du Lyonnais, however, deserve a morning on their own. The roads here are twisting and narrow, rising and falling over ridges, with sudden views toward the Alps on a clear day, and the surface can be rough and patched, with gravel in the bends and a few steep sections. Traffic is very light, except around the main market towns on Saturdays.

Fuel is not always available in small villages, and the stations in the hills are sometimes unmanned or shut on Sundays, so fill up in Saint-Symphorien-sur-Coise, Vaugneray or Lyon before heading out. A bakery or a village café will provide coffee and a snack, and the local cooking includes charcuterie, quenelles, and Lyonnais dishes with onions and cream. Walkers share the hills and the old chapels that crown many of the crests, and in autumn the chestnut and oak woods turn copper and gold.

The weather in the hills is often cooler than in the city, and fog can fill the valleys on spring and autumn mornings, so check the forecast. In summer, afternoon thunderstorms are common, with sudden downpours that make the road slippery, and in winter snow can cover the higher roads. Spring, with the orchards in blossom and the meadows green, is the best time, and the cherry season in June brings its own charm.
t.jura wine roads and cascades photo pull:
Le Péage-de-Roussillon is an industrial town of about seven thousand on the left bank of the Rhône, south of Vienne, and it has the look of a place built for work: chemical plants, warehouses, and a canal beside the river. Saint-Pierre-de-Bœuf, a village on the opposite bank, sits at the foot of the hills, where the Pilat massif drops to the river, and the Rhône here is a broad, fast, grey-green stream, carrying barges and tankers, with a cycle path, the ViaRhôna, following its banks.

The point has little glamour, and yet the area has a character of its own. To the north lies Vienne, a town with a Roman temple and a theatre, and the vineyards of Côte-Rôtie, where the vines grow on impossibly steep terraces above the river. A short way south of Saint-Pierre-de-Bœuf lies Condrieu, a village that gives its name to a rare and expensive white wine made from the viognier grape, with a scent of apricots and flowers, and a few cafés by the river where you can watch the barges pass. The slopes behind are terraced and stepped, held up by dry stone walls.

The ride named in the list, Jura Wine Roads and Cascades, belongs to a different mountain range further north-east, so this is a stage on the way from Lyon, and in practice the place serves as a sensible stop with fuel, shops and food. The roads on the west bank, climbing into the Pilat, are a delight: twisting, steep and shaded, with sudden views over the Rhône valley and its power stations and bridges, and the surface is mostly good. The east-bank roads are straighter and busier, with lorries and commuter traffic.

The weather in the Rhône valley is often windy, with the mistral coming from the north and funnelling down the valley, which can make riding tiring, particularly in winter and spring. Summers are hot, and the air can be heavy and humid, while autumn brings fog. Watch for speed cameras on the main roads, and for lorry traffic near the industrial areas. A walk by the river in the evening, with swallows overhead, rounds off the day nicely.
t.paris ile de france escapes@48.9,1.4:
Ézy-sur-Eure is a modest town of three thousand on the river Eure in Normandy, close to the border of the Eure and Eure-et-Loir, and its neighbour, Saussay, is a hamlet. The place is a few kilometres from Anet, a small town with one of the most celebrated châteaux of the French Renaissance, built in the 1540s by the architect Philibert de l'Orme for Diane de Poitiers, the favourite of King Henri II. The château, with its elegant courtyard and its famous carved entrance gate, is open to the public, and the story of Diane, who was about twenty years older than the king and ruled his heart for decades, is told in the rooms.

The Eure is a calm, clear river that runs among meadows and poplars, past mills and washhouses, and in summer people swim in the shallows and picnic on the banks, so the point is tagged for swimming. The water is generally cool and the current gentle, but check for signs, since not all stretches are supervised. The Chantilly and Ermenonville, named in the ride, lie well to the north-east, in the Oise, so this valley is a quiet western detour.

For a rider the Eure valley is a gentle place. The road follows the river with long, easy curves, passing small villages with stone houses and church towers, and now and then climbs onto the plateau for a view over the wheat fields. The surface is mostly good, and traffic is light on weekdays, with more cyclists and walkers on weekends. Because the lanes are narrow and the hedges high, watch for blind corners and farm vehicles. Fuel is available in Anet and Pacy-sur-Eure, and bakeries and cafés in the villages offer simple meals.

The region is famous for its cereals, and the plateau is covered with a patchwork of golden wheat in July. Evening is a lovely time, when the sun slants through the poplars and the river is still. In autumn the mist sits in the valley, and in winter fog and frost are common, so allow extra time. A visit to the château in the morning, before the crowds arrive, is worth the detour if you have an hour to spare.
t.milly forest roads and gatinais photo pu:
Pacy-sur-Eure is a small town of five thousand in the lower Eure valley, in the department of the same name, on the way between Évreux and Vernon, and Ménilles, a village close by, is among the quiet plateau settlements nearby. The area lies at the edge of Normandy, where the valley opens towards the Seine, and the country is a mixture of meadows, poplars and cereal fields, with villages of grey stone and tile roofs. The Eure here is a good trout stream, and the old bridges and mills add to the scene.

Vernon, a few kilometres to the north, is the gateway to Giverny, where Claude Monet lived from 1883 until his death in 1926, and where the garden he created with its Japanese bridge and water lily pond is open to visitors from spring to autumn. The village is crowded during the high season, so early morning or late afternoon is the best time. The Gâtinais and Milly-la-Forêt, named in the ride, lie to the south-east, near Fontainebleau, so this is a different part of the Île-de-France and Normandy border, but the character of the landscape is similar.

For fuel and food, Pacy and Vernon provide everything, and you can find lunch in village bakeries and cafés. The roads between here and the Seine are generally good, with long, easy curves over the plateau and sections of tree-lined avenues. The descent to the Seine at Vernon passes through chalk cuttings and woods, and the views along the river are impressive. The traffic is heavier near Vernon and on the main road to Évreux, and the speed limits in the villages are enforced by cameras.

In spring, the blossom in the orchards and the fresh green of the beech woods are lovely, and the cider and apple products of Normandy appear on the menus. Autumn mist lies over the valley and the leaves turn golden, while summer afternoons can be hot and thundery. Be careful on the wet leaves, and on farm tracks that cross the road. A short walk along the river or around the mill in Pacy makes a good break between stretches of riding.
t.paris ile de france escapes@49.5,3.2:
Blérancourt is a village of about twelve hundred in the Aisne, in the green country between Soissons and Noyon, and it houses an unexpected museum: the Musée national de la Coopération franco-américaine, in the remains of a seventeenth-century château. It was founded by Anne Morgan, the daughter of the American banker J. P. Morgan, who came here after the First World War to help the villagers rebuild, and the museum tells the story of the friendship between France and the United States, from the American Revolution to the world wars. A fine garden and a pair of pavilions survive from the old château.

Folembray, a village of about fifteen hundred, lies on the edge of the forest of Saint-Gobain, a large area of oak and beech woodland, and not far from the medieval castle of Coucy, which once had the largest keep in Europe, a cylindrical tower fifty-five metres tall, before the retreating German army blew it up in 1917. The ruins of the walls and towers still make a dramatic sight above the village of Coucy-le-Château. The country is a mix of woodland, farmland and small valleys, in the shadow of the First World War, with cemeteries and memorials scattered across it.

The point is part of a ride that centres on Paris and the Île-de-France, and it is tagged for swimming, with lakes and ponds scattered around the forest, though you should look for signed and supervised places. Laon, the hilltop cathedral city, is about thirty kilometres to the east, and Soissons and Compiègne are within easy reach. For fuel and food, Chauny, Noyon and Soissons are the nearest places of any size, and the villages may have only a bakery.

Roads through the Saint-Gobain forest are among the best in the region for a quiet ride, with long, gentle curves under tall trees and little traffic. The surface is mostly good, although forestry vehicles can leave mud, and deer cross the road without warning, especially at dusk. In autumn the colours are rich, with the smell of leaf mould and woodsmoke, and in spring the woods ring with birdsong. Fog is common in winter, and the shaded roads can be icy. Please treat the memorials and cemeteries with respect.
t.pilat ridge and rhone view photo pull of:
Roche-la-Molière and Saint-Genest-Lerpt are on the southern edge of Saint-Étienne, in the Loire department, in a landscape shaped by coal. The city of Saint-Étienne, with well over a hundred thousand people, grew on mining, steel and arms manufacture, and until recently it looked like a grimy industrial city. Today it has reinvented itself as a city of design, recognised by UNESCO in 2010, with a design biennale, a museum of modern art, and a well-preserved coal-mine shaft, the Puits Couriot, which has been converted into a museum of the mining history.

The Pilat massif, rising just to the east of the city, is the real prize of this ride. It is a regional natural park of wooded ridges and open crests, reaching 1,432 metres at the Crêt de la Perdrix, and from its edges you look across the Rhône valley towards the Alps. The road along the ridge, over passes such as the Col de la République and the Col de l'Œillon, is a favourite of local riders: well surfaced, winding, with views over the valley and plenty of bends. Chestnut woods and meadows mix with fir and beech, and the air is cooler and fresher than in the valley.

Fuel and food are easy to find in Saint-Étienne and the suburbs, and a bakery and a café will provide a decent breakfast. The local specialities include the cheese called Rigotte de Condrieu, a small goat cheese, and a type of pork sausage, and the bugnes, fried pastries eaten at carnival time. Lyon is only an hour away, which means the Pilat is popular on weekends, with many cyclists and motorcyclists, so you may want to go early or on a weekday. Police and speed cameras are used on the main approach roads.

The weather on the ridge can differ from that in the valley: fog, wind and cold are possible even in summer, and snow can fall in winter, closing or icing the higher roads. A windproof layer is wise. In spring, the broom blooms yellow on the slopes, and in autumn the chestnuts fall and the leaves turn. The viewpoints on the ridge are best on a clear morning, with the Rhône glittering below.
t.vallee de l eure easy scenic photo pull:
Cires-lès-Mello and Blaincourt-lès-Précy are villages of the Oise valley, north of Paris, in a stretch of country between Creil and the forest of Chantilly where the river cuts through soft limestone. The stone has been quarried here for centuries, and the pale blocks went into many of the buildings of Paris, as well as local churches and farmhouses, so the villages have a pleasant, honey-coloured look. Saint-Leu-d'Esserent, a short way up the river, has a fine abbey church of the twelfth century, built of the local stone, standing above the river on a hillside.

The valley is busy with industry and railways around Creil, but away from the town the roads are quiet and winding, with orchards and woods on the slopes, and views over the river meadows. The Chantilly forest and the château with its great stables, where horses were once housed in a palace of their own, lie a few kilometres to the east, and the racecourse is among the best known in France. Creil, a town of about thirty-five thousand people, has the fuel, shops and restaurants that the villages lack.

The Eure valley, named in the ride, lies well to the south-west, so this point is the northern extension of the loop. The riding is easy and undemanding, with roads climbing from the river onto the plateau in gentle curves, passing farms and stone walls. The surface is generally good, though patched in places, and the traffic is light outside the commuting hours. The larger roads along the Oise carry lorries and commuter traffic, so the quiet lanes are more pleasant.

Spring brings orchards in blossom and fresh green in the woods, while in autumn the leaves turn red and gold, and mist rises from the river in the early morning. In summer the roads are quieter in the heat of the day, and the evenings are long. In winter fog can be thick, and ice can form on shaded corners. A visit to the abbey church or a walk along the river makes a good break from the saddle, and a bakery in the village will provide a baguette and a pastry.
t.lyon rhone alpes rides@45.8,4.0:
The Lignon du Forez comes out of the Monts du Forez with a cold, clean hurry, and by the time it reaches the plain around Boën it has cut itself a shallow gorge through old volcanic rock. This is the country west of Lyon and north of Saint-Étienne that most people cross on the autoroute without noticing, and that is exactly why it is pleasant. The Forez plain is a wide, flat bowl of pasture and orchards, and the mountains stand along its western edge like a wall with the road folded into the foot of it.

The pin sits between Boën-sur-Lignon and Sail-sous-Couzan, a few kilometres from either. Sail is the one to remember: above the village a ruined medieval castle, Couzan, perches on a rock spur, and you can see it from the road long before you reach it.
