Boën is the practical neighbour, a small town with shops, a bakery or two and the usual fuel station, and it sits in the middle of the little Côtes du Forez wine area, a thin-skinned red country built on gamay. Saint-Germain-Laval, a bit further north, is a pleasant old market town. For anything larger, Montbrison is about twenty kilometres away and has everything.

The riding here is gentle rather than dramatic. Departmental roads run along the river and up into the hills with tight little bends, short climbs and a lot of blind crests where the hedges close in, so keep the speed honest. Surfaces are generally decent but patched, and farm traffic is the real hazard: tractors, loose gravel at field entrances, and mud after rain in the lower lanes. The best hours are early, when the mist lies on the plain and the hills above are already clear, and late in the day, when the light goes yellow on the stone farms.

The river is why this stop is marked for swimming. In summer the Lignon has pools below the bridges where locals wade in, but the water is mountain water, so it is bracing even in August, and levels change quickly after storms upstream. Pick a spot with a gravel bank, leave the leathers in the shade and give yourself time to warm up afterwards.

This is a fine place to start or end a day if you are heading for the Vanoise or the Jura, because you are on the quiet side of Lyon and the roads east are an easy morning's transfer away. Bring cash for the smaller villages, where the one bar may not take cards.
t.morvan southbound weekend@49.0,2.5:
Nobody plans a holiday around Goussainville, and that is fine, because this stop exists to get you out of Paris with a full tank. The pin sits on the northern edge of the Île-de-France right beside Roissy-Charles de Gaulle airport, among warehouses, logistics yards and the edges of Le Thillay, Goussainville and Gonesse. Aircraft pass low overhead on their final approach, so loud that conversation stops and restarts, and the sky is stitched with white contrails.

For a rider heading south toward the Morvan, the point is simple. Goussainville has about thirty thousand people and plenty of petrol stations, supermarkets and cafés, and Gonesse is nearly as big. Fill up and eat properly here, because the first stretch beyond Paris is motorway or fast trunk road with services that charge a premium. If you are coming back on the Sunday evening, this is also where you will find yourself stuck in the returning traffic, so a coffee before the last push into the city is not a bad idea.

There is real history underneath all the concrete, though. Gonesse was famous in the Middle Ages for its bread, which was carried into Paris to feed the city, and the town still carries the name. Goussainville has an odd survivor: the old village centre, Vieux-Pays, was largely abandoned after the airport opened in the 1970s and the noise became unbearable, and a medieval church with its tower still stands among empty houses. In June 1973 a Soviet Tu-144 supersonic airliner crashed onto the village during the Paris Air Show, killing everyone aboard and several people on the ground. Locals do not forget it, and a short detour will show you the church, although the area is quiet and residential, so keep the engine down.

As for the riding, there is little to say. Roads are flat, signalised and full of roundabouts and speed cameras, and the surface is the tired asphalt of an industrial belt. The best advice is to leave early on a weekend morning, before the delivery lorries wake up, and aim for the forests and rolling farmland south and east of Paris. The Morvan, with its granite hills, lakes and beech woods, is a long way from here, which is the whole point of stopping.
t.ende@-8.8,121.7:
Ende sits on the south coast of Flores, a long, volcanic island in eastern Indonesia, and it is a place where history has left a small, quiet mark. In 1934 the Dutch colonial government exiled the nationalist leader Sukarno here, and he lived in a modest house for four years, writing, staging plays and thinking. According to local tradition, he came to the idea of the Pancasila, the five principles that became the foundation of the Indonesian state, while sitting under a breadfruit tree on the seafront, and the spot is now a small memorial park.

The town has some 77,000 people, a busy port and a market, and behind it rises Mount Iya, a volcano whose slopes shape the weather. The coast is rugged, with black sand beaches and a harbour full of wooden boats. Fuel is easy to find in Ende, and it is the last big town before the road east climbs toward the villages of the highlands. About fifty kilometres along lies Moni, the base for visiting Kelimutu, where three crater lakes change colour from turquoise to red to black, depending on the volcanic gases and minerals in the water.

The Trans-Flores Highway, one of the great rides in Indonesia, connects the towns along the island's spine. It is mostly a narrow, twisting road, with endless bends, steep gradients and sudden views of terraced rice fields, coffee plantations and green mountains. The surface is patched and rough in places, with potholes and landslides in the wet season, from December to March, and the pace is slow. A day's progress is often measured in a few dozen kilometres.

Expect to share the road with trucks, buses, motorbikes, chickens and goats. Take it patiently, and stop often to stretch, drink coffee and talk to people, who are friendly and curious. Local food is simple and good: rice with fish, vegetables and chilli sambal. The evenings are warm, the stars are bright, and the air carries the smell of clove smoke and the sea.
t.fontainebleau@48.9,2.8:
Louis Braille was born in Coupvray in 1809, and the house where he lived is now a small museum, a short ride from this point. The pin sits near Esbly and Coupvray, in the Marne valley east of Paris, a landscape of river meadows, low wooded hills and farm villages that survives, just, in the shadow of Disneyland Paris to the south.

After a day in the Fontainebleau forest and along the Loing, it makes a quiet end. The roads near the river are flat and gentle, with long views over fields and a surface in good condition. Traffic is moderate, though weekends and holiday evenings bring heavy flows towards the theme park, so it is better to avoid the main routes and use the lanes along the Marne. The towpath by the river is popular with walkers and cyclists, and the villages along the bank have small quays and old houses.

Coupvray's church holds the grave of the man who invented the six-dot reading system, and the small village around it has changed little since his time. The Marne valley was once the scene of fierce fighting in the First World War, and the battle of the Marne in 1914, which halted the German advance on Paris, was fought not far to the east. Memorials and cemeteries are scattered along the roads.

Esbly has a railway station with direct trains to Paris Gare de l'Est, and a small centre with shops, a baker and cafes. Fuel is available in town, and a larger shopping area is closer to Marne-la-Vallée. The riverside is a good spot for a rest, with shade and benches, and in summer fishermen sit on the bank.

As the final point of a long forest loop, it is a calm place for the day to end, and well suited to a slow walk by the water.
t.lyons la foret@49.4,1.5:
Beech trees are the point. The forest of Lyons, a few kilometres from the village, is one of the largest and finest beech woods in Europe, about ten thousand hectares of tall, silver-trunked trees that stand in cathedral rows, and in spring, when the leaves are just out, the light under them is green and gold. In autumn it turns copper. The roads that cross it are some of the best in Normandy for easy riding, with long, smooth curves, a good surface and little traffic, and the sense of riding through a vast, quiet hall is hard to beat.

The village of Lyons-la-Forêt sits in a clearing at about 150 metres, and it is one of the prettiest in Normandy, with half-timbered houses, brick and flint walls and an old covered market hall dating from the eighteenth century, in the middle of the square. The film director Claude Chabrol used it as the setting for his Madame Bovary in 1991, because it looks so much like the Normandy of Flaubert's novel. A few kilometres away, the abbey of Mortemer, with its ruins and small museum, is a quiet place to stop. The village is listed among the most beautiful in France, and in summer and on fine weekends it fills with visitors from Paris, so it is better on a weekday.

Lunch here is a pleasure. Normandy is dairy country, and the food is rich: Neufchâtel cheese, a soft, white-rinded cheese in a heart shape, cream sauces, apple tart and cider or the apple brandy called Calvados. Restaurants and tea rooms around the square serve lunch until about two, and you should book on Sundays. Fuel is not found in the village itself, and I would not count on the village having any, so fill up in Gisors or Étrépagny before you come.

The forest is also home to deer and wild boar, so be careful at dusk, and in wet weather the leaves can make bends slippery. The nights are cool and the air smells of damp wood. It is a very good place to turn for home.
t.milly forest@48.6,2.7:
Fouquet's château is on your doorstep here. Vaux-le-Vicomte lies just beside Maincy, a few kilometres from the pin, and its story is one of the best in French history. Nicolas Fouquet, Louis XIV's finance minister, built it from 1656, with Le Vau as architect, Le Nôtre as garden designer and Le Brun as decorator, and in August 1661 he gave a lavish party there for the young king. Within weeks, Fouquet was arrested, and the king took the same team to build Versailles.

The pin itself sits in the countryside near Moisenay and Maincy, south-east of Melun, in the Seine-et-Marne, a country of fields, woods and small villages on the edge of the Brie plateau. Vaux-le-Pénil and Melun are close, and Fontainebleau forest begins to the south.

The ride that ends here has come out of the Milly forest and the Nemours area, so it is a gentle return. Roads are good, with long straights across the open plateau and a few twists as they enter the woods around Maincy. Traffic is light on weekdays but can be heavy near the château in summer, and early morning is the best time to see the building in soft light, when the moat is still and the gardens look their best. The grounds are open to visitors, and the garden cascade and grotto are worth the entry fee if you have the time.

Fuel is available in Vaux-le-Pénil and Melun, where there are stations and supermarkets, and a few cafes in Maincy and the neighbouring villages serve simple lunches. For a more elegant ending, the château has a restaurant, though it is expensive, and the lawns offer a place for a picnic.

The Seine is not far, and a short ride brings you to its banks at Melun for a final view. It is a worthy end to a ride that began in forest and rock.
t.lac@45.7,4.5:
Saint-Martin-en-Haut lives up to its name, which means St Martin on the heights. The pin lands a short way out of the village, in the Monts du Lyonnais, a range of rounded, forested hills west of Lyon that rise above the Rhône valley and the Gier. Aveize and the old hamlets of the area sit among meadows and orchards, and the whole region is unexpectedly rural, though it lies less than an hour from the city.

The ride here began at Lac du Bourget, far to the east, so it ends on a different note. These hills have no famous passes, but the roads are among the best in the region: they climb and dip in long, steady bends, crossing ridges that give wide views, and the surface is generally smooth. Traffic is light, except on summer Sundays when Lyonnais cyclists take over. In winter the heights can be cold and icy, and fog is frequent, so the best seasons are late spring and early autumn.

The Monts du Lyonnais are known for farming. Orchards of cherries, apricots and apples cover the slopes, and goat cheese and charcuterie are sold at village shops. The area was once a centre for weaving silk at home, and a number of old stone houses with large windows, built for looms, survive. Old chapels and calvaries stand on many hilltops.

The nearest large town is Mornant, eleven kilometres away, with a market and stations, though Saint-Martin itself has a small centre with a baker and a bar. Fuel should be taken in Mornant or Lyon before climbing into the hills. For rest, the village has a pleasant square and some benches, and several viewpoints along the road offer a place to sit.

As the finishing point of a Bourget loop, it is a calm and pastoral one, with a good view back over the Rhône valley as the light fades.
t.maumere@-8.6,122.2:
Maumere is where the Trans-Flores road runs out of island, or begins, depending on which way you ride. The pin lands on the north coast of Flores, in a town of nearly fifty thousand people, with the Flores Sea in front and the volcanic spine of the island behind. It is the biggest town in the east of Flores, a trading port with a Catholic cathedral, a busy market and a long waterfront, and the heat and humidity here hit you the moment you stop.

Coming in from Bajawa, you have ridden a long day of mountain road, with endless bends, fast descents through rice terraces and coffee plantations, and the occasional landslide patch where rain has taken a bite out of the tarmac. The surface can be rough, with potholes, loose gravel and livestock on the road, so speed is never your friend. Maumere itself is flat and chaotic, full of motorbikes, minibuses and bemos, and the last few kilometres are slower than the rest of the day.

The town is also known for a disaster. In December 1992 an earthquake and tsunami devastated the north coast of Flores, killing thousands and wiping out villages along the shore, and the memory is still strong. The area is known for its weaving, too. Sikka, a village a short ride east, is famous for its ikat cloth, hand-dyed in rich reds and browns with patterns that vary from village to village, and weavers will often show their work if you stop. Catholicism arrived with the Portuguese, and the Easter processions in Larantuka, further east, are among the most important in Indonesia.

Fuel is no problem in Maumere, with several stations, and it is wise to fill up before heading anywhere else, as villages along the road may only sell petrol from bottles. Warungs along the waterfront serve grilled fish, rice and vegetables at low prices, and fresh coconut water is available on nearly every corner. The coast around the town has beaches with coral reefs, popular with divers, and the sunset over the water is reliable.

Keep an eye on the weather. The wet season, roughly December to March, can bring heavy rain and landslides, and the dry months are far better for riding.
t.bugey lakes@45.3,4.9:
This stretch of country belongs to the border between the Drôme and the Isère, on a flat, fertile plain called the Valloire. It is a sleepy farming region, a land of walnut orchards, maize fields and low villages like Épinouze and Saint-Sorlin-en-Valloire, about fifty kilometres south of Lyon. The roads here are quiet, straight and bordered by hedges and poplars, and the air in late summer smells of cut hay and ripening fruit. It is not the Bugey, which lies far to the north-east, but the end of a long ride has a way of dropping you somewhere unexpected.

The area has one genuine marvel hidden nearby. At Hauterives, a few kilometres to the east, a country postman named Ferdinand Cheval spent thirty-three years, from 1879 onward, collecting stones on his rounds and building a fantastical palace in his garden, a riot of towers, grottoes and carved animals that he called the Palais Idéal. The surrealists admired it, and in 1969 the French state listed it as a historic monument. It is a short run from here and well worth ten minutes if you are not too tired.

For a rider, the Valloire is a restful finish. The roads are flat and fast, with long straights and gentle bends, though there are occasional tractors, so keep your eyes open. Small towns here have a bakery and a bar but not always a petrol station, so for a reliable fuel stop use Roussillon, about twelve kilometres away, or the bigger towns along the Rhône valley. Wind can pick up along the open plain, particularly in spring, and there is the odd smell of manure from the fields, a reminder that this is working land.

In September the walnut harvest begins, and you will see nets laid under the trees and trailers heaped with nuts. Local walnut oil and walnut cake are good things to buy and carry home. The landscape feels unhurried, and after a day of climbing, that is exactly what you want.
t.perche quiet roads overnight@48.7,2.3:
Paris does not let go easily. This fuel stop lies on the southern edge of the Île-de-France, in the commuter towns around Saulx-les-Chartreux and Villebon-sur-Yvette, with the motorways to Orléans and Bordeaux close by and the research campuses of the Saclay plateau a short distance to the west. It is a landscape of roundabouts, business parks and neat suburban streets, with patches of cereal field still holding out between them.

The riding does not begin here, but the day does. This is the place for the early start: fill the tank at one of the stations on the roads around, check the straps and the tyres, and aim to be moving before the commuters take over. A leisurely ride out through Palaiseau and Orsay and up into the valley of the Yvette gets you to the open country of the Chevreuse valley and, beyond it, the wooded hills around Rambouillet within an hour, if the traffic cooperates.

The place names have a little history in them. Chartreux is the old French word for the Carthusian monks, whose order built monasteries across the region, and the name hints at a past in which this plateau was church land, farmed by monks and laymen alike. Villejust and Villebon, similarly, date back to medieval hamlets that were swallowed by Paris's growth only in the last century or so.

Behind you lies the Perche, a green, hilly country of hedged fields, apple orchards and half-timbered farmhouses in the west of France, where the road quality improves, the villages are quiet, and heavy horses were once bred for the military and for the plough. The overnight ride is the chance to get there at a gentle pace, using small roads rather than motorways, and to arrive in the evening with a hungry rider and a warm room waiting.

A practical note: Saulx and Villebon have fuel, supermarkets and bakeries, and the earlier you leave on a weekend, the more peaceful the first hour will be. On a weekday, the morning rush on the roads around the A10 and the N118 is dense, so avoid it if you can.
t.perche quiet roads overnight high point@:
South-west of Paris, the land begins to lift into the hills of the Haute Vallée de Chevreuse, a regional nature park where the plateau is cut by small valleys full of woods and ponds, and this high point lies on its edge between Limours, Les Molières and Gometz-la-Ville. It is hardly a mountain pass, but at a little over a hundred and fifty metres it is among the highest ground around, and you feel the fresh air and the quiet as soon as you leave the suburbs.

The park was created to protect this corner of the Île-de-France from the sprawl of Paris, and it does a decent job. Beech and oak woods alternate with open fields, the roads dip into sheltered valleys and climb out again past stone farms, and the villages keep their old churches, wash-houses and a noticeable lack of billboards. Nearby, the ruined castle of Gometz-le-Châtel sits on a hill above the road, and the Château de Courson, a short ride away, hosts a well-known garden fair every year.

The riding is gentle, twisting and shaded, ideal for a calm morning. The roads are narrow, with tight bends between stone walls and old trees, and in autumn the leaf litter and morning damp can make them slippery, especially in shaded corners. Cyclists are everywhere at weekends, since this area is among the best loved training grounds in the Paris region, so give them room, pass wide and expect them around blind bends.

Limours is the natural stop, a town of six thousand people with a market, bakeries and a small centre of old houses, plus fuel and a supermarket on the edges. The smaller villages around have bars and boulangeries but are often shut on Mondays and in the middle of the day, so do not count on a late lunch.

The smell of this area in spring is damp earth, wild garlic in the woods and cut hay in the meadows. It is a surprisingly quiet and intimate corner of France, and a good reason to leave the motorways behind.
t.perche quiet roads overnight scenic road:
The Seine and the Oise meet at Conflans-Sainte-Honorine, and the town has never stopped looking at the water. For generations it has been known as the capital of the French inland waterways, the place where bargemen, the mariniers, tied up their péniches and where the great barge convoys from Le Havre and Rouen came to rest. A barge museum in the old castle tells that story, and you can still see working boats and houseboats moored along the quays, with the odd cargo barge slipping through.

The town climbs a steep hill from the riverbank to the old tower and the church, and the scenic road above follows the heights of the Hautil, a wooded ridge that rises over the loop of the Seine and gives wide views over the river, the poplars and the plain beyond. It is a corner of the Paris region that feels surprisingly separate, with narrow lanes, old stone walls and small plots of gardens on the slopes. Honorine, the saint of the town's name, is said to be a Christian martyr of late antiquity whose relics were carried here in the ninth century to escape the Vikings, who sailed up the Seine in the same period.

The riding here is short and pretty: tight bends up from the riverside, a mixed surface with patches that can be rough, and views that open suddenly between trees. There is more traffic than the quiet scenery suggests, because Conflans is a big commuter town of thirty-six thousand people, so the best time is early on a weekend or in the evening when the light slants across the water. Be careful on the hill in wet weather, because the cobbles and the leaf litter are slippery.

Auvers-sur-Oise, where Vincent van Gogh spent the last weeks of his life in 1890, lies a short distance up the Oise valley, and the whole area is dotted with spots that artists such as Daubigny and Pissarro painted. A ride up the river brings you past locks, bridges and fishing huts.

Fuel and food are no problem in Conflans, which has several stations and cafes along the river, and the old quarter is worth a walk if you have an hour. The river air smells of damp stone, diesel and fresh bread.
t.perche quiet roads overnight photo pull:
The valley of the Oise north of Paris has always drawn painters, and the light along this stretch explains why. This pull-off lies near Parmain, Champagne-sur-Oise and Mours, where the river curves between low wooded slopes and the water reflects the sky in broad silver bands. Early in the morning mist often lies over the surface, and by mid-morning the sun burns it off, leaving clear light and long shadows on the opposite bank.

Parmain faces L'Isle-Adam across the river, and the two towns are linked by a bridge and a long history of trade and leisure. L'Isle-Adam has a river beach where, in summer, Parisians come for a swim and a picnic, and the forest behind it is a favourite for walkers, with oak and beech under tall canopies. Champagne-sur-Oise, despite its name, has no vineyards to speak of; the name is a medieval one meaning open countryside, and the village has an elegant eighteenth-century château and a small village centre.

The riding is calm and scenic, with flowing roads that follow the river and climb gently into the forest, a good surface in general, and a few busy junctions in the towns. Traffic is thickest at weekends in summer, when day-trippers from Paris crowd the riverbank, and in the early morning on weekdays when commuters head for the railway stations. The tarmac under the trees can be damp for long periods, so stay alert for slippery patches, particularly after rain.

For photographers, the best view is looking across the water toward the church spire and rooftops of L'Isle-Adam, with the trees in autumn colour and reflections in the water. The late afternoon is the strongest time, though early morning can give something more atmospheric.

There is fuel in Parmain and L'Isle-Adam, and the little towns have plenty of bakeries and cafes. A coffee at a riverside terrace is hard to beat after a quiet morning's ride, and the smell of damp leaves and river water becomes part of the memory.
t.perche quiet roads overnight@48.8,2.8:
This part of the Brie plateau is an agricultural landscape that has largely escaped the attention of tourists, and that is much of its charm. The villages here, Neufmoutiers-en-Brie, Villeneuve-le-Comte and La Houssaye-en-Brie, are small clusters of stone and brick around a church, ringed by fields of wheat and sugar beet and bounded by small woods and hedgerows. It is the kind of country you pass through without noticing, and then remember when you are stuck in traffic somewhere else.

Brie, the region that gives its name to the soft cheese, was historically one of the granaries of Paris, and the farms here supplied the capital with grain, milk and cheese for centuries. The soil is a fertile loam over limestone, and the land is gently rolling, with long views over the plateau. Not far from here, Disneyland Paris has grown up around Marne-la-Vallée, a reminder of how fast the region has changed, though the villages retain their rural calm.

For a food stop, the realistic options are the local bakery, the bar-tabac and the larger town of Tournan-en-Brie, a few kilometres away, which has about eight thousand people, a market and a selection of restaurants. Expect simple French cooking: a plat du jour with meat or fish and potatoes, a salad, a slice of Brie with bread and a cup of coffee. Small-town bars often close in the afternoon and on Sundays, so check opening times if you can, and do not arrive late.

The roads are quiet and straightforward, with a good surface, gentle curves and little traffic outside the commuting peaks. The danger comes from tractors, farm trailers and the occasional cyclist, and from junctions where visibility is limited by hedges and crops. Early summer brings fields of ripening wheat, and the autumn light over ploughed fields is soft and golden.

The overnight ride starts to feel properly rural around here: the lights of Paris are behind you, the roads are empty, and the evening smells of cut grass and woodsmoke. Fill the tank in Tournan before heading on, since fuel in the smaller villages is not something to count on, and enjoy the quiet.
t.perche quiet@48.7,2.3:
South-west of Paris, on the high, open plain of Saclay, the coordinates land among Saulx-les-Chartreux, Villebon-sur-Yvette and Villejust. This is a landscape of big fields, wheat and sugar beet, cut through by motorways and dotted with research laboratories and business parks. The plateau is one of France's main scientific clusters, with universities and institutes that grew up around the old agricultural land, so you will see low modern campuses sitting beside barns and farm tracks.

The name Saulx-les-Chartreux hints at an older story. The Carthusians, a strict order of contemplative monks, once owned land here, and the village remembers them in its name. Many villages in this part of the Essonne grew up around a church and a few farms, and some of the old stone houses and farm courtyards can still be found down side streets. Villebon-sur-Yvette lies in the valley of the Yvette, a small river that runs through woods and meadows toward the Seine, and it still has a pleasant green corner or two.

From the plateau, the road toward the Perche runs west past Chevreuse and Rambouillet, onto smaller lanes. The ride's quiet reputation depends on avoiding the main roads, which can be badly congested at commuting hours, especially on the roads around Courtaboeuf and the A10. Use the smaller departmental roads on the plateau, where the surface is good and the bends are gentle. Fuel is not a problem: Saulx-les-Chartreux has about five thousand people, Villebon-sur-Yvette about ten thousand, and there are supermarkets with cheap petrol nearby.

The best time to ride this area is early on a weekend morning, before traffic builds, or in the evening after the commute. Autumn is gorgeous, with fields turning gold and then brown, while spring brings the bright yellow of oilseed rape. In winter, fog can lie in the valley and ice can form on shaded bends, so be careful.
t.reims@49.3,4.0:
For over a thousand years the kings of France came to Reims to be crowned, and the cathedral that still dominates the city shows why. The tradition goes back to Clovis, baptised here around the year 500 by Bishop Remigius, and some thirty-odd monarchs followed, ending with Charles X in 1825. The present Gothic building dates from the thirteenth century, its west front crowded with statues, among them the Smiling Angel, and it was damaged badly by German shelling in the First World War before being painstakingly restored. Inside, stained glass by Marc Chagall glows blue behind the apse, installed in the 1970s.

Reims is also a champagne capital, and it wears this lightly. Beneath the streets lie kilometres of chalk cellars, some of them Roman quarries called crayères, in which the great houses age millions of bottles at a steady cold temperature, and the cellars and the hillsides around them were added to the UNESCO list in 2015. Houses such as Pommery, Taittinger and Veuve Clicquot are all in town, and most offer guided tours that end, naturally, with a glass. The city also has a nice, odd claim to history: Germany's unconditional surrender in the Second World War was signed here, in a school building, on 7 May 1945. And do not miss the biscuits roses, pink sponge fingers that have been dunked in champagne since the eighteenth century.

For a ride called the Champagne Tourist Route, Reims is the right place to begin. The city is flat and busy, with a wide central square, tram lines to watch, and one-way streets, so park the bike in an underground garage if you stay. Fuel is easy, with stations on every ring road and supermarkets around the edge, and cafés open early. Leaving town, you climb quickly onto the Montagne de Reims, a forested ridge covered in vines on its flanks, where the roads wind between villages with names that appear on bottle labels.

Mornings are the best time to ride, before the day-trippers appear. The vineyards are most beautiful in autumn, when the leaves go gold and red, though harvest brings tractors and slippery grape juice on the tarmac. Spring can bring frost warnings, and night cold in the open chalk country. Wear a layer.
t.epernay@49.0,4.0:
Épernay is the sort of town that makes a bubble feel like an institution. It sits on the Marne river, in the heart of Champagne, and its main street, the Avenue de Champagne, is lined with the grand houses of famous producers: Moët and Chandon, Perrier-Jouët, Pol Roger, Mercier and others, in mansions of stone, brick and wrought iron, set behind gardens and gates. The avenue is sometimes called the most expensive street in the world, a joke based on the value of the bottles stored beneath it.

That is the real secret of Épernay: the cellars. Under the town, chalk galleries stretch for tens of kilometres, cool and damp, where millions of bottles lie on their sides, slowly developing the fine bubbles that give the wine its character. Several houses offer tours, which include a descent into the dark, a lecture on the méthode champenoise and, naturally, a glass at the end. It is best to book ahead in summer, and remember that tasting and riding do not mix.

The hills around, planted with chardonnay and pinot noir and pinot meunier, form the landscape that was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2015 for its vineyards, houses and cellars. A few kilometres to the north, in the village of Hautvillers, the monk Dom Pérignon is traditionally credited with refining the techniques of champagne production in the late seventeenth century, though the myth that he invented the wine is just that. His grave lies in the abbey church.

The riding here is a pleasure. The scenic route through the vineyards winds along the slopes of the Montagne de Reims and the Côte des Blancs, with good roads, gentle gradients, and long views over rows of vines. The best time is autumn, when the harvest is under way and the vineyards turn red and gold, but spring, with its fresh green growth, is just as good. During the harvest, expect tractors and workers on the roads.

Épernay is a town of twenty-seven thousand, with fuel stations, restaurants and parking, and the centre is compact enough to explore on foot. The suburb of Magenta is named after the battle of 1859, a small piece of Franco-Italian history in a very French town.
t.chateau thierry@49.0,3.4:
Château-Thierry lies along the Marne at a point where the river valley narrows and the hills close in, and it is the town where the poet Jean de La Fontaine was born in 1621. His house is now a museum, and the fables he spun about foxes, crows and cunning grasshoppers are still learned by schoolchildren across France. Above the river, the ruins of a medieval castle crown the hillside, with walls and towers that once guarded the road to Paris, and they give a good view over the roofs and the water.

The town has a solemn side as well. In 1918, the area saw heavy fighting in the Second Battle of the Marne, in which American troops played a significant part, defending the river crossing here and fighting at nearby Belleau Wood, to the north-west. A cemetery and memorial in the woods commemorate them, and there are other monuments around the district. The farmland near the town is rich and rolling, with fields of wheat and rapeseed, and the western edge of the Champagne vineyards begins in the hills around, making this a quiet end to the route.

On a motorcycle, the road along the Marne valley is a pleasure. It is smooth, bendy and gentle, with the river on one side and vines or woodland on the other, and it passes through villages with stone houses and old wash-houses. Traffic is light outside the commute, though lorries use the main road, so choose the smaller departmental roads when you can. The town has nearly sixteen thousand people, so fuel stations, bakeries and cafés are never far, and the riverside is a nice place for a sandwich in the sun.

Autumn brings mist on the river in the morning and the smell of woodsmoke by evening. In summer the shaded lanes are a relief from the heat. If you have time, taste a regional cheese such as Brie de Meaux from a local market, and think of La Fontaine's crow dropping hers.
t.loire castle edge@49.3,2.3:
A modest town on the little river Thérain, in the Oise département, Mouy lies about fifty kilometres north of Paris, among the low chalk hills and wooded ridges of the Picardy edge. The landscape is quiet: wheat fields, hedgerows, woodland and neat red-roofed villages, with the occasional church spire poking up on the skyline. It does not shout about itself, and there is something restful in that after the big roads of the capital.

The area is on the doorstep of two famous places. To the east, Chantilly has a grand château with a collection of paintings in the Musée Condé, a racecourse and the great stables that house horses and a museum of the horse, and the town is also known for its whipped cream. Not far away, the old town of Senlis has medieval walls, a cathedral and a cluster of narrow streets, and the forests of the Oise are full of deer. Together they make the case for ending a day here, on the edge of the château country that gives the ride its name, rather than at the far end of the Loire valley.

The riding is easy and pleasant. Roads in the Thérain valley and the surrounding plateau are smooth and lightly trafficked, with gentle bends, long views over farmland, and a pleasant rhythm of fields and woods. On weekends, cyclists and families are out in numbers. Fuel and food are no problem, because Mouy has about five and a half thousand people, with a supermarket, bakeries and a few cafés. The larger town of Creil is not far away, and has more stations. In winter, mist and ice can build in the valley, so take care on shaded bends and bridges.

In autumn, the beech woods turn deep copper, and mushrooms appear along the verges, and by evening there is a smell of leaf mould and woodsmoke. Park near the church, take a deep breath, and let the day settle. After a long ride, the peace of a small French town is hard to beat.
t.vercors balcony roads@45.9,4.9:
The Dombes plateau, north of Lyon, is one of the oddest landscapes in France. It is a flat, damp country dotted with more than a thousand artificial ponds, dug by monks and farmers over the centuries to breed carp and other fish, which are drained and harvested in rotation, then the land planted with crops for a year or two before the water returns. From the air it looks like a shattered mirror. From the road it is a tranquil country of reeds, herons and low horizons.

This fuel stop lies on its southern edge, near Civrieux, Saint-André-de-Corcy and Mionnay, small towns that have grown as commuter bases for Lyon but keep their rural roots. Mionnay has a distinguished place in French gastronomy as the home of a restaurant made famous by the chef Alain Chapel, who earned three Michelin stars here, and the Dombes still produces some of the best pond fish and poultry in the country. The Parc des Oiseaux at Villars-les-Dombes, a short drive north, is among the largest bird parks in Europe.

Be honest about the ride: the Vercors is a long way from here, a hundred kilometres or more to the south-east, and this is the approach stage. The roads around are flat and fast, with long straights and the occasional roundabout, and the pleasure comes later, when the mountains rise ahead. Fill the tank here, early in the day, because the first few hours on the Vercors roads will be demanding and you want to reach them without worrying about reserve.

Neuville-sur-Saône, a larger town about eight kilometres away on the river, has more stations and services, and the roads around the Lyon ring are busy on weekday mornings. On a Sunday morning, the Dombes is peaceful and the mist rising from the ponds in the early light is something to see.

For a coffee, the small villages have boulangeries and cafes that open early, and a croissant in the quiet of a village square is an excellent way to start a long ride. Carry some water and a light layer, because the Dombes air in the morning can be damp and cool.
Vienne is a quiet city with a dramatic past. It stands on the Rhône, south of Lyon, and in Roman times, when it was called Vienna, it was one of the major cities of Gaul, rivalling its neighbour upstream. The evidence is everywhere: a Roman theatre, still used for concerts, cut into the hillside, a temple dedicated to Augustus and Livia that stands in the middle of the town like a piece of Rome dropped in France, and a strange stone pyramid in the old circus. Every July the theatre hosts a famous jazz festival, and the town fills with musicians and visitors.

This pull-off lies a few kilometres south of the city, near Jardin, Les Côtes-d'Arey and Reventin-Vaugris, where the Rhône valley narrows and the slopes on either side are covered in vines. Across the river, on the right bank, lie the terraces of Condrieu, which produces a famous white wine from the viognier grape, and the steep slopes of Côte-Rôtie to the north, which give some of France's finest syrah. The vineyards climb in stepped rows up slopes so steep that harvesting is done by hand.

The view from the road is excellent. The Rhône, broad and slow, curves below with poplars and gravel bars, the factory chimneys and bridges of the valley mixing with the green of the slopes, and the hills of the Pilat massif rise beyond. In the evening, the light turns the river to a sheet of silver and the vineyards to a deep green, a good moment for photographs.

The riding on this section is a mix of valley road and hill road, with the main route along the river busy with trucks and cars, and the side roads climbing into the hills for quieter, more varied riding. The bends are tight in places, the surface is generally good, and there are some steep gradients as the road leaves the valley floor. Be prepared for gusts from the north, as the mistral, funnelled by the valley, can be strong, particularly in spring.

For fuel and food, Vienne is the place, with a good choice of stations and restaurants, including a number of traditional bouchons, where you can eat Lyonnais classics in a convivial atmosphere. Parking in the centre can be difficult in the evening, so use the car parks near the river.
t.vercors balcony roads@45.6,4.4:
The Monts du Lyonnais are the soft, rounded hills that lie west of Lyon, a country of small farms, pastures, woods and tidy villages, and this food stop lies in the middle of them, near Saint-Symphorien-sur-Coise and Chazelles-sur-Lyon. At between five and nine hundred metres, the hills are modest, but they feel a world away from the city, with fresh air, long views and a pleasant lack of traffic.

Chazelles-sur-Lyon has a particular claim to fame: it was for centuries the capital of French hat-making. The felt hat industry flourished here in the nineteenth century, when many workshops turned out hats for the whole country, and a hat museum in the town tells the story. Saint-Symphorien-sur-Coise, a market town of three thousand people, has a pleasant centre with an old church and a lively weekly market. Further east, at Saint-Galmier, the famous Badoit sparkling water has been bottled since the nineteenth century, and the green bottle is a familiar sight on French tables.

When it comes to food, you are in Lyonnais territory, where eating is a serious matter. Look for a local bar-restaurant offering the plat du jour, which might be a quenelle in a creamy sauce, an andouillette, a slice of rosette de Lyon sausage, or a stew of beef. For dessert, try the tarte aux pralines, a pink, sugar-laden creation that looks alarming and tastes wonderful, and cervelle de canut, a herbed fresh cheese eaten with bread. Lunch is generally served between noon and two, and kitchens close promptly, so arrive on time.

The roads here are a pleasure: narrow, winding and quiet, climbing over ridges and dropping into little valleys, with good surfaces and gentle gradients. The views from the ridges reach all the way to the Alps on a clear day, and the landscape changes with the seasons, from green pasture in spring to golden stubble in autumn. Cyclists are common, and the occasional tractor or cattle truck can slow the pace, but the traffic is rarely a problem.

Fuel is available in Saint-Galmier, which is a little under ten kilometres away, and in the larger villages of the hills, though pumps may be unmanned or card-only after hours. Carry cash for small cafes.
t.vercors@45.9,4.9:
North-east of Lyon, the land flattens into the Dombes, a plateau of glacial clay that is dotted with a thousand or more man-made ponds. Civrieux, Saint-André-de-Corcy and Mionnay sit on its southern edge, where the ponds, called étangs, glimmer among fields and woods, and herons and egrets stand in the reeds. Since the Middle Ages, the people of the Dombes have farmed fish in these ponds, draining each one every few years to harvest carp and then growing crops in the dry bed before refilling it, a rhythm that has shaped the landscape and the local menu.

It is an unusual and rather lovely part of France. Birds are the main attraction, and a large park at Villars-les-Dombes, a short way north, keeps thousands of them, while migrating species stop on the ponds in spring and autumn. Mionnay, a village of two thousand, has a place in French culinary history, because a famous restaurant here once earned three Michelin stars and drew gourmets from Lyon and further away. The local dishes include frogs' legs, carp and chicken from Bresse, the region just to the north.

For a rider, the Dombes is a calm place to end a day. The roads are flat and straight, with long lines of poplars and a lot of agricultural traffic, and it is a good area to unwind. Fuel is available in Saint-André-de-Corcy, a village of three thousand, and in the larger town of Neuville-sur-Saône, which is a bit further, so you will not run short. Bakeries and cafés are scattered through the villages, and a lunch in a village inn can be a pleasure. In mist and evening light, the ponds seem to glow, and the sky is large.

After the cliffs and balconies of the Vercors, the contrast is considerable. The ride has taken you from stone and precipice to reed and water, and the land has the quiet of a place that has been farmed for centuries. Mosquitoes can be bothersome near the ponds in summer, so carry repellent, and in autumn, fog can lie thick on the lanes in the early morning, so use your lights.
t.fontainebleau forest@48.4,2.7:
The Forest of Fontainebleau is a strange and beautiful place, a woodland of oak, beech and pine growing on a bed of sandstone that has weathered into huge grey boulders, scattered across the hillsides like the playthings of giants. It covers some twenty-five thousand hectares south of Paris, and it was a royal hunting ground for centuries before it became a place of refuge for city dwellers, climbers and painters. UNESCO designated it a biosphere reserve in the late twentieth century, recognising its rare mix of habitats.

The sandstone is the thing. Over millions of years, wind and water have carved it into rounded blocks, ledges and overhangs, and in the forest these blocks have become the world's best-known bouldering ground, with climbers from every country working the problems marked with coloured arrows. The sand itself is pale and fine, and the heaths and gorges of Franchard have an almost desert feel in dry weather. The forest also has the Mare aux Fées, a pond named for the fairies said to bathe in it.

In the nineteenth century, painters of the Barbizon school, among them Rousseau and Millet, came to the village of Barbizon on the edge of the forest to paint nature directly, working outdoors and rejecting the studio tradition, and in doing so they helped pave the way for the Impressionists. The château of Fontainebleau, a vast palace beside the forest, was a favourite of François I and Napoleon, who said farewell to his Guard in its courtyard in 1814 before going into exile on Elba.

The riding here is a very mixed pleasure. The main roads through the forest are smooth and fast, with long avenues of tall trees and dappled light, but many smaller roads are narrow, patched and strewn with leaves and sand, and sudden bends hide in the shade. Speed limits are low and enforced, and some tracks are closed to motor vehicles. Weekends bring heavy traffic, with cyclists, climbers and walkers, so go on a weekday if you can. After rain the surface can be treacherous.

Fontainebleau, a town of nearly twenty thousand people, has fuel, restaurants and parking, and is the best place to stock up. The smell of the forest, resin and leaf mould, is intoxicating on a warm morning.
t.nemours@48.3,2.7:
Nemours lies on the Loing river, in the southern corner of Seine-et-Marne, where the landscape changes from the forests of Fontainebleau to the gentler farmland of the Gâtinais. It is a town of about fourteen thousand people, with a grey-stone centre, a canal beside the river and a medieval castle that still stands guard over the bridge. A good place for lunch, in other words, with enough to look at between courses.

The castle, built in the twelfth century and extended in the fifteenth, is a solid, square fortress with round corner towers, and it houses a museum on the prehistory of the Île-de-France, as well as exhibits about the history of the town. The surrounding area is rich in prehistoric remains, thanks to the rock shelters and caves in the sandstone ridges, and the museum explains how people have lived in the region for tens of thousands of years. The duchy of Nemours, once a royal title, gave its name to a series of notable French nobles.

The Canal du Loing runs through the town, a modest waterway used for centuries to carry goods toward Paris, now mostly frequented by pleasure boats and walkers on the towpath. A seat on a terrace by the canal in summer, with a plate of simple French cooking, is hard to beat. Expect good, uncomplicated fare: a plat du jour, a steak with chips, a goat cheese salad, a tarte aux pommes, and a carafe of house wine. The brasseries around the centre are generally open for lunch from noon until two, and a lot of them are closed on Monday.

The riding to Nemours from the north runs along quiet forest roads and then across open farmland, a good mix of shaded bends and straight sections. The surface is generally good, the traffic light, and the sandstone cliffs on the edge of town give a hint of the scenery in the forest. In autumn, the leaves along the roads can be slippery, especially after rain.

Fuel is easy in Nemours and neighbouring Saint-Pierre-lès-Nemours, both of which have stations and supermarkets, and the town is a convenient base for exploring the area. If you have time after lunch, take a walk along the canal and watch the boats pass through the lock.
t.fontainebleau@48.4,2.7:
Fontainebleau is a royal town in a forest, and the combination is irresistible. The château grew over seven centuries from a medieval hunting lodge into a palace of great beauty, and François I turned it into a showpiece of the Renaissance, importing Italian artists to decorate its galleries. Napoleon was fond of it, too, and it was in the horseshoe staircase courtyard that he said farewell to his Old Guard in April 1814, before leaving for exile on Elba. The courtyard is called the Cour des Adieux, and visitors still stand on those steps for photos.

The forest surrounding the town is enormous, more than twenty thousand hectares of oak, beech and pine, with great grey sandstone boulders scattered through the trees like toys left by a giant. Climbers love it, and a local style of bouldering began here, so you will see people with crash pads and chalk-white hands. In the nineteenth century, painters lived in the village of Barbizon, on the edge of the forest, and worked outdoors, a precursor to the Impressionists. The ride's backroads through the Brie countryside and the coffee stop at Meaux set up a day of gentle riding in the cheese country east of Paris, so arriving at Fontainebleau at the end gives a fine finish.

For a rider, Fontainebleau is a good, easy place to rest. The town has nearly twenty thousand people, and Avon next door has more, so fuel, food and coffee are all easy, with bakeries open from early in the morning. Roads in the forest are smooth and gently curving, with big trees on both sides, but in places they are narrow, and the speed limits are low. Cyclists and walkers are everywhere on weekends, and deer and wild boar can cross at dusk. Leaves can lie thick on the road in autumn and make the bends slippery, so take it slowly.

The town centre fills with visitors in summer and the palace queues are long, but the forest is big enough to absorb everyone. Walk along a sandy track among the boulders for a few minutes, and you will see why the kings chose to hunt here, and why they never left.
t.chevreuse valley dawn loop@49.0,2.4:
There is no romance in the northern suburbs of Paris at dawn, but there is efficiency, and this fuel stop is a good example. It lies between Villiers-le-Bel, Écouen and Goussainville, in the Val-d'Oise, with the vast bulk of Roissy-Charles de Gaulle airport just to the east, and the roads around it fill early with lorries, vans and people in a hurry. If you want to ride the Chevreuse valley while the light is low, you need to start here, before the traffic does.

Écouen is the unexpected pleasure. On the hill above the town stands a Renaissance château built in the sixteenth century for Anne de Montmorency, Constable of France, one of the most powerful men of his day, and it now houses the national museum of the Renaissance, with tapestries, ceramics and furniture displayed in rooms that still feel like a nobleman's house. The view from its terrace takes in the plain of France, though these days you must imagine it without the warehouses.

Goussainville has a stranger story. Its old village centre was abandoned in the decades after Roissy airport opened, its streets and church left to decay, and a Soviet-built Tupolev Tu-144 supersonic airliner crashed into the town during the Paris Air Show of 1973. The church of Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Paul still stands among empty houses, an eerie sight if you take the time to look for it. Villiers-le-Bel, bigger and more ordinary, is a big commuter town with plenty of fuel and supermarkets.

For the rider, the practical points are simple. Fill up here, since the station density is high and the prices are the same as anywhere in the Paris region. The first part of the ride is on busy urban roads where the best trick is to move early and avoid the lorries. Once you have crossed the A1 and the N104, the country opens out toward the west and south, with fields and woods on the horizon.

Dawn here has its own odd beauty: a low sun on the planes taking off, the sky streaked orange behind the cooling towers, and a smell of kerosene and wet tarmac that is, in its own way, the smell of travel. A coffee from a station machine is the sort of breakfast that gets you moving.
t.chevreuse valley dawn loop scenic road@4:
The Canal de l'Ourcq is the unglamorous hero of this corner of Seine-et-Marne. Napoleon ordered it dug in the early years of the nineteenth century to bring clean water into Paris from the river Ourcq, and it was finished in the 1820s, a long, straight ribbon of water running from the east into the capital. It passes near Mitry-Mory and Villeparisis, and a ride along its banks is a good way to see how the city's outskirts are stitched together: lock-keepers' cottages, poplars, footbridges and, in the distance, the constant rumble of aircraft.

This stretch of the plain is flat and open, and the interest lies in small contrasts. A row of allotment gardens next to a warehouse; a small chapel beside a roundabout; a stand of tall oaks left standing among new housing. Mitry-Mory is a town of eighteen thousand people with an industrial history, and Villeparisis, with about twenty-four thousand, grew up around the canal and the railway. Both have everything you need and little you would put on a postcard.

The roads are straightforward: wide, mostly straight and in good condition, with roundabouts, speed bumps and traffic lights that break the rhythm. Heavy lorries serve the logistics parks, and the closeness of the airport brings buses and delivery vans, so the best moment is early on a Sunday, when the plain is quiet and the low sun lights the fields. The canal's towpath, popular with cyclists and joggers, runs parallel and is a good place to pause away from the traffic.

The scenery is not dramatic, but there is a modest pleasure in the openness of it. In spring the fields of rapeseed light up the plain with a bright yellow, and in late summer the harvested stubble smells of straw and dust. The sky is huge, and the movement of the aircraft above adds an odd, mechanical grace.

Fuel is plentiful in both towns and along the main road, and you will find boulangeries, cafes and supermarkets in the centres. This is a place to pass through with purpose, and to appreciate for what it is: the working edge of a great city.
t.chevreuse valley dawn loop high point@48:
Brie is an old hunting country, and the woods around Ozoir-la-Ferrière, Pontcarré and Gretz-Armainvilliers still carry the memory. The plateau here is hardly high, perhaps a hundred metres above sea level, but it is the top of the local world, a gently domed upland of cereal fields and big forests that the kings and, later, the bankers hunted. The Forêt d'Armainvilliers lies just to the south, a belt of oak and hornbeam where deer and boar still roam.

The great house of the district is the Château de Ferrières, a few kilometres north. It was built in the 1850s for the banker James de Rothschild, designed in a fantastical Renaissance style by the English architect Joseph Paxton, who had earlier built the Crystal Palace. The scale of the house, with its towers, galleries and enormous grounds, was meant to rival royal palaces, and the park, with its lakes and woods, is a reminder of how the Rothschilds shaped the landscape around Paris. The château is not always open, so check before visiting.

Gretz-Armainvilliers has a different claim, as an important railway junction since the nineteenth century, which explains the web of lines you cross on the way. Ozoir-la-Ferrière, the biggest of the three at twenty-two thousand people, is a commuter town with a shopping centre and a number of cafes, while Pontcarré is a quiet village with a church and a few farms.

The riding is easy and pleasant: smooth country roads through fields and woods, with long, gentle bends and few steep gradients. The forest roads are shaded and cool in summer, but wet leaves in autumn can make them slippery. Weekends bring cyclists and families out for a walk, so keep your speed under control near the forest car parks.

Ozoir is the sensible place for fuel and breakfast, with stations on the main road and bakeries open early. Morning mist often lies in the hollows, and as it burns off, the forest edges glow with a soft, golden light that makes the early start worthwhile.
t.chevreuse valley dawn loop photo pull of:
The Essonne is a modest river, but it has made a rich valley. It rises in the Beauce and winds north through the Gâtinais to join the Seine at Corbeil, passing through reeds, poplars and old mill sites, and the photo stop here lies near Mennecy, in a landscape of marshes, ponds and small fields that feels oddly rural so close to Paris. The marshes are a protected area and home to herons, kingfishers and a good many dragonflies.

Mennecy has a quiet claim to artistic fame. In the eighteenth century the town was home to a porcelain manufactory, under the protection of the Duke of Villeroy, whose château stood in a large park that is now a public garden. The soft-paste porcelain made here, with its delicate colours and small figures, is still prized by collectors, and examples are found in museums in Paris and elsewhere. The park is a pleasant place to wander, with old trees and a pond, and the town centre has a market and the usual cafes.

From a motorcyclist's point of view the interest is in the contrast between the wide, rolling plain and the intimate river valley. The roads around Mennecy are mostly straight and fast, linking Corbeil, Ormoy and Villabé, with a few bends where they cross the river or climb a little to the plateau. The surface is good, the traffic moderate, and the views over the marshes at dawn, with mist hanging over the water, are excellent. In winter fog is a real hazard and can linger until late morning.

Villabé and Ormoy are small and mostly residential, but they have an old church and a handful of shops. Mennecy, with about fourteen thousand people, is the one that has fuel, supermarkets and several cafes along the main street. The photo stop itself is best in the early morning or just before sunset, when low light picks out the reeds and the water.

Bring a layer: the damp air in the valley feels colder than the thermometer suggests, even in early summer.
t.chevreuse valley dawn loop@48.7,1.9:
Parisians have few woods they love as much as the forest of Rambouillet, and this food stop sits right at its edge. Auffargis, Les Essarts-le-Roi and Lévis-Saint-Nom lie among the woods, ponds and clearings of the Yvelines, in a landscape of oak and birch on sandy soil, with heather in the open patches and bracken in the glades. It is the sort of place where Parisians come on Sunday to walk, cycle and look for mushrooms.

A short distance away, hidden among trees in the valley of the Vaux de Cernay, stand the ruins of a Cistercian abbey founded in the twelfth century. The great gothic arches of the church still reach for the sky, roofless and covered in moss, and part of the monastery buildings has been turned into a hotel. The setting, beside a string of ponds with rocks and waterfalls, attracted painters in the nineteenth century, who called the ponds the Étangs de Cernay and set up their easels among the boulders.

For lunch, the villages have the straightforward kind of restaurant you would expect: a small inn or a family bistro with a dish of the day, perhaps a rabbit or a steak, a salad and a tart. Les Essarts-le-Roi is the biggest of the three at six thousand people and has a bakery, a market and a handful of cafes, and it is the most reliable bet for food. Smaller places may close on Sunday evenings or Mondays, so check before counting on them.

The roads through the forest are an absolute pleasure on a quiet morning: narrow, curving and shaded, with a good surface and long sight lines in the open stretches. The danger is the crowd: from spring to autumn, weekend cyclists and walkers fill the lanes, and a motorbike needs a bit of patience. Wet leaves and sandy patches on bends demand a gentle hand.

You will find fuel at Les Essarts-le-Roi, and in the bigger town of Rambouillet a few kilometres west. The air under the trees smells of pine resin and damp leaves, and the quiet is a good contrast to the noise of the capital.
t.chevreuse@49.0,2.4:
North of Paris, where the suburbs run into the flat plain of the Pays de France, the coordinates fall among Villiers-le-Bel, Écouen and Goussainville. It is a long way from the valley of Chevreuse, which lies south-west of the capital, and it tells you how a ride that starts with soft forest can end up on the opposite side of the city. Here the landscape is open and slightly bleak, big fields of wheat and sugar beet giving way to housing estates, warehouses and the giant, humming presence of Roissy-Charles de Gaulle airport to the north-east.

There is a surprising jewel on the ridge above Écouen. The château, built in the sixteenth century for Anne de Montmorency, Constable of France and one of the most powerful men of his age, is a robust Renaissance building with a moat, grand chimneys and rooms that still hold painted ceilings and monumental fireplaces. It now houses the national museum of the Renaissance, with tapestries, ceramics and weapons from the period, and from its terrace you can look out over the plain you have just crossed. The town around it has steep, quiet streets and a village feel that is hard to square with the surrounding sprawl.

Goussainville has a more haunting story. The old village centre, with its church and a few streets, was gradually abandoned in the decades after the airport opened, as aircraft noise made life unbearable, and parts of it stood empty for years, a ghost village on the edge of a major airport. Now some of it is being restored, and the church of Saint-Pierre-et-Saint-Paul stands solitary behind a fence. It is an odd, melancholy place for photographers, though you should be respectful of the houses that are still lived in.

Riding here is mostly practical. Roads are wide, with big roundabouts and trucks, and the evening queues on the A1 and the N16 can be long, but the surfaces are good and there is no shortage of fuel, with Villiers-le-Bel, Goussainville and neighbouring towns all offering several stations and supermarkets. Early mornings on weekends are the quiet time, when the sun comes up golden over the fields and the planes glitter as they climb out of Roissy.
t.romans and royans backroads@45.6,4.7:
Mornant is a market town in the hills southwest of Lyon, and it is also, quite practically, the place to fill the tank before heading south. It sits on the edge of the Monts du Lyonnais, with the Pays Mornantais, a rolling country of orchards, vineyards and pasture, around it, and the lights of Lyon within an hour's easy ride. The town has about five thousand people, a pleasant old centre and enough petrol stations, bakeries and supermarkets to prepare for a long day.

The area has a long history, and one of its best monuments is only a few kilometres away. At Chaponost, to the north, you can still see several arches of a Roman aqueduct that once carried water from the Gier valley to Lyon, then called Lugdunum, capital of the Gauls. The line ran for some eighty kilometres, with bridges and tunnels, and the remaining arches at Beaunant are a worthwhile stop if you want to see how the Romans managed water, stone and slope.

The orchards of the Mornant region are known for cherries, apricots and apples, and the spring blossom, usually in April, is a lovely sight. Taluyers and Chassagny, the smaller villages nearby, are typical Lyonnais hill villages, with a church, a few stone houses and views over the plain. The vineyards, too, produce a modest local wine, light and fruity.

The ride south, towards the Pilat and the Royans, begins here with gentle curves and low hills, and the first part is a steady climb through woodland and farmland. Traffic can be heavy in the morning around Lyon, but out here the roads thin out quickly. In summer, start early to avoid the heat, and bring layers for the hills.

Remember that this is a long route and that fuel stops thin out as you move south into the Rhône valley and the Drôme. Fill the tank here, grab water and a snack, and set off with a clear head.
t.romans and royans backroads@45.4,4.8:
The Rhône is the great river of the south-east, and it has shaped everything around Saint-Clair-du-Rhône and Les Roches-de-Condrieu. The water is broad and green, flowing between steep banks and busy with barges, while the road runs along its left side, with the hills of the Pilat on the far bank and the terraces of Condrieu rising behind. A bridge links the two banks, and from it you can see the river's whole width, with the old port of Les Roches-de-Condrieu at one end and the wooded slopes at the other.

This stretch of the valley has always been a route for traffic. Rivermen, the mariniers of the Rhône, once hauled barges upstream with horses along tow paths, and later steamers came and went. Today a long cycle route called the ViaRhôna follows the water, and the quays at Les Roches-de-Condrieu are a favourite place for cyclists to stop. The little port area has cafes and restaurants with terraces facing the river, which makes it a pleasant place to eat on a sunny day.

For food, expect the kind of cooking you find along the Rhône: fish from the river or the lakes, grilled or in a cream sauce, charcuterie, a local goat's cheese, and a glass of white wine from the Condrieu hills, made from viognier grapes, rich and aromatic. Saint-Clair-du-Rhône, a town of nearly four thousand, has a few restaurants and bakeries and a quiet centre, and the larger town of Le Péage-de-Roussillon, a short ride south, has supermarkets and fuel.

The riding in the valley is calm and flat, with long straights beside the river, but the side roads climb quickly into the hills and give far more fun. Wind is a factor here: the mistral and the northerly funnel down the valley, and a loaded bike can feel it. In midsummer, the heat on the river road can be intense, and the best time for riding is the morning.

A final word on timing: Rhône valley restaurants take lunch seriously and often stop serving by half past one, so aim to arrive by noon. Afterwards, ride on slowly, with a full stomach and the river light in your eyes.
t.romans and royans backroads photo pull o:
The stone here is the colour of honey. North-west of Lyon, in the hills around Blacé, Denicé and Cogny, the Beaujolais changes character: the buildings are made from a warm, ochre-gold limestone that glows in the evening sun, and the region is known as the Pays des Pierres Dorées, the land of golden stones. The villages sit among gently sloping vineyards, and the combination of stone, vine and soft light has made this some of the most photogenic country near Lyon.

The vines are gamay, the grape that gives Beaujolais its light, fruity red, planted on slopes of clay and limestone. Every year, on the third Thursday of November, the new vintage is released with great fanfare as Beaujolais Nouveau, and the cellars and restaurants fill with revellers. For the rest of the year, the wines are more serious, with a freshness that makes them pair well with local charcuterie and goat's cheese, and the small cooperative cellars in the villages are the place to taste.

Denicé has an old church and a few streets of golden houses, Blacé a pretty square, and Cogny a quiet centre with views across the vines. A little further on, villages such as Oingt and Theizé, among the prettiest in France, show the stone at its best, with narrow lanes, terraced gardens and old arched doorways. The towns of Villefranche-sur-Saône and Gleizé lie to the east, and are the places to find fuel and supermarkets.

The photo pull-off is best at golden hour, when the low sun turns the hillsides to amber and every wall seems lit from within. A few hours earlier or later, the light is flatter and the colours more subdued. Autumn is the most spectacular season, when the vines turn red and gold, but spring, with fresh green shoots and orchard blossom, has its own charm.

The roads here are a delight: narrow, winding and quiet, climbing between the vines with views opening and closing. The surface is mostly good, though patched, and in harvest season tractors and trailers add an element of surprise. Take it gently, stop for a taste and enjoy the scenery.
t.romans and@45.6,4.7:
The land here belongs to the Monts du Lyonnais, a range of rounded hills south-west of Lyon that rise to about nine hundred metres at their highest and are made of old crystalline rock. Mornant, Chassagny and Taluyers sit on the eastern flank, where the slope falls toward the Rhône and the soil supports orchards, pasture and, in places, vineyards. The wines of the Coteaux du Lyonnais, mostly light, fruity Gamay reds, come from these hills, and there are small producers who will sell you a bottle in a cellar with a hand-painted sign.

Mornant is a lively little market town of about five thousand people, with a church, a main street of bakeries and a Saturday morning crowd, and it is known as the centre of its own small region. Villages like Chassagny and Taluyers are quieter, with stone houses, a church and a bar. It is a landscape that does not demand attention, which is part of its charm: tiny roads between fields of maize and fruit trees, a view of far-off ridges, the sound of cowbells and tractors.

As an end point for a ride called Romans and Royans, it is a long way from the dramatic limestone cliffs of the Vercors, but a good place to finish. The roads here are narrow and bendy, rising and falling over small hills, and traffic is light except around Mornant itself. Surfaces are generally good, but cyclists are out in force, especially at weekends, and manure and gravel can lie on the bends. A little care pays off. There is fuel in Mornant, as well as bakeries and a small supermarket, and Givors, a larger town, is a short run to the east.

In the evening, the light turns the hills a soft blue and the first mist settles in the hollows. After a day on the cliffs, the gentle lanes are a welcome change. Stop for a coffee at a village bar, and chat to the regulars about the harvest. They will have an opinion, and they will be delighted to share it.
t.chevreuse valley road@48.7,2.0:
The Chevreuse valley owes its fame partly to a duchess. Marie de Rohan, Duchess of Chevreuse, was a leading figure in the plots and intrigues of seventeenth-century France, a friend and rival of cardinals and queens, who was exiled several times for her part in conspiracies against Richelieu and Mazarin. The town's name is forever linked with her, and above the roofs the ruins of the medieval castle, called the Château de la Madeleine, still stand on their rock, the remains of a fortress that guarded the valley for centuries.

The Yvette river runs through the town, a quiet stream with weirs and mill races, and the valley is lined with wooded slopes. At about a hundred metres above sea level, it is a green and sheltered trough, and the effect of being in a deep, quiet valley, only half an hour from Paris, is part of the charm. Chevreuse itself has about five thousand people, a pleasant main street, a few cafes and a market, and is an easy place to stop.

A little further east lies the abbey of Port-Royal-des-Champs, near Magny-les-Hameaux, one of the great places of French religious and intellectual history. In the seventeenth century it was the centre of Jansenism, a strict Catholic movement that attracted thinkers such as Blaise Pascal and the playwright Jean Racine, and was bitterly opposed by Louis XIV, who had the abbey destroyed in 1710. The ruins and a museum on the site give a sense of the drama.

The roads of the valley are a joy, winding along the river and climbing over the plateau, with a surface that is mostly smooth and traffic that, outside peak hours, is light. This is among the favourite cycling areas of the Paris region, so expect riders at weekends, and take care on tight bends where visibility is limited. In autumn the leaves can make the road slippery, and on cold mornings frost lingers in the shade.

Saint-Rémy-lès-Chevreuse, a short way along, has more shops and a station, and fuel is available in the larger towns around. The smell of the valley, damp earth, leaf mould and woodsmoke, is a pleasure in itself.
t.rambouillet forest@48.6,1.8:
Rambouillet forest is one of the great woods of the Île-de-France, around twenty thousand hectares of oak, hornbeam and pine that once belonged to the French crown and was kept as hunting ground. Deer and wild boar still live here, and in the quiet hours of the morning you may see them on the forest tracks. The land is gently rolling, with ponds in the hollows and sandy soil under the trees, and in spring the forest floor is carpeted with bluebells and the air smells of damp leaves. It is a favourite for walkers and horse riders, and a good place for a motorcyclist to slow down.

The town of Rambouillet, on the edge of the forest, has a château that has been a royal and presidential residence in turn. François I died there in 1547, and later Louis XVI bought the estate and built a model farm for merino sheep, which still exists as the Bergerie Nationale. Marie Antoinette was less impressed, calling the château a toad pond, but she later had a dairy built in the grounds and a charming little cottage lined with shells. Modern French presidents have used the château for official retreats, and the park, laid out in formal style with canals, is open to visitors.

The forest roads are a pleasure. Narrow, shaded and well surfaced, they run in long lines between trees and over small bridges, with only gentle bends and the occasional sandy patch on the verge. Speed limits are low and enforced, since walkers and cyclists share the space, and on warm weekends the car parks fill up. Fuel is easy in Rambouillet, a town of around twenty-seven thousand people, with several stations, supermarkets and bakeries. The market on Saturday morning is excellent and a good place to buy bread, cheese and fruit for a picnic.

Come in autumn if you can. The beech and oak turn gold and bronze, mushroom hunters appear along the tracks, and the light filters through the branches in long shafts. In summer, the shade is a relief. Park at a clearing, switch off the engine and listen. After a minute or two, the forest begins to speak, with birdsong, rustling leaves and the creak of branches.
t.dampierre castle sight@48.7,2.0:
Dampierre sits in the soft green fold of the Chevreuse valley, and its château is one of the most elegant in the Île-de-France. The present building was rebuilt in the seventeenth century by Jules Hardouin-Mansart, the architect of Versailles, for the Duc de Luynes, and the family still owns it today after nearly four centuries. The pink brick and pale stone, the tall slate roofs and the long moat-like canals give it a calm, symmetrical look, and the formal gardens were designed by André Le Nôtre, who also laid out the gardens at Versailles. Inside, a salon was painted by Ingres, the nineteenth-century master of line, in a project that was left unfinished.

The village that surrounds the château is tiny, with just over a thousand people, a handsome main street and a parish church. Lévis-Saint-Nom, nearby, is a small village of similar charm. The whole area belongs to the Haute Vallée de Chevreuse regional park, created to protect the valley from the sprawl of Paris, and it shows. Meadows, woods and ponds fill the valley floor, and the hills on either side are covered in oak and beech. Horses graze in fields, and the roads between villages are lined with old stone walls and hedges.

For a motorcyclist, this is a lovely stretch of country. The valley roads are narrow and winding, with gentle bends, wooded sections and glimpses of water, and the traffic is light on weekdays. At weekends the roads fill with cyclists, walkers and families heading for the château, so keep your speed down and watch the blind corners. There are cafés and restaurants in the village, and in Chevreuse you can find a good bakery.

Check opening times if you plan to visit the château, since the interior is usually open on selected days and in the afternoon, and the grounds may have a separate ticket. Even if the doors are shut, the exterior is worth a walk along the canal, where the building reflects in the still water, and the geese are in charge.
t.saint remy@48.7,2.1:
Saint-Rémy-lès-Chevreuse is the sort of town you are glad to find after a morning in the forest. It lies on the river Yvette, in the heart of the valley, with a main street of bakeries, bistros and small shops, and it is big enough, with about eight thousand people, to feel lively, but small enough to keep a village rhythm. It is the last stop of the Paris RER B line, so on weekends the pavements fill with walkers and cyclists in hiking boots and Lycra, heading for the hills. The surrounding slopes are wooded and green, and the air has a pleasantly damp, earthy smell.

The valley has a serious history. A few kilometres away, in the hollow of Port-Royal-des-Champs, a community of nuns and scholars became a centre of Jansenism in the seventeenth century, a stern and intellectual current of Catholicism that clashed with the king, and the philosopher Blaise Pascal and the playwright Jean Racine both had ties to the place. Louis XIV had the abbey destroyed in 1710, and only ruins remain. Chevreuse, next door, has the ruins of a medieval castle on a hill above the town and a pleasant old centre of half-timbered houses.

As a food stop, Saint-Rémy is straightforward. The main street has a good number of cafés and restaurants with terraces, and bakeries sell sandwiches and pastries for a picnic.
