You will find a market here a couple of times a week, with local cheese, vegetables and bread. Fuel is available in town, with a station or two on the main road, and Chevreuse is close if you need more. Parking for bikes is easy near the centre, and the streets are calm enough to leave the machine and wander.

The roads in and out of the valley are among the best in the region for a gentle ride, winding through woods and meadows with small bridges and stone walls. They are busy on fine weekends, so an early start gives you the best of the quiet. Order something hot, sit outside if the sun is out, and watch the cyclists puff past.
t.barbizon village pause@48.4,2.6:
Barbizon is a single long street on the western edge of the forest of Fontainebleau, and it is a village that owes everything to a handful of painters. In the 1830s and 1840s, artists began to arrive from Paris, tired of academic studios, and set up easels among the oaks and boulders to paint nature directly. They included Théodore Rousseau and Jean-François Millet, who painted peasants at work in the fields, including his famous Gleaners, and their approach, known as the Barbizon School, paved the way for Impressionism. The village's Auberge Ganne, where many of them lodged and covered the walls with paintings, is now a small museum.

A walk along the main street gives you a feel of how the place has changed. Galleries, antique shops and restaurants now occupy the old farmhouses, and the walls are covered in roses and wisteria. Robert Louis Stevenson spent time here in the 1870s and wrote about the forest. The Fontainebleau château is about eight kilometres away, and the village has the air of a quiet corner that has never quite recovered from being so photogenic.

For a rider, Barbizon is a pleasant pause rather than a long stop. Roads from Fontainebleau, which skirt the forest, are smooth and gently twisting, shaded by tall trees, with speed limits that are strictly applied. At the village, parking is simple on the side streets, though on fine weekends it can be busy. Fuel is not usually available in the village itself, so use the larger town of Fontainebleau, which is close by and has several stations. There are cafés and restaurants on the main street, some quite smart, and a coffee at a pavement table is a civilised way to rest.

Come on a weekday morning if you can. The light in the forest is soft, the crowd is thin, and you can walk a short way into the woods to see the boulders and heather where the painters worked. In autumn, the leaves glow, and a few of the old oaks stand with their branches bare against a grey sky.
t.nemours food window@48.3,2.7:
Balzac set a novel here, and if you ride into Nemours at midday you can see why he found it a good stage. Ursule Mirouët, one of the quieter books in his huge Human Comedy, takes place among the notables, notaries and doctors of a small provincial town on the Loing, and Nemours, with its grey stone, its canal and its slow, watchful streets, still has something of that atmosphere. It is a town where people know each other's business and where lunch, at midday, is a fixed point.

The town has about fourteen thousand inhabitants, and together with neighbouring Saint-Pierre-lès-Nemours it forms a pleasant, practical base for the ride. The Loing flows through the middle, split into channels by the canal, and the quays are lined with plane trees and cafes. The castle, which stands on the river, gives the place a bit of scale, but the pleasure lies mostly in the ordinary things: a baker with a queue, a market stall, a fishmonger.

For lunch, the usual French rhythm applies: restaurants serve from noon until about two, and after that the kitchens close, so the food window is real. The food of the Gâtinais, the region around, is plain and good, with a plat du jour of roast pork or chicken with potatoes, vegetable soup, a cheese plate and a fruit tart. The honey of the Gâtinais is well known, a pale, creamy honey made from rapeseed and wild flowers, and a pot makes a good souvenir.

The riding in this part of the Loing valley is quiet and easy, through farmland and woods with long views and light traffic. The roads are generally good, though some are patched, and the main hazard is the tractor or the cyclist on a narrow lane. In autumn, mist can lie in the valley until late in the morning, and in winter, black ice on bridges is a risk.

Bagneaux-sur-Loing, a few kilometres away, is a quieter village, but Nemours has everything: stations, supermarkets, cafes, and a bakery on nearly every corner. Eat well, take a short walk along the canal, and ride on refreshed.
t.barbizon@48.4,2.6:
Barbizon comes back at the end of a day with a different face, once the day-trippers have gone. The shops close, the terraces empty and the village slows to the pace of the forest behind it. The sandstone ridges around Barbizon, the Gorges d'Apremont and the Franchard area, are a short ride away, and they catch the evening sun in layers of grey and orange, with heather and silver birch growing between the boulders and the sandy tracks. It is wild country, in the middle of a densely populated region, and it is a strangely quiet place when the light is low.

An ancient wood, the Bas-Bréau, lies on the edge of the village, and it contains some of the oldest oaks in the forest, some of them hundreds of years old. The painters of Barbizon came to sketch them, and a few of the trees were given names and protected as early as the nineteenth century, when the forest became one of the first protected landscapes in the world. In 1861 a decree set aside part of the forest as an artistic reserve, one of the earliest protected landscapes anywhere, reflecting how seriously the painters took their woods.

The ride from Fontainebleau along the forest road is the nicest way to arrive or leave. The surface is smooth, bends are gentle, and tall trunks flash past on both sides, with the road dipping in and out of shadow. Be wary at dusk, when deer and wild boar cross the road and the low sun can dazzle, and watch for cyclists and walkers without lights. In the village, a couple of restaurants stay open into the evening, and sitting on a terrace under the trees is a fine end to a day's ride.

Sleep, if you can, nearby, and wake early. Mist often hangs between the trunks at dawn, and a rider setting out from Barbizon at first light feels the whole forest holding its breath.
t.nemours old road turn@48.3,2.7:
Before the motorways, there was the Nationale 7. The road ran from Paris to the Riviera, through Fontainebleau, Nemours, Lyon and Avignon, and in the years after the war it became the route des vacances, the holiday road, jammed in August with families, caravans and overloaded Citroëns heading south. Charles Trenet immortalised it in a cheerful song in 1955, and for a generation of French people the very name conjures up long drives, picnics at the roadside and the smell of hot tarmac.

Nemours was one of the towns the old road passed through, and the turn at this point follows the old line, now partly bypassed by the A6 motorway, with the traffic of lorries and cars reduced to a murmur. You can still see traces of the past: old garages, faded signs on buildings and the odd roadside inn that once served weary travellers. The road is wide and straight in places, and winds gently in others, following the contours of the Loing valley.

The riding is a pleasure of a nostalgic kind. The surface is generally good, the corners are wide and easy, and the road has a certain quiet dignity. A motorcycle on the old route feels like the right tool, slow enough to take in the details, fast enough to cover ground. Speed limits are strictly enforced in the towns, and you should watch for cameras, since this is a busy road for local traffic.

The country on either side is a mixture of sandstone ridges, pine and oak woods and fields, with the forest of Fontainebleau to the north and the hills of the Gâtinais to the south. At about sixty metres above sea level, the valley is low and often misty in the early morning, and in summer it can be hot and humid.

Nemours has fuel in plenty, and the neighbouring town of Saint-Pierre-lès-Nemours has more, as well as a few bakeries and cafes. A coffee on the roadside, with the sound of passing traffic, is the best way to feel the history of the road.
t.dampierre en yvelines bends@48.7,2.0:
Dampierre-en-Yvelines is dominated by a house that thinks it is bigger than the village, and it is right. The Château de Dampierre, built in the seventeenth century by Jules Hardouin-Mansart, the architect of Versailles, for the Duke of Chevreuse, is a grand brick-and-stone palace set in a formal park with a long canal. It has belonged to the Luynes family ever since, and inside, one gallery contains murals painted by the great neoclassical artist Ingres, a rare example of his work on a domestic scale. The château is open for visits at certain times of year, and is worth a stop.

The village itself is small, barely a thousand people, but the setting is lovely: stone houses, an old church and, behind the château, a long avenue of trees. The area around is part of the Haute Vallée de Chevreuse regional park, and the valley is a patchwork of woods, meadows and ponds. At about a hundred and fifteen metres above sea level, it is not high, but the sheltered position and the shade of the old trees give it a cool, peaceful feeling.

The bends in question are a pleasant string of curves on the lanes between Dampierre, Lévis-Saint-Nom and Chevreuse. They are not dramatic, but they are well-surfaced and well-cambered, and a rider can find a nice rhythm on a quiet morning. The road runs along the edge of the park wall for a while and then dips into the wooded valley, with a view of the church spire coming and going between the trees.

Be careful in autumn, when leaves, mud from farm vehicles and wet stone walls can make the road slippery, and at weekends, when cyclists and walkers arrive in numbers. Cattle and horses graze in the surrounding fields, and there are a few blind corners where a tractor can appear without warning.

For fuel and food, Chevreuse is the nearest town of any size, a few kilometres away, with stations, bakeries and cafes. Dampierre itself has a bar or two and a bakery, and the smell of woodsmoke in the cooler months is a pleasant companion on the ride.
t.abbaye des vaux de cernay@48.7,1.9:
The Vaux de Cernay is a quiet, rocky, wooded valley in the Haute Vallée de Chevreuse, and the abbey in its hollow is one of the prettiest ruins within an hour of Paris. A group of monks founded it in 1118, and in 1147 it joined the Cistercian order, the austere reformers who preferred remote valleys, running water and hard work. For centuries the abbey prospered, owning mills, fish ponds and forests, until the Revolution scattered the monks and the buildings fell into decay. Gothic arches, a ruined church and sections of cloister now stand among the trees, and ivy has crept over much of the stonework.

In the nineteenth century, the Rothschild family bought the estate and turned it into a country retreat, adding a château and enlarging the lakes, and today the property is a hotel with a restaurant and spa. The ruined abbey church lies in the grounds, and it is usually possible to see it, though access and opening hours vary, so check before you go. Close by, the stream tumbles over boulders through a small chaos of mossy rocks and beech trees, and the valley's ponds reflect the sky. Painters from Paris came here in the 1800s, drawn by the same quiet light that attracted artists to Barbizon, and a Cernay school of landscape painters grew up in the nearby village.

The roads are what make the valley special for a motorcyclist. They are narrow, winding and well shaded, with a succession of short bends, small bridges and old stone walls, and the surface is generally good. Speed limits are low, and cyclists and walkers are common, particularly on weekends, but early in the morning the valley belongs to riders and deer.

Come in autumn, when the beeches burn copper and the air smells of damp earth and fungi, or in early spring, when wild daffodils cover the banks. The lakes are good for a short walk, and a coffee on the hotel terrace is an easy way to spend half an hour.
t.rambouillet forest loop@48.6,1.8:
Rambouillet is the town where a king died and a president spends his summers. François I, the Renaissance monarch who brought Leonardo da Vinci to France, died in the château of Rambouillet in 1547, and the building, a mix of medieval towers and later wings, has been a royal and then presidential residence ever since. It is surrounded by a large park, partly formal and partly wild, and by one of the largest forests in the Paris region, over twenty thousand hectares of oak, beech and pine.

The estate holds some real oddities. In the park stands the Laiterie de la Reine, a dairy built for Marie Antoinette as a pleasure house, in the fashion for playing at country life, with a grotto and a little temple. Not far off is the Bergerie Nationale, a sheep farm founded under Louis XVI, who imported Spanish merino sheep to improve French wool, and the breed is still kept there today. A visit gives you a very different view of royal life from the glitter of Versailles.

The forest is the main attraction for riders. Its roads, many of them straight and lined with tall trees, run through tunnels of green, with dappled light and the smell of resin and leaf mould, and it is a pleasure to ride on a quiet weekday morning. The surface is mostly good, but narrow in places, and wet leaves, sandy patches and fallen branches can be treacherous. Deer and wild boar live in the woods, and a boar crossing at dusk is a real possibility.

Rambouillet itself, with nearly twenty-seven thousand people, has everything: fuel, supermarkets, cafes and a pleasant market on Saturdays. The old centre is quiet and tidy, with a few good restaurants, and the park is an excellent place to stretch out on the grass after a ride. The photo spot is at the forest edge, where the trees open to a view across a pond or a clearing, best in the soft light of early morning.

Weekends in fine weather bring many walkers and cyclists, so ride with care and expect to share the road. In winter, the forest can be cold and misty, with ice on the road in shaded sections.
t.beaujeu vineyard roads@46.2,4.6:
Beaujeu gave its name to the whole region, and then quietly let the more famous towns take the credit. The lords of Beaujeu were powerful in the Middle Ages, and their lands, the Beaujolais, were named after the town, which was the capital until the sixteenth century. Today it is a calm, small place of about two thousand people, with a main street of old houses, a Romanesque-Gothic church, a handful of cafes and a sleepy confidence that comes from knowing its own worth.

The town hosts one of the Beaujolais's most colourful events, the Sarmentelles, a festival held just before the release of the Beaujolais Nouveau in November, with a parade, music and wine tastings, in which the town celebrates the end of the harvest. The name comes from sarments, the vine prunings that were once burned in bonfires. It is a rowdy, cheerful tradition and a good time to be here, if you can find a bed.

Around Beaujeu, the vineyards roll in every direction. To the south-east rises Mont Brouilly, a conical hill crowned with a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Grape, a place of pilgrimage for winemakers, and the slopes around it produce the Côte de Brouilly. Nearby villages such as Quincié and Villié-Morgon are the home of famous wines, the first with the Brouilly vineyards and the second with Morgon, a deep, powerful gamay that can age for years. The hills here are steeper and the wines more serious than in the south of the region.

The riding is excellent. Narrow lanes wind between the vines, climbing and dropping with views over the valley to the Saône plain, the surface is generally good, and the traffic is light outside harvest. In spring, the vineyards are a fresh green, in summer a dense dark green and in autumn a blaze of red and gold. Rain makes the lanes slippery, and the grapes dropped from trailers at harvest make an unpleasant surprise.

Belleville, about thirteen kilometres away, is the nearest large town for fuel, and Beaujeu itself has cafes, a bakery and a small market. Stop for a tasting at one of the small producers, and bring a spare bag for the bottles, because it is easy to leave with more than you meant.
t.macon river food@46.3,4.8:
Mâcon turns its face to the Saône, and the river is the reason to stop. The town stretches along the west bank of the slow, wide river, with quays lined with plane trees, a long stone bridge to the village of Saint-Laurent-sur-Saône on the opposite bank, and terraces where you can eat and watch the barges. It is a town of about thirty-five thousand people, the capital of the Mâconnais wine country, and it has a pleasant, easy-going air that suits a food stop.

The poet Alphonse de Lamartine was born in Mâcon in 1790, and the town celebrates him with a statue and a quay bearing his name, since he was the great Romantic voice of French poetry, famous for his lyrical verses about nature and love. On the other side of the river, the Bresse begins, the country of the famous chickens, and the food on this bank takes the best of both regions. A plate of poulet de Bresse in cream, with a glass of white Mâcon or the more famous Pouilly-Fuissé, is the thing to order.

The wines of the Mâconnais are mostly chardonnay, grown on limestone slopes to the west, with a freshness and minerality that suit river fish, goat's cheese and local ham. Not far from town, the great rock of Solutré rises over the vineyards, a limestone cliff that gave its name to a prehistoric culture, and a ride to its foot is a fine afternoon's excursion. The old story is that, for thousands of years, hunters drove wild horses over the cliff, though the details are debated.

The riding around Mâcon is a pleasant mix of river road and vineyard lane. The surface is generally good, traffic is moderate, and the best moment is early morning when mist lies on the Saône and the light turns soft and golden. In summer, the quays are busy with walkers and cyclists, so ride slowly.

Fuel is easy at the edge of town, with several stations near the bridges, and parking along the quays is possible but busy at midday. Aim for a table by the water, order the plat du jour and let the river do the rest.
t.yzeron ridge roads@45.7,4.6:
Lyonnais like to escape to the hills on Sundays, and the Yzeron valley is one of their favourite exits. It lies to the west of the city, in the Monts du Lyonnais, a range of rounded, wooded hills that reach about nine hundred metres at their highest, and the roads here, little more than lanes, climb out of the suburbs into a landscape of meadows, chestnuts and old stone farms. The village of Yzeron gives its name to the stream and the valley, and it has been a weekend retreat for generations.

The Monts du Lyonnais are an old, worn-down range, geologically a western neighbour of the Alps and not part of them, made of ancient granite and gneiss, and they are home to a quiet rural life of dairy farming, orchards and woodland. Signs of an older life remain: dry stone walls, wash houses and small chapels, and now and then a hay barn or a stone cross at a crossroads. Thurins, Courzieu and Saint-Martin-en-Haut are typical small towns of the area, with a few shops and a Saturday market in the larger ones.

The ridge roads are the point. Narrow, winding and often steep, they follow the crests of the hills, with views over the Rhône valley to the east and the Pilat massif to the south, and on a clear day the Alps, with Mont Blanc a faint white shape on the horizon. The surface is variable, from smooth to patched, and gravel and mud on the bends need attention. Traffic is light, apart from cyclists, who treat these hills as their training ground.

In winter, the heights can see snow and ice, and the roads become hazardous, while in summer the hills are green and cool, a relief from the heat of the city. Fog often fills the valleys in autumn, and you can ride above it into clear sun.

For fuel, fill up before leaving Lyon's outskirts, since the villages have few stations. Craponne, about eleven kilometres away, has everything, and Saint-Martin-en-Haut is the best place for a coffee and a pastry along the way.
t.sainte croix en jarez@45.5,4.6:
Sainte-Croix-en-Jarez is a village inside a monastery, which is a sentence that does not make sense until you see it. Béatrix de Roussillon founded a Carthusian charterhouse here in 1280, in a hollow of the Pilat hills, and for five centuries, monks lived in solitary cells around a cloister, as the Carthusians do. When the Revolution dispersed the community, the buildings were sold, and the villagers moved into the monks' cells and the service buildings, so today ordinary houses, a bakery and a café share the old walls, and the village's streets follow the cloister. The church, the chapter house and the great gate are still there, and some of the cells are open to visitors.

The village is listed among the most beautiful in France, and it feels like a place where time has been layered, with medieval stone and farmhouses leaning into each other. The surrounding landscape is the Pilat regional park, a rounded massif of old rock and forest that rises between Lyon and Saint-Étienne, with chestnut woods, pastures and a few ridge-top viewpoints. The Gier valley runs below, once heavily industrial, now greener, with the town of Rive-de-Gier as its centre.

Getting here is half the pleasure. The roads climb from the valley through woodland and meadows in a sequence of short, tight corners, and they are narrow, with occasional gravel and wet leaves. Traffic is light, except on fine weekends when cyclists and walkers fill the hills. Fuel is not available in the village, so fill up in Rive-de-Gier, about six kilometres away, which has nearly fifteen thousand people, several stations and supermarkets. There is a small café in the village, and a restaurant or two that serve local food, such as Pilat cheeses and chestnut desserts.

The ridge road toward Pilat and Saint-Étienne is one of the nicest in the region, and the village makes a good halfway stop. In winter, snow can fall on the high ground, and mist is common in the valley, so check the conditions. The best time is a soft autumn afternoon, when the stone glows and the smell of woodsmoke drifts along the lanes. Take your helmet off and listen to the quiet. There are no cars in the cloister, and the silence feels earned.
t.pilat viewpoint@45.4,4.6:
The Pilat is the last high ground before the Rhône, a rounded massif of granite and forest that rises abruptly from the river valley to its highest point, the Crêt de la Perdrix, at about fourteen hundred metres. It is a regional nature park, a place of beech and fir woods, heather moors and open pastures, and it feels more remote than its position, between Lyon and Saint-Étienne, would suggest.

This viewpoint, above Pélussin, looks out across the valley to the Alps, and on a clear day, particularly in winter or after rain, Mont Blanc stands on the horizon, small and white, well over a hundred kilometres away. Closer, the Rhône winds through its valley, with factories and vineyards along its banks, and the scale of the view makes the whole region feel miniature. The best conditions are early in the morning, when the air is cold and clear, and after a storm has cleaned the dust from the sky.

The Pilat has its own history. In a high side valley stands the Charterhouse of Sainte-Croix-en-Jarez, a Carthusian monastery founded in the thirteenth century, which after the Revolution was sold off and gradually turned into a village, with the monks' cells becoming houses. Pélussin, a small hill town, has an old centre and a few good bakeries, and the Pilat's slopes produce a number of local specialities, from cheese to chestnuts, and a white wine called Condrieu on the Rhône side.

The roads here are twisting, climbing and descending between forest and field, with a good surface and fine views. Cyclists are everywhere on summer weekends, and the wind on the high ridges can be strong, so a loaded bike needs a firm grip. Mist can drift up from the valley and cut visibility to a few metres, and in winter the upper roads can be icy.

The nearest large town for fuel is Saint-Chamond, around twelve kilometres away, though Pélussin has stations too. Carry a layer, because the temperature at the top is often ten degrees below the valley.
t.col de la republique@45.3,4.5:
The Col de la République is a pass with a political name and an unexpected role in cycling history. At about eleven hundred and forty-five metres, it carries the old main road from Saint-Étienne to Annonay across the Pilat massif, and it has been climbed by the Tour de France more than once, while the steady grade through the beechwoods has made it a training favourite for local clubs. The pass lies in the Parc naturel régional du Pilat, between the industrial valley of Saint-Étienne and the Rhône basin.

The name speaks of the republic, and the pass has the plain, civic feel that goes with it. It is not a dramatic one in the Alpine sense; it has no famous hairpins and no view of glaciers, but the road climbs steadily through a forest of beech and fir, and the top is a wide, open saddle with a small restaurant and a few buildings. It is a place for stopping, drinking and looking at the sky.

For the rider, the road is a pleasure. The gradient is gentle, the bends are long and smooth, and the surface is generally excellent, which makes for a relaxed, rhythmic climb and descent. Heavy lorries and cars share the road, though, so keep an eye on the traffic. In winter the pass can be icy or snowy, and on the east side fog from the valley sometimes climbs up to meet you. The temperature at the top is often several degrees cooler than at the bottom.

Nature here is subtle but rich: the forests have deer and roe deer, and in spring the meadows are full of wild flowers, with orchids, gentians and buttercups. The air smells of resin, damp earth and mown grass, and in autumn, the beeches turn a copper-gold that lights the slopes.

For fuel, Bourg-Argental, about seven kilometres down the east side, has stations and shops, and La Ricamarie, thirteen kilometres west toward Saint-Étienne, is the bigger centre. There is nothing at the top beyond the restaurant, so fill up in advance and pack a layer.
t.yzeron@45.7,4.6:
Yzeron sits on a hillside high in the Monts du Lyonnais, a village of stone houses and a church spire among pasture and spruce woods, with views over the folded hills toward Lyon. It is a cooler, quieter place than the city, which is only about twenty-five kilometres away. In summer, people from Lyon drive up to escape the heat, and in winter a dusting of snow sometimes falls on the high ground, giving the villages an Alpine air. The landscape is made of rounded ridges and wooded gorges, cut by little rivers like the Yzeron itself, which runs down toward the city through a long green valley.

The Monts du Lyonnais are a farming region, known for dairy, orchards and small family businesses, and their villages have kept a lot of their character. Courzieu, Thurins and Saint-Martin-en-Haut each have a church, a bakery and a market day, and the area has long been popular with cyclists, who use the steep local climbs for training. The old stone walls and farm courtyards are common, and the hills are often swathed in morning mist that drifts out of the valleys and clears by mid-morning, leaving a clean, bright sky.

For riders, this is excellent practice country. The roads are narrow, quick and full of bends, rising and falling over small ridges and dropping into wooded valleys, and they are often quiet in the morning. The surface is usually good, though patches of gravel and wet leaves collect on shaded corners, and tractors and cyclists can appear without warning. Fuel is limited in the smallest villages, so it is better to top up in Craponne, a larger town of about eight and a half thousand people, or in Saint-Martin-en-Haut, which has a few thousand and basic services.

If you have time, take a break at a village café and talk to the owner, who may have strong views on the best route to Lyon and a certain pride in the local cheese. The sun sets late in summer, and the light on the hills is soft and golden. After a day on the bike, the lights of Lyon spread out in the dusk like an orange carpet, and the air smells of cut grass and wood smoke.
t.paris north west edge@48.9,2.2:
On the north-western edge of Paris, where the Seine makes one of its great loops, the coordinates fall at Bezons, Houilles and Colombes. It is a hard-working suburban landscape of tower blocks, tram lines, small houses with allotments and the grey sheen of a river that has seen a lot of traffic. La Défense's towers lift above the horizon to the south, and the Seine runs wide and sluggish, with barges and the occasional rower. It is not a place to linger, but for a morning ride it is a useful starting point, close to the motorway and the fast roads west.

The area has some surprises. Colombes is home to the old Olympic stadium Yves-du-Manoir, which hosted the 1924 Games, the ones in the film Chariots of Fire, and it was used again for hockey during the 2024 Games. Bezons, a town of nearly twenty-eight thousand, has its own tram link, the T2, which brings city people out to the riverbank, and the old Seine boating tradition of guinguettes, riverside dance halls, was strong along this stretch in the early twentieth century. A couple of Sunday cafés on the water still carry on that spirit.

Leaving this corner of Paris is easier than it sounds if you know your way. From Bezons, follow the Seine downstream, then take the roads over the bridge toward Montesson and Chatou, and you reach the forest of Saint-Germain-en-Laye and the open land of the Yvelines in half an hour. The ride's targets are the Lyons Forest in Normandy and the white chalk cliffs of the Seine valley, a long loop to the north-west that is well worth the early start. Fuel is plentiful here, at stations along the main roads and in the big supermarkets, so fill up before leaving, because the roads in the countryside beyond have fewer.

Weekday mornings are slow with commuter traffic, so aim to be out before seven, and on Sundays the streets are almost empty. The light at dawn on the Seine, when mist lies on the water and the first trams hum past, has a strange industrial beauty.
t.vexin ridge road@49.1,1.9:
The Vexin is a frontier country, and it shows. The plateau between the Seine and the Oise was for centuries the border between the kingdom of France and the duchy of Normandy, and the river Epte, which flows along its western edge, marked the line. In 911, the Viking chief Rollo and the French king Charles the Simple agreed at Saint-Clair-sur-Epte to give Normandy to the Norsemen, and the Vexin was the buffer between them. The history gives the villages a particular character, with fortified churches and the remains of castles.

This ridge road, at about a hundred and twenty metres, runs along the crest of the plateau between Seraincourt, Vigny and Oinville-sur-Montcient, in the Vexin français regional park. The landscape is open and agricultural, with huge fields of wheat, barley and rapeseed, divided by lines of trees and low stone walls, and long views over the countryside. The soil is chalky and light-coloured, and the fields glow in the sun.

The riding is easy and open: long, gentle curves and straights, a surface that is generally smooth, and very little traffic. On a clear day, you can see for miles over the plateau, and the church spires of the villages mark the horizon. In spring the rapeseed paints the fields a startling yellow, in summer the wheat turns gold, and in autumn the ploughed land is a deep brown. The wind is the main factor: across the open plateau it can be strong, and a crosswind can push a loaded bike.

The small villages have an old church, a few stone houses and a bakery or a bar, and some have farm shops selling local produce, such as honey, cider, and cheese. Seraincourt and Oinville are quiet and unassuming, and give a good sense of rural life. The area is popular with cyclists at weekends, so be prepared to share the road.

Meulan-en-Yvelines, about nine kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel and shops, and you should fill up there. The smell of the plateau in summer, dry grass and warm earth, is a pleasant companion, and the long evenings make it a good place to end the day.
t.la roche guyon seine view@49.1,1.6:
Above La Roche-Guyon, the Seine swings through a great meander, and the view from the cliff road takes in a wide loop of the river, green islands, poplar lines and pale chalk bluffs. The valley here is cut into thick white limestone, and the river has carved long, steep walls on the outer bends, which glow almost pink in the late afternoon. Barges pass slowly below, and the fields on the flat plains inside the loops are patched with wheat, rape and maize. It is one of the most peaceful panoramas anywhere within an hour or so of the capital.

The cliff itself holds history. Some of the houses in the village of Haute-Isle, a few kilometres east, are cut straight into the chalk, with doorways, chimneys and even a chapel hollowed out of the rock, and people have lived in these troglodyte homes for centuries. The cliff and the river were also strategic, and the château of La Roche-Guyon, built against the slope with a medieval tower on the hill above, controlled the road from Paris to Normandy for centuries. Monet's garden at Giverny lies a short ride downstream, and many painters followed the same light along this valley.

The riding is a pleasure. The D913 runs beside the river, under overhanging cliffs and through small villages, with gentle curves and a smooth surface, and it is one of the classic scenic roads of the Vexin. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, with cyclists and sightseers, and in places the road is narrow, with chalk dust on the bends. Fuel is not available at the viewpoint, and the nearest stop is Mantes-la-Jolie, a large town about twelve kilometres away, which has stations and supermarkets. Smaller villages along the road have bakeries and cafés.

Come on a weekday, and in the late afternoon if the weather is clear. The river catches the sky, swallows dart around the cliffs and the chalk turns a warm cream. It is a good place to open the visor, let the engine tick, and look at the water.
t.gisors@49.3,1.8:
Gisors is a Norman town that stands guard on the border with the Île-de-France. It lies on the Epte, the old border river, and its great castle, a motte-and-bailey fortress with a tall octagonal keep, was built by the Normans in the late eleventh century and strengthened by the kings of England, before it fell to the French king Philip Augustus in the twelfth. It was one of the key strongholds on the frontier, and the walls and keep still dominate the town. A local legend says that the Knights Templar hid treasure in the castle, and it has kept treasure hunters busy for generations, though nothing has been found.

The church of Saint-Gervais-et-Saint-Protais, a large, richly decorated building that mixes Gothic and Renaissance styles, stands in the centre, and its richly carved facade is among the finest in the region. The town has about twelve thousand people, a market, a handful of restaurants and a pleasant, slightly sleepy feel. In the nearby village of Neaufles-Saint-Martin, the ruin of a huge round tower stands on a mound above the houses.

As a return gate, Gisors is practical: it has fuel, supermarkets and a railway station, and the road to Paris is clear. The route home follows the valley of the Epte and the plateau of the Vexin, a quiet, open landscape with a good surface and light traffic. The air smells of hay and warm stone in summer, and woodsmoke in autumn.

The riding in this region is relaxed and unhurried, with long views and not much to disturb you. The Lyons Forest, to the north, is among the finest beech forests in France, and the cliffs of the Seine, to the south, are a dramatic sight, which makes this a good place to turn for home with a sense of a day well spent.

A word of caution: fuel stations in the smaller villages can be few, so take advantage of Gisors before heading south. The temperature here can be several degrees colder than Paris in winter, and fog is common in the valleys.
t.paris@48.9,2.2:
The ride that began on the north-west edge of Paris comes back to the same place, and there is a pleasure in returning to a starting line after a long loop. The coordinates are the same suburbs of Bezons, Houilles and Colombes, with the Seine running wide beside them, and the lights of La Défense glowing beyond. It is a hard-working landscape of tram lines and tower blocks that looks better in the evening, when the sun sinks behind the towers and the river takes on a pale glow.

A few minutes upstream lies the Île des Impressionnistes, an island at Chatou where the Maison Fournaise, a riverside restaurant, once hosted the painters of the Impressionist circle. Renoir painted his Luncheon of the Boating Party on its balcony in 1880, and the building has been restored as a small museum. The island is a pleasant place for a walk if you have a quarter of an hour, with a path along the water, benches and a few cafés. It shows that the Seine here was once a weekend playground of Parisians, who came out by train to row, swim and dance.

After a day in the country, the last miles back are mostly about patience. The main routes into Paris from the west, the A86 and the N13, fill up with commuter traffic from about four in the afternoon, and weekends see long queues of returning day-trippers. Smaller roads along the river are more relaxing, with plane trees and old walls, and traffic lights that, at least, keep you moving. Fuel is no problem, with a choice of stations, and cafés and bars open late. A cold drink and a sandwich by the water is a decent way to wind down.

If you finish before dark, walk to the riverbank and watch the barges slide by, heavy with sand and grain. The Seine here still works for a living, and the lights on the water look very good after a long day.
t.la roche guyon@49.1,1.6:
La Roche-Guyon is squeezed between the Seine and a wall of chalk, and the village has the look of a place that has been fitted into the only space available. The château, one of the oldest in the area, backs straight into the cliff, with rooms and a stairway hollowed from the rock, and a medieval keep on the crest above is linked to it by a long covered passage. For centuries, it belonged to the La Rochefoucauld family, whose most famous member, the seventeenth-century moralist, wrote his sharp little maxims about human vanity, and the family still has links to the house.

The château has a darker chapter too. In the spring of 1944, Field Marshal Erwin Rommel made it his headquarters while he prepared the German coastal defences against an Allied landing, and the caves in the cliff behind were used as shelters and offices. After the Normandy landings, the Allies advanced quickly along the Seine, and the village was liberated in August. Today the château is open to visitors, with a fine kitchen garden and a museum of the 1944 episode, and the village has been named one of the most beautiful in France.

It is also a gateway to the Vexin Français regional park, a plateau of wheat fields, orchards and small stone villages above the river. The hills nearby produce apples and cider, and local farms sell fruit and honey from roadside stalls. The roads here are some of the best in the region for relaxed riding, with long views, smooth tarmac and a pleasing rhythm of villages, though the D913 along the river is narrow and can be crowded on sunny weekends. The village streets are tight, so park near the river and walk the last part.

Fuel is not available in La Roche-Guyon itself, so use Mantes-la-Jolie to the west, a larger town with several stations. A café on the main street serves coffee and pastries, and several restaurants offer lunch. Try a slice of tarte aux pommes with a cup of strong coffee, and sit watching the barges slide past on the Seine, as they have for centuries. The village is calm outside July and August, and the cliff glows in low sun.
t.vetheuil seine bends@49.1,1.7:
Claude Monet moved to Vétheuil in 1878, and the village has never forgotten it. He was poor, his wife Camille was ill and the family shared a house with another household, but the Seine here, curving gently under the chalk bluff, gave him a subject that he painted again and again: the church on its hill seen across the water, the river in winter ice, the poplars and the light on the islands. Camille died in 1879 and was buried in the village cemetery, and Monet left in 1881, settling at Giverny two years later, where he would spend the rest of his life.

The photo spot is right for that view. From the road on the opposite bank, near Lavacourt, you look across the Seine to the village, with the Gothic and Renaissance church of Notre-Dame rising above the roofs, a view that has changed surprisingly little in a century and a half. The best light is early in the morning, with mist on the water, or in the late afternoon, when the sun turns the stone to honey.

The river here loops in a series of broad meanders, bounded by chalk cliffs and wooded slopes, and the countryside is a mix of fields, orchards and small villages. The Vexin plateau rises behind, and the road along the river is quiet, winding and pleasant. The surface is generally good, with some patches, and traffic is light outside weekends, when visitors come to see the village and the Monet sites.

The nearest towns of any size are Limay and Mantes, where you will find fuel, supermarkets and cafes, while Vétheuil itself has a bakery, a bar and a couple of restaurants. The village is small and steep, with narrow streets, so parking is limited and a walk to the church is a good idea.

In the cooler months, mist often lies on the river until mid-morning, and the damp air can make the road slippery, particularly on the lower bends. Bring a layer, a camera and a little patience.
t.blois@47.6,1.3:
Blois is a town built on a slope, and the château is the reason you see it from miles away. It rises above the Loire on a spur of rock, a jumble of different eras in a single courtyard: a medieval hall, a Gothic wing from the time of Louis XII in brick and stone, a Renaissance wing with a spectacular open spiral staircase, built for François I, and a classical wing by François Mansart. Four centuries of French taste, neatly stacked, and all of it was at one time a royal residence.

The château was also the scene of one of the great dramas of French history. In December 1588, King Henri III had the Duke of Guise, his rival and the leader of the Catholic League, murdered in the royal apartments, and the Duke's brother, the Cardinal, killed the next day. Catherine de' Medici, the king's mother, died in the château a few weeks later. A few years earlier, in 1429, Joan of Arc had her standard blessed in Blois before setting out to relieve Orléans, and a statue of her stands near the cathedral.

The town has other pleasures. The old centre has steep, narrow streets and half-timbered houses, and the Maison de la Magie, a museum of illusion, honours Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin, the conjuror born in Blois who inspired the name of Houdini. A stone bridge links the two banks of the Loire, and from it the view of the town, stacked on its hill, is the one you want for a photograph, best in the late afternoon.

For the rider, Blois is the hub of the châteaux country. Chambord, Cheverny, Chaumont and Amboise all lie within an hour's ride, on quiet roads through forest, vineyard and farmland, with a smooth surface and gentle curves. Traffic is heavy in July and August, with tour buses at the major sites, and it is much better to ride in spring or early autumn, when the light is soft and the crowds thin. The levees along the river carry some of the best roads, with views of the water and the white tufa cliffs.

With more than fifty thousand people, Blois has everything: fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and parking, though the old town is steep and the cobbles in the centre can be slippery in rain. The smell of the river and warm stone, and the sound of church bells over the roofs, make it a very pleasant place to stop.
t.auvers sur oise art@49.1,2.2:
Vincent van Gogh arrived in Auvers-sur-Oise in May 1890, and he was dead by the end of July. In those ten weeks, he painted about seventy canvases, among them the dark, restless wheat fields, the crooked village church and the portrait of his doctor, Paul Gachet. He died on 29 July 1890 of a gunshot wound, and he is buried in the small cemetery on the hill, next to his brother Theo, with a bed of ivy over both graves. The room he rented above the Ravoux inn, number five, is preserved almost empty, which makes it more affecting than any display.

The village on the Oise had drawn painters long before him. Charles-François Daubigny settled here in the 1860s and painted from a floating studio on the river, and Pissarro, Cézanne and Berthe Morisot all worked in the area. The light is soft and silvery, with the river and the open sky, and the village still feels like a country town with old stone houses and quiet lanes. Paths lead up to the wheat fields on the plateau, where a stone marks the place thought to have inspired his last paintings, and the view over the valley rewards the short climb.

For a rider, Auvers is easy to reach and pleasant to leave. The roads along the Oise and across the Vexin plateau are smooth and quiet, with gentle bends, old stone walls and villages with church spires. Weekends see cyclists and visitors, so slow down in the village, where the streets are narrow and parking is tight. Fuel is available in Méry-sur-Oise next door, which has about nine and a half thousand people, as well as stations on the main road, and the village has a few cafés and a bakery.

Visit early or late, since the main sights, such as the Ravoux inn and the church, are most crowded at midday, and check opening times, as some sites close for lunch and on certain days. In autumn, the fields are ploughed brown, the sky turns heavy and grey, and the wheat of the paintings feels very far away. Even so, it is easy to understand why a painter felt something here.
t.vetheuil river sweep@49.1,1.7:
The Seine below Vétheuil is a river in no hurry. It swings in long, lazy loops between chalk cliffs and poplar-lined banks, the water slow and green, and the road that follows it, the D913 on the north side, is one of the best easy rides in the Île-de-France. The Vexin plateau rises on one side, topped with fields and woodland, and the river flows below, with islands, barges and the occasional pleasure boat.

The chalk is the story. Over millions of years, the Seine has cut through the Cretaceous chalk, leaving white cliffs that glow in the sun, and in places the rock is riddled with caves. At Haute-Isle, a village a few kilometres downstream, people lived in houses dug into the cliff until recent times, and some are still used, their chimneys poking out of the rock face. At La Roche-Guyon, a little further, a castle with a medieval keep carved into the cliff and a later house at its foot stands above the road. In 1944, Field Marshal Rommel made it his headquarters, during the defence of Normandy, and the underground passages that served his staff are still there.

Behind these cliffs, the villages of the Vexin, Freneuse and Gasny, have a quiet, rural air, with stone houses, churches and fields of wheat and rapeseed. The Vexin français regional park protects the plateau, and cyclists and walkers are a common sight on the riverside lanes. Limay, across from Mantes, is the nearest sizeable town, with about eighteen and a half thousand people.

The riding along the river is a series of easy curves, with the cliffs on one side and the water on the other, and a surface that is generally good. In the evening, the cliffs glow gold and the river turns to silver, and it is the best time to go. Mist on cold mornings can linger on the water, and the road under the cliffs is damp and sometimes slippery. Be careful of falling stones in winter, when frost splits the chalk, and watch for cyclists on summer weekends.

Fuel and shops are in Limay and Mantes, so fill up there before heading along the river. The smell of river water, damp stone and wild garlic in spring is pleasant company, and the whole stretch is a calm, quiet end to a day.
t.la roche guyon cliffs@49.1,1.6:
The Seine does something unusual below Mantes: it stops running in straight lines and starts to loop, and at La Roche-Guyon it presses right up against a wall of white chalk. The cliff is the whole point of the stop. It rises behind the village in pale, stained tiers, with houses and garages tucked into its foot, and some of those rooms are caves rather than rooms, cut straight back into the rock. At about thirty metres above sea level you are on the river's own floor, and the cliff makes it feel like the bottom of a bowl.

The riding here is gentle and rewards a slow pace. The riverside road follows the bend with long, easy curves, plane trees and poplars on one side, rock on the other, and the odd barge sliding past at walking speed. Traffic thickens on fine Sundays because Parisians come out for exactly this view, so an early start gives you the village almost to yourself. The surface is decent chalk-country tarmac, but after rain the cliff drips onto the lane in places, so respect the shaded sections.

The château is what turns this from a pretty bend into a story. A medieval keep climbs the cliff behind the village, reached by a stair cut into the rock, while the later house sits below it, partly built into the cave dwellings. In 1944 the German commander Erwin Rommel made his headquarters in the château during the build-up to the Normandy landings, which gives the quiet streets an odd weight. The village is listed among the most beautiful in France, which is fair, and also small enough that you will see all of it in half an hour.

Gasny and Freneuse are a few kilometres away and are small towns, so check the tank before you commit; Mantes-la-Jolie, about twelve kilometres off, has everything. Claude Monet's gardens at Giverny are not far upriver, so on a summer weekend this whole stretch carries coaches and cyclists, and patience on the narrow bends is part of the deal.
t.magny en vexin food window@49.2,1.8:
Magny-en-Vexin sits where the Vexin plateau tips toward the Epte valley, on a patch of limestone farmland that nobody outside the Paris region thinks about much. That is its charm. The Vexin is a wide, open country of wheat and rapeseed fields, small stone villages and church spires that show up a long way off, and Magny is its market town: a sensible, well-kept place of about five and a half thousand people, with the sort of high street where the baker and the butcher still know each other's business.

As a food stop it does the job without fuss. You will find a boulangerie within a minute of the centre, a few cafés and brasseries with tables out when the weather allows, and a bench or two if you prefer to eat your sandwich in the sun. Lunch in France keeps hours, so try to arrive before one o'clock, or be ready to settle for a baguette and a pastry until the kitchens reopen. Being a real town, it also has fuel, which is the reason to note it on a day that otherwise runs through villages with none.

The roads around here are some of the most relaxed you can find within an hour of Paris. The fields are big and the visibility good, so the lanes between villages are fast and open, with long straights broken by gentle bends and the occasional dip into a wooded valley. In summer the crops stand high at the verges and in spring the rapeseed floods the horizon yellow. The wind can be steady across the plateau, since there is little to stop it, so a tank bag and a tucked-in elbow help.

The Vexin français is a regional nature park, and it is worth knowing that the villages here were built from the local pale stone, which glows in low evening light. Keep an eye out for old washhouses, lime-washed barns and the occasional château behind a wall. Chars and Vigny are the next small settlements on the map if you want somewhere quieter, but for a proper stop with a counter and a till, Magny is the one.
t.beaujeu vineyard road@46.2,4.6:
Beaujeu is the old capital of the Beaujolais, and the region takes its name from this small town rather than the other way round. You would not guess it from the size: just over two thousand people, a few streets climbing a hillside, a church and a good deal of cellar space under the houses. The valley of the Ardières runs right through it, and the vineyards start almost at the last house, their rows following the slopes in neat stripes of green, then yellow, then rust as the year turns.

The grape here is Gamay, which loves the granite soils of this northern end of the Beaujolais. The famous crus of Brouilly, Fleurie and Morgon lie a short ride to the south and east, and the road between them is the real treat of the day: short, well-surfaced and winding, with the rows of vines on both sides, small stone villages every few kilometres and, in early autumn, tractors dragging trailers of grapes along the same lanes. They are not fast, and they are not apologetic, so settle into the rhythm. The harvest happens in September, and the whole district smells of crushed fruit and woodsmoke.

Every November Beaujeu hosts the celebration of the new vintage, the Sarmentelles, when the first wine of the year is brought out with parades and a lot of noise, and the town fills. Outside that week the town is quiet and easy: a couple of cafés and bakeries near the centre, a few restaurants that serve the sort of lunch a Lyonnais would be happy with, which means plenty of charcuterie, a good salad with lardons and a glass of the local red, though a rider will want to pour that sparingly if the afternoon holds another forty kilometres.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Beaujeu is small, and although a village of this size may have a pump, you should not count on it. Belleville, about thirteen kilometres away, is the nearest proper town, and Villefranche-sur-Saône is bigger still. Fill up there and enjoy the lunch with an easy mind.
t.col des echarmeaux@46.2,4.4:
Écharmeaux is a pass in the French sense of the word: a gap in a rounded range of green hills, not a gasp of rock and snow. The col sits in the hills that separate the Beaujolais vineyards from the upper Loire country, a watershed where streams to the east head for the Saône and the Rhône and those to the west, near Chauffailles, join the Loire. You climb through pastures and cattle, past dark plantations of Douglas fir that the Beaujolais hills are known for, and arrive at a modest saddle with no drama at all.

The drama comes from the approach. On the Beaujolais side the road climbs through a series of tidy bends, with the wooded slope close on one side and long views opening out over the Saône plain on the other. It is a road for rhythm rather than speed: medium-radius corners, a clean surface in most places, and the odd farm tractor to remind you whose lane it is. The western side, towards Chauffailles, drops into softer, more open land, with the Charolais cattle you may know from the beef trade grazing the fields.

Weather matters more than the number on the sign would suggest. The hills catch cloud, and on a cold morning you can ride from sunshine at the bottom into a damp white mist at the top and out again. Summer is the best season, though late spring is lovely, with the meadows full of flowers. Snow is not unknown in winter, and the col is usually passable but can be slick, so treat it with caution outside the warm months.

Chauffailles, about eight and a half kilometres away, is a small town of four thousand with a station and shops, while Belleville, on the Saône side, is the bigger option at some distance. If you want coffee, plan it for one of the villages rather than the pass itself. What you get at the top is a quiet moment in the trees, a view back toward the vines, and the satisfaction of having crossed a divide you never knew was there.
t.cluny stone town@46.4,4.7:
For several centuries, the biggest church in Christendom stood in this small Burgundian town, and today most of it is gone. The Abbey of Cluny was founded in 910 by William of Aquitaine, who gave the land to the monks and, unusually, freed them from any lord's control, answering only to the pope. Under a series of long-lived abbots, Cluny became the centre of a network of over a thousand monasteries across Europe and a powerhouse of medieval religion, art and politics. The third abbey church, begun in the late eleventh century, was the largest in Europe until St Peter's in Rome overtook it, with five aisles and two transepts.

The Revolution ended all that. The abbey was sold off in the 1790s, and the great church was dismantled for building stone, leaving only one arm of a transept, a tall octagonal tower and some cloister buildings. The ruins are still impressive, and a visit gives a sense of the scale of what was lost, and of how the town was built from its stones. Cluny is a quiet, golden-stoned town of about four and a half thousand people, with a handsome old centre of narrow lanes and Romanesque houses, a national stud farm and a market.

The countryside around is the Mâconnais, a land of rolling vineyards, limestone ridges and small villages with Romanesque churches, and the roads are among the most peaceful in Burgundy. The curves are gentle and the surfaces mostly good, with occasional farm traffic. Nearby Taizé, a few kilometres north, is home to an ecumenical community that draws young pilgrims from around the world. Fuel is available in Cluny, and the larger town of Mâcon is about twenty-five kilometres east, with more options.

For lunch, ask for a local dish, such as jambon persillé, ham set in parsley jelly, or a plate of Charolais beef, and wash it down with a glass of white from the Mâconnais. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with warm light and quiet streets. In the evening, the stone glows pale gold against the dark roofs, and the great tower seems to hold up the sky.
t.macon river@46.3,4.8:
Mâcon is the point where the Saône changes character. Upstream it is a slow, reedy river through meadows, and here it becomes a proper waterfront, with stone quays, a long bridge and the flat Bresse plain stretching away on the far bank. The town is the capital of the Mâconnais wine country, home to the poet Alphonse de Lamartine, and for a rider moving between Burgundy and the Beaujolais it is the natural place to do the dull but necessary things.

The fuel stop itself is by the river, close to the main routes, which means you are in and out without wading into the old centre. Mâcon is a town of thirty-five thousand people, so it has plenty of stations, supermarkets and cafés, and it is open on a Sunday more reliably than the villages in the hills. If your tank is running low, this is the place to fill it, because the next stretch of small roads north and west into the vineyards offers little in the way of pumps.

If you have time to spare, walk along the quay. The Saône here is wide and calm, and the view across to Saint-Laurent-sur-Saône, which belongs to a different département and a different province, reminds you that this river was once a frontier. The wines of the Mâconnais, especially the white from Chardonnay grown on the limestone slopes to the west, including Pouilly-Fuissé, are a short ride away, and a bottle in the pannier is a fine souvenir if your luggage allows.

The riding in and out is plain town traffic, with roundabouts, lights and the occasional lorry, and it demands a little patience in the early evening. Once you leave the ring road to the west the landscape lifts quickly, with the rounded, rocky hills of the Mâconnais showing stone villages and vine terraces, and the ride becomes a different animal entirely. The river is a handsome reason to stop, but you will not regret the climb out.
t.oingt@45.9,4.6:
Oingt is a village built of a stone that seems to have been dipped in honey. The limestone in this part of the Beaujolais is coloured by iron oxide, and in low sunlight it glows from pale cream to deep orange, which is why the region is known as the Pierres Dorées, the Golden Stones. Oingt perches on a hilltop, its old houses wrapped around a medieval keep and a church, with narrow cobbled lanes that curve and climb between walls hung with wisteria and roses. It has been named one of the most beautiful villages in France, and a handful of artisans' workshops and galleries occupy the old houses.

Around it lie the villages of Théizé, Le Bois-d'Oingt and Cogny, and the Beaujolais vineyards run in neat lines across the hills, with Gamay vines growing on granite and limestone. The Pierres Dorées wines are mostly lighter and fruitier than the famous crus further north, and many growers sell directly from their cellars. The view from the hilltop looks across a patchwork of vines, orchards and woods to the Monts du Lyonnais and, on a clear day, the Alps.

A motorcycle suits these hills. The roads are narrow, twisting and quick, with short climbs and drops between villages, and the surfaces are generally good, though some are rough where tractors have passed. The Beaujolais gets busy on fine weekends, especially in harvest season, so a weekday ride is better. In September and October, vendange tractors crowd the lanes, and grape juice and mud can make corners slippery. Fuel is not available in Oingt itself, and the nearest sizeable towns are Gleizé and Villefranche-sur-Saône, which are about ten kilometres away.

Spend a few minutes walking up through the village to the keep and look out over the roofs. A café near the entrance serves coffee and a glass of local wine, and a stall sometimes sells goat's cheese and honey. After the cliffs and gorges of a day's riding, the soft hills and warm stone make a gentle, cheerful ending.
t.drome provencale weekend@45.6,4.7:
Givors is not a town anyone chooses for its beauty, and it makes no pretence of it. It sits on the Rhône south of Lyon, where the Gier valley joins the great river, squeezed between the water and the first hills of the Monts du Lyonnais and the Pilat. The railway, the motorway and a canal all pass through, and the place has the working look of a town that has made things for centuries. The label on this stop says fuel gate, and that is fair: it is a handy place to fill a tank before the day's real roads begin.

It has a history worth a minute of thought. Givors was a glass town, with a glassworks that employed much of the population for generations, and it was the terminus of the Canal de Givors, an early canal built in the eighteenth century to carry coal from the Saint-Étienne basin to the Rhône. The coal, glass and iron that came through here helped feed the industrial region around Lyon, and you can still see the legacy in the old brick and the long, low buildings by the water.

For riding, Givors is a gateway rather than a destination. From here you can go up the Gier valley toward Rive-de-Gier and the Pilat, or climb west into the Monts du Lyonnais, where the roads wind between orchards and farms. Early morning is the best time to leave, since the town road network is busy with commuters from Lyon, and the first few kilometres of any route out are slow. Once the hills begin the traffic thins and the corners improve.

With eighteen thousand people, Givors has plenty of fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries, so there is no difficulty about stocking up. Chassagny and Montagny are small settlements beside it with fewer services. Expect noise, concrete and a certain gritty honesty, then take the first road up into the hills and leave the Rhône behind.
t.drome provencale weekend high point@45.6:
This is high country by the standards of the Lyon hinterland, a rolling plateau on the edge of the Monts du Lyonnais where the land lifts above the Rhône valley and the air changes. The villages nearby, Saint-Didier-sous-Riverie, Saint-Maurice-sur-Dargoire and Saint-Joseph, are small and stone-built, strung along ridges and spurs, and the whole district is a patchwork of orchards, pasture and small woods. The highest summit of the Monts du Lyonnais, the Signal de Saint-André, tops out a little under a thousand metres, so you are in the same family of hills, if not at the roof.

What makes the riding good here is variety over short distances. The roads follow the folds in the land, so you drop into a wooded valley, climb out through fields, pass a church and a few farms and then do it again. The corners are mostly open and well sighted, the surface is usually decent, and the traffic outside commuting hours is light. Farm vehicles and cyclists are common, particularly at weekends, since the Lyonnais love these hills as much as riders do.

History runs under the whole district. The Romans carried water to Lugdunum, the capital of the Gauls, by a long aqueduct from the Pilat that passed through this country, and fragments of arches and channels survive in the fields around Chaponost and elsewhere along its route. It is the kind of detail you only notice when someone points it out, and then it changes the way you see the hills: a landscape in which people have been moving water, stone and goods for two thousand years.

Practical points are simple. The air is noticeably cooler than in the valley, a relief in summer and a bite in the cold months, so carry a layer. A short stop here is mostly for the quiet, the smell of cut grass and the feeling of having climbed out of the city's orbit.
Here the stone turns gold. Around Le Bois-d'Oingt, Chessy and Theizé, the southern Beaujolais leaves behind the grey granite of the north and moves onto limestone coloured by iron, a warm ochre that glows in the light and gives the area its nickname, the country of the golden stones. Walls, houses, church towers and barns are all built from it, and on a sunny afternoon the whole district looks as if someone has turned a dimmer up.

The roads are what you came for. They wind between vineyards and small hills, climbing to hamlets and dropping to stream beds, with a mixture of open bends and tight turns through villages. Surfaces are generally good, though patches of broken tarmac appear where the farm traffic is heavy, and in September you will share the lanes with grape trailers. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with the light low and the vines in leaf or colour. Summer can be hot on the south-facing slopes, but the shaded hollows are a relief.

There is real history in these villages. Oingt, a short distance away, is among the prettiest of the golden-stone villages and is worth a detour if you have time. Chessy has a more unusual claim: the old copper mines there produced a vivid blue mineral that mineralogists still call chessylite, a name taken from the village. It is the sort of fact that makes the place feel less like a postcard and more like a working landscape with a long memory.

For fuel and food, Le Bois-d'Oingt is a small town with basic services, and Anse, about nine kilometres away on the Saône, is bigger and a safer bet for a full tank. The villages are good for coffee and a pastry, and several of the local restaurants serve classic Lyonnais dishes in generous portions. If lunch is part of the plan, arrive a little before noon and expect to be sitting for a while. The quiet and the warm stone make it hard to hurry.
t.drome provencale weekend photo pull off@:
There are places along the edge of the Beaujolais where the land drops away and the whole Saône valley opens out eastwards, a wide, flat plain stitched with fields, poplars and roads, and beyond it the Dombes country and, on the best days, the pale line of the Alps. This pull-off sits on that edge, above Saint-Georges-de-Reneins and Arnas, with Villefranche-sur-Saône a few kilometres to the south. It is a place to take a photograph and then to look at it again for a while, because the scale of the view is hard to catch on a phone.

Light is everything. In the morning the haze lifts slowly off the plain and the slopes are soft and silvery, while late afternoon lays long shadows across the vine rows and turns the hills a deep green. Autumn adds red and gold to the vines, and a clear, cold day after rain can bring the distant mountains into view. In summer the heat haze often hides them. Wind is usually modest, but the exposed ridge can be breezy.

The Beaujolais has been wine country for a very long time, and the landscape shows it. Terraces and low walls climb the slopes, and the rows are planted close, for Gamay is a hungry plant that likes to be worked by hand on steep ground. Villefranche, the commercial heart of the region, was founded in the Middle Ages and is still known for its long main street, lined with old houses and courtyards. It is a good place for lunch or a proper break.

For practical needs, the villages around here are small but Saint-Georges-de-Reneins and Arnas have basic shops and, in all likelihood, a station or two, while Villefranche-sur-Saône is a bigger town of about thirty-three thousand with every service you could want. Take care at the pull-off itself. Pulling in on a narrow road with traffic behind you needs some thought, so check the shoulder and keep your helmet on until you are properly stopped.
t.drome provencale@45.6,4.7:
This is the industrial southern edge of Lyon, where the Gier valley meets the Rhône at Givors, a town of eighteen thousand people with a working past. Givors was once a centre of glassmaking, with a large factory that produced bottles for the wine trade, and a canal built in the eighteenth century linked it to the coalfields and ironworks of Rive-de-Gier, carrying coal to Lyon. The canal has largely disappeared, but its line can still be traced in the streets, and a few locks and old warehouses survive beside the river. The town has a slightly worn, honest look, with tall chimneys and river wharves.

Behind Givors, the hills rise quickly. Chassagny and Montagny sit on the slopes above the valley, with views over the Rhône and the long trains and barges that pass below. Orchards and small vineyards cling to the terraces, and the first spurs of the Pilat massif rise to the south, covered in woodland. It is a quiet and unglamorous corner of the region, rarely visited by tourists, which gives it a certain authenticity.

For a ride called Drôme Provençale, the end of the day here feels like a descent from the sunny south back into practical France. The roads south of Lyon along the Rhône are straightforward and fast, though busy with lorries, and the climbs into the hills offer more fun, with tight bends and views over the valley. Surfaces are generally good, but watch for gravel on the smaller lanes. Fuel is plentiful in Givors, with several stations and big supermarkets, so there is no need to worry.

If you have a few minutes, take the small road up to one of the viewpoints and watch the sun go down over the Rhône. The river is wide and slow here, and the light on the water turns it a dark gold. Behind you, the hills smell of pine and warm stone, a faint echo of Provence.
t.dombes lakes easy scenic@45.9,4.9:
Flat country, thousands of ponds, and nothing in a hurry: the Dombes is the plain north-east of Lyon where, for roughly eight centuries, people have dug shallow lakes, raised carp and pike in them, drained them, planted a crop of grain for a year and flooded them again. The result is a chequerboard of water and reeds, dotted with herons, grebes and storks, and a district that looks unlike anything else in the Rhône valley. Saint-André-de-Corcy, where this stop sits, is on its southern edge, and the nearest hills are a long way off.

For a rider, the Dombes is an easy day rather than a thrilling one. The roads are straight or gently bending, lined with poplars and hedgerows, and the speed limits are generally low. You will cross causeways between ponds, pass farms built of brick and timber, and catch glimpses of water through the trees. It is a place to relax into, with long sightlines and a feeling of great sky, and the light in the early morning, with mist on the lakes, is the best reason to start early. In winter the wind comes straight across the plain, so be ready for it.

The towns on the edge, Saint-André-de-Corcy and Mionnay, are small and unglamorous but have a sharper place in culinary history than you might expect. Mionnay was the home of one of France's best-known restaurants of the late twentieth century, which helped to put the Dombes' fish and poultry on the map. Local menus still feature frogs' legs, pike dumplings called quenelles, and carp, and the district's Bresse chickens are protected by their own appellation just to the north.

Fuel is easy here. Saint-André-de-Corcy has more than three thousand residents and the usual stations, shops and bakeries, and Neuville-sur-Saône, about ten kilometres to the south-west, is a larger town if you need more. This is a good place to fill the tank before heading into the open ponds, where services thin out noticeably. Take a warm layer if the day starts cool, because damp air hangs over the water until mid-morning.
t.beaune@47.0,4.8:
Beaune is a walled city that has turned itself into a wine cellar. The ramparts survive almost all the way round, and behind them the streets are a mixture of cobbles, courtyards, shopfronts and tasting rooms, with the great Burgundy houses sharing alleys with cheese shops and mustard sellers. At the south end of the Côte d'Or, it is where the grand cru road begins, and for a rider it is as much a pause in history as it is a stop for fuel and food.

The Hospices de Beaune is the thing to see, even if only from the outside. The hospital was founded in the fifteenth century by Nicolas Rolin, chancellor of the Duke of Burgundy, and its roof of coloured glazed tiles in diamond patterns has become the emblem of Burgundy. Inside, the old wards and the great hall are open to visitors, and the hospice still owns vineyards whose wine is sold at a famous charity auction every November. If you arrive on that weekend, the city will be heaving and rooms will be impossible, so plan accordingly.

North of town, the Route des Grands Crus runs along the foot of the slope through villages whose names are on wine lists around the world: Pommard and Volnay just to the south, Savigny-lès-Beaune to the north-west, and on toward Nuits-Saint-Georges and Dijon. The road is more a scenic drift than a sports ride, with low walls, small plots and the vines turning gold in October. Early morning light on the slope is the best time, and weekdays are quieter than weekends.

Beaune has twenty-four thousand people and all the services you could want. Fuel is easy at the stations on the ring road, and there are plenty of cafés in the central squares. Parking for motorcycles is usually manageable at the edge of the old town, though a boulevard slot fills early on a fine day. Burgundy lunches run long, so decide before you sit down if you are riding on afterwards, and choose the glass accordingly.
t.col de l oeillon ridge@45.4,4.6:
On the map the Pilat looks like a small bump south of Saint-Étienne, but on the ground it is a proper mountain massif, with a high ridge, deep forests and views down into the Rhône valley. The Col de l'Oeillon sits at around thirteen hundred metres, on the road that climbs from Pélussin up toward the main crest, and it is one of the best-known climbs for riders in the Lyon region. The highest point in the range, the Crêt de la Perdrix, is a short walk away at about fourteen hundred and thirty metres.

The road up is the draw. From Pélussin, it climbs steadily in a long series of bends, with hairpins and open corners in a good rhythm, through chestnuts and then beech and fir forest, finally breaking out onto the crest with long views east over the Rhône valley and, in clear conditions, to the Alps. The tarmac is usually good, traffic is light on weekdays, and the gradient stays reasonable. On sunny weekends, expect cyclists and other motorcycles, which makes it sociable but demands attention on the tighter bends.

The Pilat is a regional nature park, and the ridge has an Alpine feel: cool air, wet grass, wildflowers in June, fog on autumn mornings. At the foot of the slopes, on the Rhône side, steep terraces grow the grapes of Condrieu and Saint-Joseph, two of the best-known wines of the northern Rhône, so there is a nice contrast between the vines below and the forest above. A pause at the top gives you time to take in how high you have climbed from the river.

Fuel is not available on the col. Pélussin has about three and a half thousand residents and basic services, but do not count on it open late or on a Sunday, and Maclas is smaller still. Saint-Chamond, about thirteen kilometres away, is the largest town nearby with full services. Bring an extra layer even in summer, because the ridge is breezy and the wind can be cold, and in winter snow can close the upper road for days at a time.
t.pilat forest bends@45.4,4.6:
Down in the forest on the southern and western flanks of the Pilat, the road forgets about views and concentrates on bends. This stretch, near Saint-Julien-Molin-Molette and Bourg-Argental, runs under big stands of beech and fir, with the light falling in patches on the tarmac and the air noticeably cooler and damper than anywhere on the Rhône side. If the high ridge is the postcard, this is the quiet backstage, and some riders will tell you it is the better ride.

The corners are tight and continuous, one after another, with few places to overtake and plenty of reasons not to try. The surface is mostly good but gets slippery under shade, particularly in autumn when wet leaves and moss lie in the apexes, and after rain a patch of mud from a forestry vehicle is not unusual. Mornings are the best time, as the forest is quiet, and wild animals such as deer sometimes cross the road. In winter, ice lingers in shaded bends long after the sun has warmed the fields.

This area also has a working history. The Pilat was once a centre of silk-throwing, the process of twisting raw silk into thread, and the mills in the valleys here, driven by fast little rivers, supplied the weavers of Lyon and Saint-Étienne. Saint-Julien-Molin-Molette takes its name partly from the mills, and old buildings from this period still stand beside streams in the area. Timber, too, has long mattered, with the forest managed for wood and the roads built to haul logs.

Practical matters need care. Saint-Julien-Molin-Molette is a village of just over a thousand people, and Bourg-Argental, a few kilometres further, is a small town with shops, cafés and basic services. Fuel is limited, so top up in Saint-Chamond or at a larger station before entering the forest section. Mobile reception is patchy in the valleys, and there are long stretches with no villages at all, which is part of the charm.
