t.condrieu food by river@45.5,4.8:
Condrieu is a small town on the right bank of the Rhône, and its fame rests on a grape. Viognier, a fragrant white variety with notes of apricot and blossom, was almost lost here in the twentieth century, when only a few hectares survived on the steep granite terraces above the town, and the wine from this tiny area has since become one of the most sought after in France. The vines cling to slopes so steep that they are held by dry-stone walls, and in autumn the terraces blaze yellow above the river.

The town also gives its name to a small goat's cheese, the Rigotte de Condrieu, which is protected by a designation of origin and is often eaten fresh with a slice of bread and a glass of the local white. The quayside has a row of restaurants and cafés with terraces facing the river, and in summer it is a lively place to sit, with river cruise boats mooring at the pier and barges passing with a slow rumble. Opposite, across the water, the hills of the Ardèche rise in blue folds. Les Roches-de-Condrieu, next door, has a small port and a modern feel, while Saint-Clair-du-Rhône is a quiet village just beyond.

The area was once the heartland of the Rhône boatmen, the mariniers, a close community that lived and worked on the river. Old houses along the quay have wide doorways where barrels and bales were hauled in and out. Behind the town, the lanes climb into the Pilat massif, a forested ridge where the roads wind through chestnut woods and offer one of the better rides in the region. Condrieu has about thirty-six hundred people, so fuel is available in town, and Le Péage-de-Roussillon, about ten kilometres south, has more stations and shops.

For a good meal, choose a table by the water, ask for something from the river or the hills, and order a glass of Condrieu, which has a scent of peaches and a surprisingly long finish. Traffic on the main road along the Rhône is heavy, so linger on the quay until the evening rush is over. The light on the water, with the Ardèche hills behind, is lovely just before sunset.
Beneath the quiet village of Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, in the Marne valley east of Épernay, lie cellars cut into the chalk, and they are where the story of champagne is really told. The wine is made in two stages. The first ferments in vats in the autumn, and the second takes place in the bottle, down in the cool and dark, for months or years, and the chalk is the perfect place for it, holding a steady ten degrees all year and breathing out a faint damp, mineral smell. The tunnels, hewn by hand centuries ago, branch and bend beneath the vineyards, lined with bottles stacked neck to base.

The vineyards above are among the best in Champagne for Pinot Noir. The village faces a south-facing slope, and the walled vineyard known as the Clos des Goisses, set on a precipitous hillside above the Marne canal, is one of the steepest and most celebrated plots in the region, with a pronounced chalky soil that gives its wines an intensity of flavour. Aÿ, only a short way along the road, was prized by kings and was said to have been a favourite of Henry IV of France. The Marne flows nearby, with a canal alongside it, and the landscape is a patchwork of vines, poplars and small villages.

The area is well suited to riding. The roads that run between villages along the foot of the slope are gentle, with easy bends and smooth surface, and the higher roads over the Montagne de Reims offer longer views. Harvest in September brings tractors and pickers, and the roads are sticky with grape juice, so go carefully. Épernay, a town of twenty-seven thousand people, about six kilometres away, has fuel and supermarkets, while the small villages have little more than a bakery.

Tours of the cellars generally need to be booked in advance, and some producers close in the middle of the day or at weekends, so check before you go. Bring a jacket, because even on a hot day the cellar is cool. After the visit, sit outside with a glass, and notice how the sunlight on the vines makes the chalk glow white.
t.caves pommery@49.2,4.1:
Eighteen metres below the streets of Reims, a stone staircase of a hundred and sixteen steps leads down into one of the most remarkable wine cellars in the world. The Pommery caves were dug as Roman chalk quarries, the crayères, whose tall, pyramid-shaped galleries were later linked by tunnels into a network about eighteen kilometres long. When a widow, Madame Pommery, took over her late husband's champagne business in 1858, she saw the potential of the chalk pits and built her cellars there, as well as a huge neo-Gothic and Elizabethan-style estate above ground.

She was a daring businesswoman. In the 1870s, she created one of the first dry champagnes, a brut, at a time when the English and Russian markets liked sweeter wine. Down in the galleries, carved reliefs were cut into the walls by a sculptor, and the bottles lie in dark racks that disappear into the distance, a quiet army of green glass. During the First World War, locals sheltered here from bombardment, and the cellars have also been used for art installations in recent years.

The caves are on the outskirts of Reims, close to the town of Cormontreuil, which has about six and a half thousand people and fuel stations, though it is easier to find a wide choice of stations on the main roads into Reims. Visits are guided, usually booked in advance, and last around an hour, ending with a tasting. Tickets can sell out in high season, so book ahead if you can. The cellars hold a steady temperature of around ten to twelve degrees, so wear a jacket under the helmet, and leave the gloves outside, because steps and rails can be damp.

For a rider, it makes a fine stop before or after a day among the vineyards, since the caves are a few minutes from the ring road and have parking. Do not drink and ride, of course, but a tasting is best saved for when the bike is parked for the night. The glow of the glass in the dim galleries is unforgettable, and the cool air is a pleasure in July.
t.colline de vezelay@47.5,3.7:
Vézelay rises from the top of a hill in the northern Morvan, a long street of pale stone houses ending in a great Romanesque basilica, and from far across the countryside it looks like a ship riding on a green sea. The Basilica of Sainte-Marie-Madeleine was built to house relics said to be those of Mary Magdalene, brought here in the ninth century, and it became one of the great pilgrimage sites of medieval Europe. It is also the start of one of the main French routes to Santiago de Compostela, and pilgrims still set out from its doors, shells on their backpacks.

The history is formidable. In 1146, Bernard of Clairvaux preached the Second Crusade on this hillside before a huge crowd, and in 1190, Richard the Lionheart and Philip Augustus met here to launch the Third. The basilica's greatest treasure is its carved capitals, close to a hundred of them in the nave, showing scenes from the Bible and from daily life with vivid, sometimes humorous detail. On the summer solstice, a line of sunlit patches runs down the centre of the nave in perfect alignment, a feature that draws visitors every year. UNESCO listed the hill in 1979.

The hill is the reason for the stop, but the landscape below is just as good. The valley of the river Cure runs between wooded slopes, and the roads are small, quiet and full of gentle curves. The climb up to the village itself is steep and cobbled in the final stretch, and cars are restricted, so leave the bike in the car park below the hill and walk up the main street, which takes ten minutes. Fuel is not available in the village, and the nearest larger town is Avallon, about twelve kilometres away, which has stations and supermarkets.

Early morning and evening are the best times, when the day-trippers have gone and the light turns the stone gold. A glass of Bourgogne Vézelay, a local white wine, goes well at a table near the basilica, and from the terrace behind it you can look out over a wide sweep of countryside, field upon field, wood after wood, rolling into the haze.
t.corbigny@47.5,3.7:
These coordinates actually sit in the Cure valley close to Vézelay, some twenty-odd kilometres north of Corbigny itself, and the whole area belongs to the northern Morvan, a region of oak and beech woods, small farms and clear rivers on the edge of Burgundy. Avallon and Clamecy are the towns around, and in between lie meadows full of white Charolais cattle, stone villages with slate-grey roofs and the ruins of a hundred old mills along the streams.

Corbigny is a small town of the Nièvre, on a branch of the Canal du Nivernais, which was dug in the nineteenth century mainly to float firewood and timber to Paris. The wood was cut in the forests of the Morvan and sent downstream in huge rafts, a trade that lasted for centuries and made Clamecy its capital, and the writer Romain Rolland was born in Clamecy in 1866. The town has a medieval abbey church, Saint-Léonard, and a quiet market, and it is the sort of place where the café owner knows everyone by name.

The ride is named for the Climats, the little vineyard plots of the Côte d'Or that UNESCO recognised in 2015, a good hundred kilometres to the east. They are some of the most precisely mapped vineyards in the world, each one with its own name, and the Burgundy wines grown on them have been prized for a thousand years. Here, in the Morvan, the landscape is wilder and much more rural, and you will find riding that is quiet and unhurried. The roads are small, with gentle curves, patchy surfaces and a lot of agricultural traffic, and the signposts point to villages with names you might have to say twice.

Fuel is a point to plan. Avallon, with nearly nine thousand people, is the nearest town with several stations, and smaller places like Joux-la-Ville offer little. Stock up before heading into the hills, and pack a thermos. After a day in the vineyards, the forest feels cool and wide, and the wind in the beech trees makes a sound like the sea.
t.lyon@45.8,4.8:
Lyon sits on two rivers, the Rhône and the Saône, which meet at the southern tip of the narrow peninsula at the heart of the city, and it has been an important place for two thousand years. The Romans founded it in 43 BC as Lugdunum, and made it the capital of the three Gauls, and you can still sit in the Roman theatres on the hill of Fourvière, where plays are held on summer nights. Above them stands the white basilica, visible from everywhere, and below them, the old town of Vieux Lyon has Renaissance houses and the covered passages called traboules, which cut through blocks and courtyards and were used by silk workers and later by the Resistance.

The city grew rich on silk, and across the Saône the hill of the Croix-Rousse was once crowded with workshops, whose weavers, the canuts, rose in revolt in the 1830s. Lyon also has a reputation as the capital of French food. Small restaurants called bouchons serve hearty local dishes such as andouillette, quenelles and salade lyonnaise, with a glass of Beaujolais, and the late chef Paul Bocuse made the city a pilgrimage for gourmets. The Lumière brothers, who invented cinema in 1895, were from here, and the festival of lights on 8 December sets the streets glowing with candles and projections.

For riders, Lyon is a hub, with the Alps, the Massif Central, the Beaujolais and the Rhône valley all within a short ride. The centre is busy, with trams, one-way streets and a low-emission zone that can restrict older vehicles, so check the rules and use a secure car park if you are staying. Fuel is easy on the outskirts, and plenty of stations lie on the ring road. The ride in question visits Firminy, where Le Corbusier built a large cultural centre and a concrete church, which makes the afternoon a tour of twentieth-century architecture.

Leave in the morning, before the commuter traffic builds, and come back in the evening, when the old town is glowing. A glass of wine on the riverbank, with the cathedral lit up behind, is a fitting end to a day.
t.lascaux@45.1,1.2:
On 12 September 1940, a dog vanished down a hole above the Vézère valley, and the four teenagers who went after it found the way into one of the great finds in the history of art. The cave of Lascaux, near the town of Montignac, holds hundreds of paintings and engravings of horses, bulls, stags and ibex, some of them several metres long, made by Palaeolithic people around seventeen thousand years ago. The animals are drawn with astonishing confidence, in red, yellow and black pigments, and they seem to gallop across the curved walls of the chambers. It was opened to the public after the Second World War, and for fifteen years, thousands of visitors a year came to see it.

The visitors were the problem. Their breath and body heat brought carbon dioxide, humidity and algae to the cave, and the paintings began to fade, so in 1963, it was closed to the public to save them. Today the original is protected, with access limited to scientists, and visitors see exact replicas. The newest, Lascaux IV, a large facility opened in 2016 at the foot of the hill, reproduces the whole cave with precise detail and is well worth a visit.

The Vézère valley is known as the capital of prehistory, with a string of caves, rock shelters and museums around Les Eyzies, and the roads that wind through it are a treat. They run beside a clear river, under limestone cliffs and past stone villages, with gentle bends and a smooth surface. Le Cap Blanc, a rock shelter nearby, holds a frieze of carved horses that stands out in relief on the stone wall. In summer, coaches and caravans are common, so aim for an early start. Fuel is available in Montignac, a town of about three thousand people, and in Terrasson-Lavilledieu, which has more stations, to the north.

Tickets to Lascaux IV are best bought in advance, and the visit is guided in part. Spring and autumn bring cooler weather and thinner crowds, and in the evening, the stone of the valley takes on a warm glow. Sit by the river in Montignac with a coffee, and think of the first people who stood in the dark with a burning lamp, painting a bull.
t.vichy@46.1,3.4:
Vichy has been a spa town since Roman times, and it still wears the elegance of its glory days in the nineteenth century, when emperors and aristocrats came to take the waters. Napoleon III visited several times in the 1860s and had a row of chalets built for his use by the river Allier, and his patronage made the town fashionable. Wide avenues lined with plane trees, a grand opera house of 1901, covered galleries and a park of springs recall that age. In the Hall des Sources, visitors can still fill a glass at the fountains and taste the mineral waters, which are fizzy, salty and warm.

The name carries other associations. In 1940, after the fall of France, the government of Marshal Pétain made its seat in Vichy's hotels, and the town gave its name to the collaborationist regime of the following four years, a dark chapter that the town now acknowledges in its museum and public life. Today it is a calm, green place, a bit sleepy in winter, famous for its pastilles, little mint-flavoured sweets first made in 1825, and for the cosmetics industry that grew from its waters.

Riding around Vichy is easy. The Allier valley is flat and wide, and the roads along it are smooth and quick, with the hills of the Bourbonnais to the east and the volcanic chain of the Auvergne rising to the west. Cusset, next door, has a medieval centre with a clock tower, and the little villages beyond have châteaux and Romanesque churches. The town has twenty-seven thousand people, so fuel stations and supermarkets are on every approach, and the cafés and brasseries in the centre stay open late. In the old thermal quarter, parking is straightforward and the pavements are wide enough to wander.

The ride from Clermont-Ferrand brings you through fields of sunflowers and wheat, and it is a pleasant change from the volcanic puys. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, when the plane trees are in leaf and the crowds are thin. Buy a tin of pastilles, sit under the covered gallery with a coffee, and imagine the carriages arriving in the evening.
t.kelimutu@-8.8,121.8:
Kelimutu is a volcano on the island of Flores, in Indonesia's Nusa Tenggara, and it has three crater lakes that change colour. At the summit, about sixteen hundred metres above the sea, the three lakes sit side by side in a rocky landscape, one a deep turquoise, one a milky green and one a dark, almost black, though the colours shift over the years, from blue to green to red to brown, apparently according to volcanic gases and minerals in the water. Nobody can predict when or how they will change, and that is part of their pull.

The local people, the Lio, regard the lakes as the resting place of the dead. According to their belief, the souls of the young go to one lake, those of the old to another, and those of the wicked to a third, and the area is treated with respect. The national park around the volcano protects forest, with orchids, tree ferns and birds, and the lakes are reached by a short walk from the car park at the end of the road. Sunrise is the best moment, when the first light touches the water and the clouds drift in the craters below you.

The road from Moni to the lakes is a short climb, about thirteen kilometres, with a series of bends through forest, and it is generally in good condition, though narrow and wet in places. Mornings are cold, and mist or cloud often covers the lakes by mid-morning, so an early start is essential. In the dry season, from about May to September, the chances of a clear sunrise are best, and the rainy season brings thick cloud and heavy showers.

Fuel is a concern in this part of Flores. Ende, the large town on the south coast, about nineteen kilometres away in a straight line but much further by road, has proper fuel stations and shops, and it is wise to fill up there. Small shops in the villages sell petrol in bottles, but quality and supply vary. Carry water and snacks, because the park has little more than a few stalls, and wear warm clothes for the dawn.
t.moni@-8.7,121.9:
Moni is a small village at the foot of Kelimutu, a cluster of homestays, guesthouses and tiny restaurants strung along the road, in a cool green landscape of rice terraces, coffee bushes and banana trees. At about a thousand metres, it is noticeably cooler than the coast, and the evenings bring a damp chill that sends everyone into their rooms with a pot of hot tea. Most travellers come to sleep before the sunrise climb to the lakes, but the village has a quiet charm of its own.

The surrounding countryside is worth a little time. The people of the area weave ikat cloth, with patterns of dyed thread that vary from village to village, and you can see the weavers at work, or buy a piece from a roadside stall. A short ride away is a waterfall, and nearby there are hot springs where you can warm up after a cold morning on the volcano. The fields around the village are green, and the smell of woodsmoke and coffee hangs in the air.

The road to Moni, part of the Trans-Flores route, is a tough but rewarding ride. From Ende, it climbs into the hills in a long series of bends through forest, rice fields and villages, and the surface varies from good tarmac to broken patches, with landslides, potholes and animals on the road. Rain can make it slippery, and the corners often come with little warning, so a measured pace is wise. The scenery is excellent, with views over the green ridges to the sea.

Moni has a handful of small shops, but no proper fuel station that I would rely on, so fill up in Ende before you go. Small roadside stands sell petrol in bottles, though the price is high and the quality uncertain. Homestays often include dinner and breakfast, with rice, vegetables, eggs and strong local coffee, and the hosts can arrange early transport to the lakes. Bring a warm layer, a torch and a little cash, since cards are rarely accepted.
t.rouen food@49.4,1.1:
Rouen is the kind of city you do not mind stopping in. It sits on the Seine in Normandy, about an hour and a half from Paris on the motorway, and it has a lot of ground to cover for a town of its size: a great Gothic cathedral, a medieval centre of half-timbered houses, and a history that reaches from the Vikings to the Second World War. The cathedral's cast-iron spire, finished in the nineteenth century, is the tallest in France, and Claude Monet painted the west front in dozens of canvases at different hours, trying to catch the light on the stone. Stand in the square at sunset and you will understand the obsession.

This is also where Joan of Arc was tried and burned in 1431. A modern church on the old market square, the Place du Vieux-Marché, stands where she died, and a simple cross marks the spot. The Gros-Horloge, an astronomical clock set in an arch over a pedestrian street, dates from the fourteenth century and is as much a symbol of Rouen as the cathedral. The old streets around it are cobbled and mostly closed to traffic, so you will park and walk.

For a rider, Rouen is a good gate. It has fuel on every approach, and the food scene is solid. Normandy cooking leans on butter, cream, apples and the sea, so you can have duck done in the Rouen style, with a sauce made from its own blood and liver, which is rich and not for everyone, or go lighter with fish, moules or a tarte normande with a glass of cider. There are bakeries all through the centre if you need something simpler. The neighbouring towns of Bihorel and Mont-Saint-Aignan sit on the hill above the centre and have the university and more modern cafes.

The ride out toward the coast is the reason many people come. The roads follow the Seine through loops and chalk cliffs, and the Route des Abbayes, a signposted route along the river, passes the ruins of Jumièges and Saint-Wandrille, two great Benedictine abbeys. In the other direction, the plateau of the Pays de Caux runs to the sea, with fields, flint farmhouses and white cliffs at Étretat. In the city itself, watch for tram tracks, which are slippery when wet, and for the one-way systems around the river.
t.cambremer@49.2,0.0:
Cambremer is where apple country begins to show its hand. The village lies in the Pays d'Auge, in the Calvados department of Normandy, a green, rolling land of orchards, hedgerows, half-timbered farmhouses and fat dairy cows, and the roads that wind between them are lined with apple trees. There are only about a thousand people, so it is a small place, with a church, a few shops and the sense of being in no hurry. The surrounding farms are the true attraction, because this is the heart of the Route du Cidre, a signposted trail past dozens of producers who sell cider, pommeau, perry and calvados directly from the farm.

The cider is not the sweet fizzy drink of the English pub. It is a dry, complex, slightly cloudy drink, made from a blend of bitter, sweet and acid apples, often with a gentle sparkle, and the best bottles come from small producers with old orchards. Calvados is the apple brandy distilled from it and aged in oak, and in the Pays d'Auge the spirit is double-distilled, giving it depth. Pommeau, a blend of apple juice and young calvados, is sweet and rich. Of course, a rider should taste with discipline, spit or sip, and buy a bottle to take home.

The region is also famous for cheese, with Camembert, Livarot and Pont-l'Évêque all made within a short distance, and a lunch of cheese, bread, butter and cider is the correct thing here. The half-timbered buildings, called colombages, have walls of oak beams and white or ochre plaster, and many of them are centuries old. In late April and early May, the orchards bloom in white and pink, and in autumn the fruit is picked and the air smells of fermentation.

The riding is about leisure. The lanes are narrow and winding, with high hedges, farm gates and tractors, and it is easy to find yourself on a tiny road with grass down the middle. Take it slowly, because there are cows crossing and mud on the corners after rain. Fuel is not in the village, so top up in Lisieux, thirteen kilometres away, or Dozulé, and expect shops to close at lunch. The weather is mild and often damp, and a waterproof jacket is wise even in summer.
t.beuvron en auge@49.2,0.0:
In the heart of the Pays d'Auge, Beuvron-en-Auge looks the way Normandy ought to look in a children's book. The half-timbered houses, with their dark beams, pale plaster and tilting upper storeys, date mostly from the fifteenth to seventeenth centuries, and they cluster around a covered market hall in a village of a couple of hundred people. It is on the list of the most beautiful villages in France, and for once the label is deserved. The geraniums are suspiciously tidy.

The reason to ride here is the cider. The Pays d'Auge is a protected area for cider, pommeau and calvados, apple brandy distilled and aged in oak, and the Route du Cidre winds between the orchards on small lanes, with farm signs inviting you to stop and taste. Many producers sell directly, so you can buy a bottle of farmhouse cider or a small flask of calvados, if your panniers have room. The cheeses of the region, Camembert, Livarot and Pont-l'Évêque, are made within a short ride, and a plate of them with bread and a glass of cider is a very good lunch.

The riding is gentle, hedged and curving, with lanes that lead through apple orchards, along hedgerows and past cows grazing in lush pasture. The roads are narrow, and corners hide slow tractors and wandering cyclists, so keep your speed sensible. Wet weather is likely at any time of year, because this is Normandy, and a waterproof is not a luxury. Late April and May bring apple blossom in clouds of pink and white, and autumn brings the harvest, with the smell of crushed fruit hanging over the villages. Summer is warm but rarely hot.

Beuvron is small, so fuel is better found elsewhere. Dives-sur-Mer, about eleven kilometres away, has stations and supermarkets, and the closer village of Dozulé has some services. In the village itself, the market hall and the little shops around it sell local products, and a couple of cafés serve food and drink in season. Park at the edge, as the central streets are narrow. The Normandy coast, with the beaches of Cabourg and Deauville, lies a short ride to the north.
t.bonnebosq@49.2,0.1:
Bonnebosq is a small village in the rolling heart of the Pays d'Auge, a place of orchards, hedgerows and thick-walled farmhouses, and it is the kind of stop that rewards you for not expecting very much. There is no famous monument here and nothing you have to see. What you get is Normandy at its most ordinary and best: black-and-white Normande cows in damp green fields, apple trees in rows across the hillsides, and half-timbered manors tucked behind banks of hedge and old stone walls.

The roads that link Bonnebosq with Cambremer and Dozulé are narrow, winding lanes, often lined with hedges that block the view on corners. The riding is relaxed, with gentle gradients and a surface that varies from good to patchy. In wet weather, which is common, mud and wet leaves can make the lanes slippery, and tractors regularly appear around blind bends, so keep to a sensible speed and stay alert. Dawn and dusk bring the best light, a soft slanting gold over the orchards. In spring the blossom turns the fields white, and in autumn the apples are gathered and pressed.

This is cider country, and the habit of tasting at the farm gate is strong. Look for signs advertising cidre fermier, farm cider, along the road, and stop if one catches your eye. Pommeau, a blend of apple juice and calvados, is the local aperitif, sweet and surprisingly strong, and a glass with a slice of local cheese makes a very good snack. Calvados itself is aged for years in oak, and the older bottles are for sipping rather than gulping. For a rider, the tasting is best done on foot, or kept for the evening.

Lisieux, about thirteen kilometres away, is the nearest large town and the place to fill up with fuel, buy supplies and see the huge basilica built in the twentieth century in honour of Saint Thérèse, a major pilgrimage site. Smaller villages nearby have bakeries and cafés, though opening hours in rural France are short and many places close for a long lunch and on Mondays. Plan ahead and carry a snack.
t.beaumont en auge@49.3,0.1:
Beaumont-en-Auge hangs on a hillside above the Touques valley, and the view over the valley is the first thing you notice. The village is small, only a few hundred people, with a main street of half-timbered houses, a church and a steep lane down to the river, and it has the look of a place that has been admired for a long time. A Benedictine priory once stood here, and some of the older buildings keep traces of it. In the Pays d'Auge, a land of orchards, meadows and cows, it is among the prettiest of its kind.

Its most famous son is Pierre-Simon Laplace, the mathematician and astronomer, born here in 1749 into a farming family. He later became one of the great figures of French science, known for his work on celestial mechanics and probability, and he is said to have been one of Napoleon's examiners. A bust of him stands in the village, and the local school bears his name, a nice reminder that big ideas can start in a small place.

The Normandy cider route comes to a quiet end here, after a day of lanes, farms and tastings. The road down the valley follows the Touques toward Pont-l'Évêque, a cheese town with a long history, and toward the seaside resorts of Trouville and Deauville, with their casinos, racecourses and beaches, about ten kilometres off. The contrast between the orchards and the glamour of the coast is striking, and one can easily ride from one to the other in an hour.

Beaumont has few services, so use Pont-l'Évêque, six kilometres off, for fuel, bakeries and supermarkets, and Trouville for restaurants and a seafood lunch. In spring the hillsides are white with blossom, and the farm shops open for the season, while in autumn the apples are heaped in barns and the smell of fermenting juice drifts out. Be careful on wet roads, since mud from tractors can make the corners slippery, and fog often fills the valley in the early morning. The best way to end is a table outside in the late sun, with a glass of cider and a plate of cheese.
t.verzenay@49.2,4.1:
Verzenay is a Champagne village that decided to build a lighthouse in the middle of a sea of vines. The Phare de Verzenay, put up in 1909 by a local Champagne merchant as an advertisement, stands among the vineyards on the northern slope of the Montagne de Reims, a long way from any actual coast. It is a delightful piece of folly, and you can climb it for a view across the rows of Pinot Noir to the plain of the Marne and the spire of Reims cathedral on a clear day. A small museum inside tells the story of the vine.

The Montagne de Reims is not really a mountain. It is a wooded plateau rising a few hundred metres above the surrounding plain, with vineyards on its slopes, and Verzenay sits on its northern edge, where the chalk subsoil and the exposure give a rich, firm Pinot Noir. The village is classed grand cru, one of the top-rated in Champagne, and its fruit goes into some of the most famous bottles in the world. The whole landscape, the hillsides, houses and cellars of Champagne, was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2015, and the chalk cellars dug beneath the villages run for kilometres.

On a motorcycle, the Champagne Tourist Route is a gentle pleasure rather than a thrill. The lanes wind among the vines in easy bends, past low stone walls and grower houses with their names painted on gates, and the surface is generally good. Speeds are low because the road is narrow and tractors work the rows. September and early October are the busiest and most fragrant time, when the grape harvest fills the villages with pickers and trailers heavy with fruit. Spring brings fresh green shoots and risk of late frost, and the vines are bare and brown in winter. Summer is warm and quiet.

The forests above the village hide a curiosity: at Verzy, a short way along, the Faux de Verzy are a grove of dwarf, twisted beech trees whose branches droop and tangle, found in very few places. They are worth a short walk if you have time.

For practical stops, Verzenay itself is tiny, with a few cafés and growers who offer tastings, so book ahead for a visit to a cellar. Fuel and supermarkets are better found at Cormontreuil, about nine kilometres away, or in Reims. Remember that tasting and riding do not mix, so keep your tasting small or save it for the evening.
t.hautvillers@49.1,3.9:
Dom Pérignon, the monk who is said to have invented Champagne, is buried at Hautvillers. The story is not quite true, since sparkling wine was being made long before him, but the truth is better in some ways. Dom Pierre Pérignon was cellarer at the Benedictine abbey here from 1668 until his death in 1715, and he is credited with refining the art of blending different grapes and making a better white wine from black grapes. The line about drinking the stars is a later invention, but nobody minds. His tomb lies in the abbey church, and the abbey itself now belongs to the Champagne house Moët & Chandon.

The village stands on a hillside above the Marne, between Épernay and Dizy, and everything about it is neat. Narrow streets climb between stone houses covered in vines, and the shop and restaurant signs are wrought-iron works of art, hanging from the walls like a sculpture gallery. A tiny village with such a vast reputation can feel crowded in high season, but most visitors are gentle ones, and on a quiet morning you can walk the lanes and hear nothing but birds and distant tractors. The church of Saint-Sindulphe is worth a visit, and the viewpoint at the edge of the village looks across the vineyards to the river.

The route to Hautvillers from Épernay climbs gently through vineyards on a narrow road with a handful of bends and a lot of grapevines at the edge of the tarmac. It is easy riding, and a good one for a slow afternoon, though be careful in the harvest season when trailers of grapes crowd the lanes, and mud from the vineyards can slick the road. The best seasons are spring and early autumn. The slope faces south, so it warms up quickly, and the vines turn gold and red in October.

The Marne valley below is a wide, calm river plain, and the chalk hillsides of the Côte des Blancs and the Montagne de Reims line the horizon. The soil is chalky and well drained, and the vines are mostly Pinot Meunier and Chardonnay, planted tightly and pruned low.

There is fuel in Épernay, about five kilometres away, and the Avenue de Champagne there is lined with famous houses offering cellar tours, some of which need booking ahead. In Hautvillers itself, a few small restaurants and a bakery are usually open. Save the glass for the end of the day, and perhaps buy a bottle from a small grower rather than the biggest names.
t.orleans@47.9,1.9:
Orléans is the city of Joan of Arc, and it takes this seriously. In the spring of 1429, during the Hundred Years' War, the English had besieged the city for months, and a seventeen-year-old peasant girl who claimed to hear saints arrived with a relief force and, in the space of nine days, lifted the siege. The victory turned the war, and the city has celebrated it every year since, with a festival held between 29 April and 8 May. A statue of Joan on horseback stands in the main square, the Place du Martroi, and a reconstructed house of the period shows how she lived while she was here.

The city stands on the northernmost bend of the Loire, and for centuries it was a major river port, with boats carrying wine, salt and other goods to and from the interior. The quays along the water are pleasant for a walk, and the great cathedral of Sainte-Croix, with its soaring Gothic towers, rebuilt after the Wars of Religion, dominates the old town. Orléans was also famed for vinegar, made here from the wine that came down the river, and the town's cuisine includes sweet tarts, local cheeses and the Loire's freshwater fish. About a hundred and twenty thousand people live in the city, so fuel, bike shops and restaurants are everywhere.

The Loire Valley, from here to the west, is a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, a long stretch of river, vineyards and châteaux, built by kings and nobles who found the climate gentle and the hunting good. Chambord, Blois, Amboise and Chenonceau are all within a day's ride. The roads along the river are flat and easy, with long, soft bends, poplars along the banks and fields of sunflowers and wheat, so the Loire is more about the pace of the day than about riding thrills.

Leave the city early, because Orléans is a busy place at rush hour, with tram lines, roundabouts and impatient drivers. Once on the levee roads, traffic eases, though weekends in summer bring cyclists and caravans. Spring is lovely, with new green on the vines, and autumn is golden. The river can flood in winter, and fog is common in the mornings. Stock up on supplies in the city, then head west and let the river lead you, with a stop for a goat's cheese lunch.
t.chambord@47.6,1.5:
Chambord is absurd in the best way. François I began it in 1519 as a hunting lodge, and what rose out of the flat forest of the Sologne was a château with some four hundred rooms, a skyline of turrets, chimneys and lanterns like a miniature city, and a famous double-helix staircase in the centre, where two people can climb at once without ever meeting. Legend credits Leonardo da Vinci, who spent his last years not far away at Amboise, with the idea. Scholars treat the attribution with caution, but it is a good story and nobody has proved it wrong.

The king hardly lived here. He visited only for brief hunting parties, and the great rooms stood mostly empty and unfurnished, a pattern that continued for centuries. Molière's company staged the first performance of Le Bourgeois gentilhomme here in 1670, with Louis XIV watching, and later the estate passed through the hands of exiled princes, marshals and finally the state. Despite all that neglect, the building has survived in remarkable shape.

What makes the visit as a rider is the setting. The château stands in the middle of a walled forest park of more than five thousand hectares, the largest enclosed park in Europe, with a wall about thirty kilometres long. The roads that approach it, the D84 and the lanes through the Sologne woods, run flat and straight between oak and pine, with deer in the clearings at dawn and a mist in autumn that makes the towers float. The riding is calm, not demanding, and the main hazards are cyclists, tourist coaches and the slow summer queues on the approach. Come early or late, or in the quieter months, and the long avenue to the front gives a lovely view.

The Loire itself flows a few kilometres to the south, and the villages along it, such as Saint-Dyé-sur-Loire, have small cafés, a quay and a gentler pace. Wild boar and red deer still live in the forest, and you can hear stags roar in the rutting season in September and October. The surface of the roads here is generally good, though agricultural traffic is common, and rain is possible at any time of year.

For fuel, the nearest sizeable town is Mer, about ten kilometres to the south-west, and Blois is a short ride beyond. There are cafés and a restaurant near the château, and an ice cream and a coffee on the terrace in the sun is a good way to take in the view.
t.chenonceau@47.3,1.1:
Chenonceau is the château built across a river, and nothing prepares you for how elegant that looks. A long gallery, two storeys high, spans the Cher on a row of arches, so that the building seems to float on the water, with the slow green current flowing underneath. It is called the Ladies' Castle, and the label is earned, because for centuries women shaped it. Thomas Bohier, a royal financier, began the main block around 1513, and his wife Katherine supervised the work. Then Henry II gave the château to his mistress, Diane de Poitiers, who laid out the gardens and built the bridge across the river.

When the king died in 1559, his widow, Catherine de' Medici, forced Diane out and took the château for herself. She added the gallery on top of the bridge, where she held lavish fêtes, with fireworks, masques and mock naval battles. The rivalry between the two women is one of the best-known stories in French history, and each of their gardens is still there, in a formal layout on either side of the entrance.

The château has a second claim to a place in history. During the Second World War, the Cher formed part of the demarcation line between occupied and Vichy France, and the south end of the gallery opened onto the free zone. It was used by the Resistance to help people cross, while the main entrance stayed under German control. In the First World War the gallery was turned into a military hospital.

The approach is by an avenue of plane trees, a classic piece of French garden design, and the village roads around it are quiet, rolling lanes through vines and farmland. The riding is easy: gentle curves, a decent surface and little traffic apart from the tourist season, when coaches and cars crowd the car park by mid-morning. Early morning and late afternoon give the best light, and the château is less crowded than later in the day. The wines of Touraine, light whites from Chenin Blanc and fresh reds from Cabernet Franc, are produced nearby.

Amboise, about twelve kilometres to the north-west, is the nearest large town for fuel and supplies, and Civray-de-Touraine, much closer, has a few small shops and cafés. There is a restaurant and a café at the château itself, though prices reflect the setting.
t.amboise@47.4,1.0:
Leonardo da Vinci is buried in Amboise, in a small chapel in the grounds of the château, and he came here at the invitation of François I, who gave him the manor house of Clos Lucé, a few hundred metres away, and a pension. He died there in 1519, aged sixty-seven. The house is now a museum with models of his inventions, built from his drawings, and a garden where some are displayed outdoors. Whether the bones in the chapel are really his is debated, since the church where he was first buried was largely destroyed in the Revolution, but the place has its own quiet dignity.

The château itself stands on a rocky spur above the Loire and has seen a good deal of drama. Charles VIII, who rebuilt it in the late fifteenth century with Italian craftsmen, died here in 1498 after, the story goes, hitting his head on a low doorway. In 1560 the Amboise conspiracy, a failed Protestant plot to seize the young king Francis II, ended in a bloody revenge, with hundreds executed and hung from the balconies. In the nineteenth century the Algerian leader Abd el-Kader was held here in captivity with his family and followers.

The town runs along the river below, with a bridge, tidy quays, shops and cafés, and a narrow-street centre with half-timbered houses and tall roofs of slate. The stone is tuffeau, a soft, pale limestone quarried from the hills around, which gives the Loire châteaux their creamy glow. Many houses in the district are built into caves in the cliff, an old tradition in Touraine, and wine cellars are dug into the same soft rock.

On the bike, the Loire valley roads are some of the gentlest in France. The D751 follows the river on its south bank, flat and smooth with wide views of the water and the sandbars, and the lanes in the hills behind the town wind through vineyards and woods. Expect traffic and parking trouble at the town centre in summer, but early morning is pleasant and quiet. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with soft light and fewer crowds.

Amboise is big enough to have everything a rider needs, including fuel stations, supermarkets and plenty of places to eat. Try the local goat's cheese, rillettes, a glass of Vouvray or Montlouis and a slice of tarte Tatin if you can.
t.tours@47.4,0.7:
Tours is a graceful city at the meeting of the Loire and the Cher, with a population of about a hundred and forty thousand and a long history of being the place where things happened. In the fourth century, a Roman soldier named Martin, who famously cut his cloak in half to share it with a beggar, became bishop here, and his tomb drew pilgrims from across Europe throughout the Middle Ages, making Tours one of the great spiritual centres of the Frankish world. The basilica built in his honour has been destroyed and rebuilt, and today two towers of the old church still stand beside a modern basilica.

The old town is a delight, with narrow streets and half-timbered houses around the Place Plumereau, a square full of café tables and student life. The cathedral of Saint-Gatien, a Gothic building with a flamboyant façade, took centuries to complete, and its stained glass is among the finest in the region. Tours was also the home of Balzac, who was born here in 1799 and wrote about provincial France with a ferocity that locals find amusing now. Food here is rich and traditional, with rillettes, pork spread in jars, cheeses from goat's milk and white wines from the Vouvray hills, made from the Chenin Blanc grape.

The ride from Orléans ends here after a leisurely stretch of the Loire, and it is a ride of châteaux. Within easy reach of Tours are Amboise, where Leonardo da Vinci spent his last years, Villandry with its remarkable formal gardens, Azay-le-Rideau on its island, and Chenonceau, built across the river Cher. The roads between them are gentle, flat and pretty, with the river often in view, and there is no great challenge to the rider, only a slow, pleasant day. Expect crowds at the big châteaux in July and August, so choose the lesser ones for some peace.

Fuel and services are easy in Tours, and La Riche, on the western side, is closer to the road out. The city has a tram and heavy traffic, so give yourself time. The Loire here is wide and shallow, with sandbanks and herons, and in late summer the water can be very low. Winters are mild and often damp, and spring brings blossom. A glass of Vouvray, a plate of rillettes and a view of the river is a fine way to end the day.
t.meursault@47.0,4.8:
Meursault makes white wine of a style that is hard to describe except to say that people who love Chardonnay often name it as the finest. The wines are rich and round, with hazelnut, butter and a mineral spine, and they are made from grapes grown on the lower slopes of the Côte de Beaune, south of the town of Beaune. There are no grands crus here, but premiers crus such as Perrières and Genevrières have a reputation that equals many of the grands crus of other villages.

Every November, the village hosts La Paulée de Meursault, a huge lunch held on the Monday after the Hospices de Beaune auction, to which growers bring their own bottles to share with friends and guests. It is the third of the Trois Glorieuses, the three great days of Burgundy wine, and the atmosphere is one of boisterous celebration, with toasts, songs and the pouring of rare vintages. Visitors may not be invited, but the village comes alive that weekend.

The village itself is attractive without being showy. Its town hall, with a roof of glazed multicoloured tiles in the Burgundian style, stands on the main square, and the church has a tall Gothic spire that can be seen from the vineyards. A château and cellars of local growers line the lanes, and in summer, cafés set tables outside under the trees. Many of the lanes are narrow, and tourist traffic is heavy at times, so take your time.

For a rider, the Route des Grands Crus here is a gentle, undulating road, with the D974 running along the base of the slope and smaller lanes climbing between the vineyards. Surfaces are good, and the bends are easy, but the real attraction is the setting, with rows of vines in orderly stripes, limestone walls and the pale stone of the villages. In autumn the leaves turn gold and red, in spring the vines flush bright green, and in July the heat can be intense, so early morning rides are best. Cycling is popular here, and you will share the road with groups of riders on the quieter lanes. Park for tastings and keep the bike for the road. Many estates offer tastings by appointment, so ask at the local tourist office or at the cellar doors, and be prepared to buy a bottle in return.

Beaune, about seven kilometres to the north, is the nearest big town, and it has fuel, supermarkets and the famous Hôtel-Dieu, the Hospices de Beaune, a medieval almshouse with a spectacular tiled roof. Meursault itself is small but has a few restaurants and wine shops.
t.santenay@46.9,4.7:
Santenay is the last stop on a very famous road. The Route des Grands Crus runs south from Dijon through the Côte d'Or, a thin strip of limestone hills facing east, and passes through villages whose names are on wine lists across the world: Gevrey-Chambertin, Vosne-Romanée, Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet. By the time it reaches Santenay, the great names have mostly fallen behind, but the vineyards are still lovely, with neat rows of Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and the wines here, less expensive and less grand, are often fine value. The village is small, with a pretty church, a few cellars and a thermal spa that dates back to the nineteenth century.

The wine of Burgundy is shaped by tiny differences in soil, slope and exposure, and the vineyards are divided into plots called climats, each with its own character and history, which UNESCO listed as a World Heritage Site in 2015. Monks, especially Cistercians and Benedictines, spent centuries tending these slopes and recording which plots made the best wine, and their descendants, the family estates, still hold to the system. The names on the labels are not just brands but places, and you can walk or ride through them and see the stone walls and small huts that mark the boundaries.

The ride is all about pace. The roads run through villages and vineyards, with stone houses, low walls and cellar signs inviting you in for a tasting, but a rider must be disciplined: sip and spit, or buy a bottle for later. Traffic can be slow, especially during the harvest in September and early October, when tractors and trailers fill the lanes, and the smell of crushed grapes hangs in the air. In spring, the vines are bright green, and in autumn the leaves turn red and gold, which is the loveliest time.

Chagny, about four kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with fuel and supermarkets and a handful of excellent restaurants. Burgundian cooking is rich and slow, with beef braised in red wine, snails baked in garlic butter, the cheesy puffs called gougères and a pungent cheese called Époisses. Many cellars close at lunch and on Sundays, so telephone ahead if you want a tasting. Weather is changeable, with hail a risk in summer, and a sudden storm can ruin a vintage and a ride at once.
t.the retreat reflection garden@31.2,120.7:
The name says almost everything. Tuisi Garden, the Garden of Retreat and Reflection, was built in the 1880s in the water town of Tongli by an official named Ren Lansheng after he was dismissed from his post, and he called it after the old idea that a man out of office should withdraw and think about his faults. What he actually created was one of the most graceful small gardens in the region: pavilions and halls arranged around a pond as if they were floating on it, with rockeries, covered walkways and windows that frame views like paintings.

It stands among the classical gardens of Suzhou on the UNESCO list, and it rewards a slow visit. Tongli itself is a canal town of stone bridges, whitewashed houses with black-tiled roofs and boats nosing under willow branches. Early morning, before the tour groups arrive, it can feel genuinely peaceful, with the smell of steamed buns drifting from the doorways. The surrounding lake country south of Suzhou is flat, watery and green, laced with canals, fish ponds and the bigger lakes such as Taihu.

As a riding destination, the area is more about atmosphere than corners. The roads are flat and straight, the towns busy, and in many places motorcycles are restricted while electric scooters swarm every lane. Foreign riders on their own bikes need permits and usually a guide, and expressways are off limits to motorcycles. If you do ride, the lake roads around Taihu and the canal country towards Zhouzhuang and the Jiangnan water towns offer gentle, scenic cruising, ideally on weekday mornings.

Food is a big part of any visit. In autumn the region is famous for hairy crab from Yangcheng Lake, steamed and eaten with ginger and vinegar, and all year round you can find sweet-braised pork and freshwater fish. Fuel is no issue anywhere nearby. Spring and autumn are comfortable, summer is humid, and the plum rains of June can soak you for days, so pack accordingly and give yourself time to sit in a garden pavilion while the rain falls.
t.west lake cultural landscape of hangzhou:
There is a Chinese saying that in heaven there is paradise, and on earth there are Suzhou and Hangzhou. The West Lake, on the western edge of Hangzhou, has inspired poets, painters and garden designers for more than a thousand years, and its blend of water, hills, causeways, pagodas and temples became a model for landscape gardens across China, Japan and Korea. UNESCO inscribed it as a cultural landscape in 2011. The Su causeway, built by the poet-governor Su Dongpo in the eleventh century, and the Bai causeway, named after the Tang poet Bai Juyi, cross the lake, lined with willows and peach trees.

Around the lake, the Leifeng pagoda, rebuilt in modern times, recalls the Legend of the White Snake, one of China's great folk tales, in which a snake spirit falls in love with a human; the Lingyin temple, one of the most important Buddhist temples in China, sits in the hills with its cliff carvings; and the tea plantations of Longjing, home to the famous Dragon Well green tea, cover the slopes to the south-west. The lake is particularly beautiful in the early morning mist, or in the evening when the lights come on.

Riding in Hangzhou is restricted: like many Chinese cities, it limits motorcycles in its central areas, and foreign riders need a Chinese driving licence. The roads around the lake are busy, with heavy traffic and many pedestrians and cyclists, and the best way to explore the lake itself is on foot or by bicycle. Outside the city, the hills of Zhejiang offer winding roads through tea plantations and bamboo forests, and the Qiantang river is known for its tidal bore, best seen in autumn.

Hangzhou is a vast city, and services are no problem, though parking a motorcycle anywhere near the lake can be. The food is famous in its own right: West Lake fish in a sweet vinegar sauce, Dongpo pork braised until it melts and named after the poet-governor, and shrimps stir-fried with Longjing tea leaves. Visit the tea villages in the hills to drink the tea where it grows, ideally in spring when the first leaves are picked, and take a boat to the islands in the lake to see it as the poets did.
Fontainebleau is the palace French kings actually lived in, as opposed to the one they built to impress, and for that reason it feels more human than Versailles. Almost every monarch from the Middle Ages to Napoleon III added a wing, a staircase or a garden, so the place is a jumble of styles, held together by its forest and its long ponds. Napoleon called it the true home of kings, and in April 1814 he said goodbye to his Old Guard in the courtyard that is still known as the Cour des Adieux, at the foot of the horseshoe staircase.

The town of Fontainebleau sits around the palace, with Avon next door, about sixty kilometres southeast of Paris. It is the usual place for Parisian riders to escape to, and the attraction is the forest that surrounds it: some twenty thousand hectares of oak, beech and Scots pine on sandy soil, scattered with weird sandstone boulders that climbers come from all over Europe to scale. The roads through it, the old N6 and N7 alignments and the smaller forest routes, are smooth and flowing, shaded on hot days and lovely in October when the beeches turn copper.

Be warned, though: the forest roads are popular with everybody, limits are low and enforced, and on Sundays you share them with cyclists, walkers, horse riders and families pulling into the car parks. Deer and wild boar cross at dawn and dusk. Ride it early or on a weekday and it is a pleasure; ride it at Sunday lunchtime and it is a procession. The Seine valley to the east, around Samoreau and Samois, gives some quieter curves along the river.

The painters of Barbizon on the western edge of the forest, Millet, Rousseau and friends, worked outdoors here in the mid-nineteenth century and helped open the door to Impressionism; their village is a short detour. Practically, Fontainebleau has everything: fuel on the main roads in and out, plenty of cafes and brasseries around the palace and the main street, and a big park to rest in. Palace grounds are free to walk; the interiors need a ticket and a couple of hours, which is time well spent if the weather turns.
t.provins@48.6,3.3:
Provins rises out of the wheat fields of the Brie like something from a film set, and the odd thing is that it is almost entirely real. In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries this was one of the four great fair towns of the counts of Champagne, where merchants from Flanders, Italy and beyond met to trade cloth, spices and money. When the fairs declined, Provins simply stopped growing, and so its ramparts, its gates and its medieval upper town survived the centuries more or less intact. UNESCO listed it in 2001 as a rare surviving example of a medieval fair town.

The Tour César, a squat twelfth-century keep with an odd octagonal top on a square base, is the landmark you see from the road, and from its top you look across the roofs of the upper town and out over a plain that seems to go on forever. Beneath the town lies a network of tunnels and cellars cut into the soft rock, once used for storage and later for all sorts of rumoured secret purposes. The red rose of Provins, said to have been brought back from the crusades, turns up in jams, sweets and honey in every shop.

The roads in are a lesson in how to enjoy open country. From Fontainebleau or Paris you cross the plateau of the Brie on long straight roads lined with poplars, with big skies and very little traffic away from the main routes. It is not a place for corners, but the minor roads along the Voulzie valley and towards Donnemarie-Dontilly have some gentle dips and bends. Wind across the plateau can be strong, and in harvest season you will meet slow farm machinery and mud on the road.

Provins, with nearly thirteen thousand people, has all the practical things: fuel at the supermarkets on the edge of town, cafes in the lower town, bakeries and a weekly market. The upper town gets busy on summer weekends, especially during the medieval shows, and the cobbled lanes are steep and polished, so park below and walk up. A slice of Brie de Meaux, the local cheese, with fresh bread on the ramparts, is the correct lunch.
t.palace and park of versailles@48.8,2.1:
Louis XIV wanted a stage on which the whole French nobility would have to perform for him, and Versailles is what that ambition looks like in stone, gilt and gravel. His father's modest hunting lodge on a damp plateau west of Paris grew, over decades of building, into the palace you see now, and in 1682 the court moved out here for good. The Hall of Mirrors, the chapel, the endless enfilade of state rooms: all of it was designed so that a duke had to queue to watch the king get dressed. A long way from the Paris mob, too, which was rather the point, until the mob walked out here in October 1789 and fetched the royal family back to the city.

The gardens are the work of André Le Nôtre, and they are the real reason to come on a bike, because you arrive with a sense of scale already in your body. Ride the long axis to the Grand Canal, then out to the Trianons and Marie Antoinette's little play farm, the Hameau, and you begin to understand how much land a king could bend to a straight line. History did not stop with the Bourbons: the treaty that ended the First World War was signed in the Hall of Mirrors in 1919, in the same room where the German Empire had been proclaimed in 1871.

As riding goes, be honest with yourself. This is the outer Paris region, so the approach is suburban traffic, roundabouts, traffic lights and the occasional delivery van parked in your lane. The nicer way in or out runs through the forests that ring the town, Fausses-Reposes to the east and the Forêt de Marly to the north, where the roads narrow, the trees close over and the air suddenly smells of leaf mould instead of exhaust. From there it is a pleasant run down to the Seine and Poissy, where Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye sits on its white stilts, a twentieth-century answer to all this baroque excess. Carry a Crit'Air sticker for anything near Paris; the low-emission rules are enforced.

Versailles itself is a proper city, so fuel, cafés, bakeries and bike parking are no problem; the streets around the Notre-Dame market are good for a long lunch. Go early on a weekday if you want the palace without the coach crowds, and save the park for the late afternoon, when the low sun turns the gravel gold and the fountains, on show days, are running.
t.shangyu yuyaosection of zhedong canal@30:
The Grand Canal is usually thought of as the great waterway linking Beijing and Hangzhou, but it did not stop there. From Hangzhou, the Zhedong Canal, the canal of eastern Zhejiang, continued east through Shaoxing, Shangyu and Yuyao to the port of Ningbo, linking the inland waterway system with the sea and maritime trade. The Shangyu to Yuyao section, a waterway of rivers and canals through the flat, fertile plain south of Hangzhou Bay, is part of the Grand Canal World Heritage site, inscribed in 2014. Along it, boats carried rice, silk, tea and porcelain for centuries, and towns grew up along its banks with bridges, locks and warehouses.

The Cao'e River, which flows through Shangyu, takes its name from a legend: in the second century, a girl named Cao E threw herself into the river to search for the body of her drowned father, and she became a symbol of filial devotion, honoured by a temple on the riverbank. Yuyao, to the east, is the birthplace of Wang Yangming, one of the most influential philosophers of the Ming dynasty, and near the town lies the Hemudu site, where remains of a Neolithic culture that cultivated rice around seven thousand years ago were found, among the earliest known rice-growing communities in the world.

The plain here is densely populated and industrialised, with towns, factories, rice paddies and fish ponds crisscrossed by canals and roads. The riding is flat and busy, with heavy traffic of trucks, cars, electric scooters and tricycles, and it is not a place for pleasure riding. To the south, however, the hills of Shaoxing and the Siming mountains offer winding roads through bamboo forests and tea plantations. As everywhere in China, foreign riders need a Chinese licence and properly registered vehicle, motorcycles are often banned from city centres, and expressways are closed to them.

Shangyu, Yuyao and the nearby towns have fuel, shops and restaurants. The food of Zhejiang is light and delicate, with plenty of fish, shrimp and vegetables. Try Shaoxing wine, the famous yellow rice wine of the region, and the stinky tofu, a speciality of Shaoxing that tastes much better than it smells. Yuyao is also known for its yangmei, red bayberries, which ripen in early summer.
t.amiens cathedral@49.9,2.3:
Amiens Cathedral is huge. Built mostly in the thirteenth century, Notre-Dame d'Amiens is the largest Gothic cathedral in France by interior volume, with a nave rising over forty metres, and its west front is covered with hundreds of carved figures, saints, prophets and kings, which were once brightly painted. In summer, a light show projects the original colours onto the facade at night, bringing back the medieval look. The cathedral is a World Heritage Site, and its interior, with its soaring columns and stained glass, is a masterpiece of Gothic architecture.

Amiens is the capital of Picardy, on the Somme river, and the city has a pleasant old quarter, Saint-Leu, with canals, restaurants and cafés. The hortillonnages, floating gardens on a network of canals, are a unique sight, explored by flat boats. The writer Jules Verne lived in Amiens for many years, and his house is a museum. The Somme valley, east of the city, is the site of the First World War battles, with cemeteries and memorials scattered across the countryside.

Riding in and out of Amiens is mostly flat, with straight roads through open farmland, and the city itself has ring roads and traffic. The Somme valley offers pleasant riding along the river, with villages and views, and the coast, at the Bay of Somme, is about an hour away. Wind can be strong on the open plains.

Inside, look down as well as up. The nave floor holds a great octagonal labyrinth laid in black and white stone, which pilgrims once followed on their knees, and the choir stalls are carved with thousands of tiny wooden figures from the early sixteenth century, a whole medieval world of craftsmen, peasants and saints. The cathedral came through both world wars largely intact, protected by sandbags around the most precious parts, while much of the surrounding city was destroyed. Tradition holds that it also keeps a relic said to be the head of Saint John the Baptist, brought back from Constantinople after the Fourth Crusade, which made the building a magnet for pilgrims in the Middle Ages.

Fuel and services are plentiful in the city. Local specialities include macarons d'Amiens, an almond biscuit, and ficelle picarde, a crepe filled with ham and mushrooms. The city is busy, but parking a bike near the cathedral is usually possible.
t.suzhou section of jiangnan canal@31.2,12:
The Grand Canal is the longest artificial waterway in the world, running from Beijing to Hangzhou, and the Jiangnan section through Suzhou is one of its most storied stretches. Here, the canal winds through a landscape of water towns, rice fields and lakes, past ancient bridges, temples and gardens. It is part of the World Heritage site that recognises the canal as one of the greatest engineering achievements of the pre-industrial world.

The canal was built over centuries, with major sections completed during the Sui dynasty in the early seventh century, to transport grain and goods between the fertile south and the political capitals in the north. Suzhou flourished as a commercial and cultural centre, known for its silk, its scholars and its classical gardens, several of which are also World Heritage sites. Along the canal, you can see stone bridges like the Baodai Bridge, with its many arches, and old towpaths where boats were once pulled by human labour.

Riding here is a different kind of experience. The area around Suzhou is densely populated, with heavy traffic, busy roads and many restrictions on motorcycles in urban areas. Foreigners need special permits and often a guide to ride in China. The roads are generally flat and straight, with occasional bridges and elevated highways. The best way to see the canal is often by boat or on foot, exploring the water towns like Tongli, Zhouzhuang and Luzhi, where life still revolves around the waterways.

The landscape is shaped by water. Lake Tai, one of the largest freshwater lakes in China, lies to the west, and the area is crisscrossed by canals, rivers and ponds. In spring, the fields are green with rice and rapeseed, and in autumn, the hairy crabs of Yangcheng Lake are a famous delicacy. The air can be humid and hazy, especially in summer.

Suzhou is a major city with all services, including fuel, food and accommodation. Songling, part of the Wujiang district, is about five kilometres away. Try Suzhou-style noodles, sweet and sour mandarin fish, or a cup of Biluochun green tea, grown on the hills by Lake Tai.
t.ningbo section of zhedong canal@30.0,121:
East of Hangzhou, the Grand Canal does not simply stop. A further waterway, the Zhedong Canal, carries on across the coastal plain of eastern Zhejiang through Shaoxing and Yuyao to Ningbo and the sea, linking the inland canal system to one of China's great ports. This point sits on the Ningbo section, in a flat, intensely worked landscape of rivers, locks, villages and factories between Yuyao and the city.

Ningbo's place in history comes from that link. For more than a thousand years, goods carried down the canal from the interior were loaded here onto ships bound for Japan, Korea and South-east Asia, and the city became one of the starting points of what is now called the Maritime Silk Road. The heart of the old port is Sanjiangkou, the Three Rivers Mouth, where the Yao and Fenghua rivers meet to form the Yong, which flows on to the East China Sea. The Tianyi Pavilion in the city centre, built in the sixteenth century, is one of the oldest surviving private libraries in Asia.

The plain around here is old as well as busy. Near Yuyao lies Hemudu, the site of a Neolithic culture some seven thousand years old, where archaeologists found some of the earliest evidence of rice farming, along with wooden houses on piles and lacquered bowls. Yuyao is also the home town of Wang Yangming, the Ming philosopher whose ideas about the unity of knowledge and action are still studied across East Asia.

Be realistic about the riding. This is one of the most densely built parts of China, with expressways, ring roads, industrial zones and heavy traffic, and riding a foreign motorcycle here requires permits, a local licence or temporary permit and usually a guide. Many cities, Ningbo among them, restrict motorcycles in urban areas. The pleasant riding is south of the plain, in the green hills of Siming Shan and towards Fenghua, where roads climb through bamboo forests and tea gardens to small mountain villages.

Ningbo is a large city with every service. Yuyao, closer to this point, is a sizeable town in its own right. In season, Yuyao is famous for its yangmei, red bayberries, sold in mountains by the roadside in June, and Ningbo's tangyuan, sweet glutinous rice balls filled with black sesame paste, are known across China.
On a gentle rise above the Seine at Poissy, set back from the road in a meadow ringed by trees, a white box floats on thin columns. Villa Savoye is perhaps the most famous house of the twentieth century, designed by Le Corbusier and his cousin Pierre Jeanneret for a wealthy family as a weekend retreat and completed in 1931. It is the purest built expression of Le Corbusier's five points of a new architecture: pilotis, a free plan, a free façade, horizontal ribbon windows and a roof garden. Since 2016 it has been part of the World Heritage site of his architectural work, along with the small gardener's lodge at the entrance, a miniature echo of the main house.

Inside, a ramp climbs gently from the ground floor to the living spaces and on to the roof terrace, so that moving through the house becomes a kind of promenade. The rooms are bright and spare, with built-in furniture and a bathroom that is almost a sculpture. The family lived in it only for a few years before the war; it then suffered damage, neglect and plans for demolition before being rescued, classified and restored by the state. Today it is a museum.

The location is convenient for a ride out of Paris. Poissy is on the western edge of the metropolis, and the roads here are busy, with traffic lights, roundabouts and suburban sprawl. Head west along the Seine valley or north into the Vexin français, a regional natural park of plateaus, valleys and villages, and the riding becomes much more pleasant, with winding country roads, old stone farms and churches. The forest of Saint-Germain-en-Laye, just south, is a large woodland with straight roads and shady paths.

Poissy itself is an old royal town, the birthplace of Saint Louis, King Louis IX, in 1214. It has a fine Gothic collegiate church where he was baptised. Saint-Germain-en-Laye, a few kilometres away, has a château with a national archaeology museum and a long terrace with views over the Seine and Paris.

Poissy, under two kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Chambourcy and Saint-Germain-en-Laye also have plenty of options. Book or check opening times before visiting the villa, and take your time: the house rewards slow looking, especially when the light moves across the white walls.
t.beffroi d amiens@49.9,2.3:
Amiens built its belfry to say something, and the message was independence. Rising above the town hall in the early fifteenth century, the belfry housed the bell that called citizens to assembly and warned of fire and enemy, and it became the symbol of a town that had won its freedoms from the king and the local lords. UNESCO listed the belfries of northern France and Belgium together in 1999, and the Amiens tower is one of the finest, topped later by a baroque lantern. A short walk away stands the cathedral of Notre-Dame, the largest Gothic cathedral in France by volume, which was listed in 1981.

The city sits on the Somme, a river that gave its name to a very different history. Between 1914 and 1918 the battlefields lay to the north and east, and Amiens was a vital railhead and a base for British and Commonwealth troops. The Battle of Amiens in August 1918 turned the tide of the war. Today the Somme valley is quiet and green, with reedbeds, ponds and market gardens. In the old quarter of Saint-Leu, canals run between the houses, and the hortillonnages, a patchwork of floating gardens, can be explored by flat-bottomed boat.

A short ride in any direction brings you to chalk plateaus, big skies and straight roads lined with poplars. The riding is flat and fast, and it is not complicated, but it has a calm rhythm, and the Somme memorials, with their rows of white headstones, are moving. The wind sweeps across the open land, and weather rolls in from the sea, so check the sky. Spring brings green fields and poppies, and autumn brings mist on the river.

Amiens has well over a hundred thousand people, so fuel, food and accommodation are no trouble. It was also the home of Jules Verne, who lived here for decades and served on the town council, and his house is a museum. For something sweet, try the macarons d'Amiens, a soft almond biscuit that has been made here for centuries. Park near the town hall, climb the belfry if it is open, and look out across the roofs to the cathedral's great spire.
t.the master of nets garden@31.3,120.6:
Suzhou has been famous for gardens for about a thousand years, and the Master-of-Nets Garden is often called the best of them, though it is among the smallest. It was first laid out in the twelfth century by a retired official and rebuilt in the eighteenth, and the name means fisherman, a modest title for a retiree who wanted to live like one. Everything is arranged to make a small plot of land feel limitless. A pond sits at the centre, with halls, pavilions and covered walkways around it, rocks piled like mountains, a zigzag bridge, and views that are framed by windows cut into walls in the shape of fans, moons and vases. One of its courtyards was copied in New York's Metropolitan Museum as the Astor Court.

The garden is part of the UNESCO listing of Classical Gardens of Suzhou. The best time to visit is early morning, before the tour groups arrive, or in the evening, when on some nights the garden hosts small performances of music and opera in the pavilions, lit by lanterns. Look at the details, the carved doors, the paving laid in patterns of pebbles, the old pines trained into shapes, and the way a single bamboo against a white wall becomes a picture.

Suzhou lies on the old Grand Canal, in the Yangtze delta, and the city is known for silk, canals and stone bridges, and for a gentle, wet climate. Riding here is not the point, and an honest account should say so. The urban roads are busy with electric scooters, taxis and buses, the lanes between the old houses are narrow, and foreign riders face a maze of licence, registration and permit rules in China, so most visitors arrive by taxi or metro. Spring, with its blossom, and autumn, with chrysanthemums and mild weather, are the most pleasant times. Summers are very humid, and a visit in plum rain season in June can mean drizzle for days.

Everything you need is within a short distance, and Suzhou is a large city of several million. The old quarter around the garden has tea houses and restaurants serving local dishes such as sweet and sour mandarin fish, crab-roe noodles and osmanthus cakes. Tickets for the garden are cheap and sometimes limited, so arrive early. The canals are best explored by boat or on foot, and a walk along Pingjiang Road in the evening, with its lanterns and waterside cafés, is a pleasant way to end the day.
t.area of city site@30.4,120.0:
Five thousand years ago, on the plain south of Lake Tai, a society built a city without metal tools. Liangzhu, now in the suburbs of Hangzhou, was a centre of a culture that carved jade into ritual objects, tubes called cong and discs called bi, and that grew rice in irrigated fields, and that built a complex water system of dams, dikes and canals, on a scale that no one expected from a Neolithic culture. UNESCO listed the Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City in 2019, and the entry covers the city walls, the palace area, the waterworks and the burial grounds of the elite.

The high dams at the mouth of the valley, to the north-west of the city, are the focus of this part of the listing. The dams held back the water from the hills, controlling floods, and the artificial lakes made a transport network and a reservoir. They were made of layers of clay and straw-wrapped earth, and they have since become low grassy ridges in the bamboo woods. You will not see towers or temples here, only low earth banks and the shape of a landscape, which is the point. The evidence is in the soil and the display halls of the museum, with its jade treasures.

The hills north-west of Hangzhou are a pleasant place, wooded with bamboo, tea bushes and small reservoirs, and the roads here are often narrow and winding, with villages of white houses. Moganshan, a summer hill resort loved by Shanghai residents a century ago, is not far, and its road climbs in tight hairpins through bamboo. As elsewhere in China, foreign riders face licence and registration hurdles, so most go by car or train. Spring brings green tea harvest, and autumn is clear. In summer, rain and humidity are heavy.

Deqing, about seventeen kilometres away, is a town of nearly ninety thousand, with fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and Hangzhou has everything else, including the West Lake and its tea houses. Try the Dragon Well tea from the hills, and dishes of river fish and bamboo shoots. The museum at Liangzhu is worth time before you visit the ruins, as it gives the context. Bring water and good walking shoes, as the site covers a large area and most exploring is done on foot or by electric cart.
t.the couple s retreat@31.3,120.6:
