The Couple's Retreat, Ou Yuan, is a small garden in the Qing style, tucked in a lane in the old quarter of Suzhou and often missed by visitors who head for the larger gardens. The name refers to its layout, which is divided into two parts, east and west, that are joined by a covered walkway, a bit like two halves of a household, and the pairing of the pavilions on each side gives the place its romantic title. It was laid out by a Qing dynasty official and is part of the UNESCO list of Classical Gardens of Suzhou.

What the garden does well is intimacy. The pond is small, the rockeries are compact, and the halls are close to each other, so that you feel more like a guest in a family house than a tourist in a monument. Windows frame views of bamboo and plum trees, with latticed patterns that cast shadows on the floor. A pavilion beside the water is a good place to sit, listen to the sounds of the neighbourhood over the walls and take in the scent of osmanthus in autumn. It is the kind of place where you can imagine a husband and wife arguing over where to put a rock.

As in the rest of Suzhou, riding is not a sensible plan for a visitor. The old streets are narrow and thick with scooters and pedestrians, and foreign riders are hampered by Chinese licence and registration rules. The best way to see the quarter is on foot, by canal boat, or by rented bicycle, and to use taxis and the metro for the rest. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, because summers are hot and sticky and winters are chilly and damp.

You are in the middle of the city, with a shop, a noodle stall or a tea house on every corner, and several million people living nearby. Fuel stations and repair shops are on the outskirts and ring roads. Try the local pastries, such as the sweet green rice balls and the small meat buns called xiaolongbao, and a pot of green tea from nearby Dongting hills. The garden is small and quiet, so visit in the morning on a weekday, and be considerate in the narrow walkways, since a crowd of tour groups makes it feel crowded.
t.routes of santiago de compostela in fran:
At the heart of Paris, beside the rue de Rivoli, stands a Gothic tower that belongs to a church that no longer exists. The Tour Saint-Jacques is all that survives of the church of Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie, built in the early sixteenth century in the flamboyant Gothic style, and it was the traditional gathering point for pilgrims leaving Paris for Santiago de Compostela in northwest Spain. The church was demolished after the Revolution, but the tower was saved, and it now stands in a small garden, topped by a statue of Saint James.

UNESCO inscribed the Routes of Santiago de Compostela in France in 1998, as a series of monuments, hospitals, churches and bridges along the four main paths that cross the country on the way to the Pyrenees. The Paris route, called the Via Turonensis because it passes through Tours, is one of the four, and it links Paris to Orléans, Tours, Poitiers, Bordeaux and the Basque country. Pilgrims have walked these roads for a thousand years, carrying a scallop shell as a badge, and many still do, with the shell hanging from their packs.

The tower itself is a pleasure to look at. It rises about fifty metres, with rich stonework, niches, gargoyles and carved saints, and on a bright day the stone seems to glow. The garden at its foot is a rare patch of calm in the middle of the city, with benches where Parisians eat their lunch. The tower is sometimes open for guided visits in summer, so check before you plan to climb.

A motorbike is a good way to cross Paris, but the city has its quirks. The centre has low-emission zone rules, which require an air-quality sticker called Crit'Air, and parking is limited, though motorbikes can often use designated spaces on the pavement edge. Traffic is dense and aggressive, the cobbles can be slippery in the rain, and tram lines and painted road markings are slick when wet. Early on a Sunday morning is a great time to ride through.

Fuel is available at stations around the ring road, but there are few in the centre, so fill up before you enter. Cafés and bakeries are everywhere.
t.the garden of cultivation@31.3,120.6:
Suzhou is a city of canals and gardens, and the Garden of Cultivation is one of the smaller and quieter examples of an art that the Chinese took to extraordinary lengths. A scholar's garden here was not simply a plot of flowers. It was a miniature world, a landscape of rocks, water, trees, pavilions and walls, arranged to suggest mountains and rivers and to make a visitor feel they had stepped out of the city. UNESCO listed the classical gardens of Suzhou in 1997, adding more in 2000.

The Ming dynasty, in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, saw many of these gardens built by retired officials and wealthy merchants, who used them for poetry, painting, music, tea and conversation. Their design follows careful principles: no single view should be seen all at once, paths twist, windows frame scenes, and pools reflect the sky. Walking through, you pass through moon gates, zigzag bridges and covered corridors, and every turn is a new composition.

The city around the gardens is large, with over five million people, and Suzhou has a long history as a centre of silk production and scholarship. Old canals still run through the centre, with white-walled houses and stone bridges, and boats glide past in the early morning mist. The old saying is that there is heaven above and Suzhou and Hangzhou below.

A word of honesty about riding. In Chinese cities, motorcycles are heavily restricted, and many cities ban them in central areas. Foreign riders usually need special permits and licensing, so riding here is not a casual matter. Most visitors get around by metro, bus or taxi, and the gardens are best explored on foot in any case. Fuel and food are plentiful in the city, and local dishes include sweet and sour mandarin fish and noodles with a clear, delicate broth. Come early in the morning to enjoy a garden before the tour groups arrive, and in spring or autumn, when the weather is mild. Take your time, and sit for a while in a pavilion.
t.the humble administrator s garden@31.3,1:
Wang Xianchen was a retired imperial official who, around 1509, in the Ming dynasty, bought a piece of marshy land in Suzhou and made a garden. He named it after a line in an ancient essay about how a humble man can learn to govern his own small plot, and the name has a modest, ironic ring: the Humble Administrator's Garden is the largest in Suzhou, covering about five hectares, and is regarded as one of the finest in China. It belongs to the group of classical Suzhou gardens that UNESCO inscribed in 1997.

Water is the heart of the design. Pools, streams and lotus ponds cover about three-fifths of the area, and pavilions and covered walkways stand on the edge or on islands, so that you move through a landscape of reflections. A zigzag bridge crosses the water, a hall for viewing lotus faces the central pond, and the surrounding rocks, bamboo and pine trees are arranged like a painting, with views framed by round and hexagonal windows. The effect is of a large country estate shrunk into a city block.

The garden had many owners, passing from the original family to a gambler, then to officials and merchants, and for a time it served as a rebel palace in the nineteenth century. Today it is one of the most visited places in the city, and in peak season, it is crowded, so go early, on a weekday and in spring or autumn. The azaleas in April and the lotus in July are the high points.

Riding is not really part of a visit to Suzhou, since motorcycles are restricted in the city centre, and foreign riders face licensing barriers. The best way to travel is by metro, bus or taxi, and the old centre is compact enough to walk. Fuel and food are no problem, and the city has a rich cuisine, from noodles and dumplings to the sweet, slightly sour flavours of Jiangsu cooking. Bring water and a hat in summer, and allow at least two hours for the garden. Tea is served in a teahouse by the pond, and it is pleasant to sit there for a while.
t.the lion forest garden@31.3,120.6:
If you want to know why Chinese gardens love rocks, go to the Lion Forest Garden. Built in 1342, during the Yuan dynasty, by monks of a Buddhist monastery in Suzhou in honour of their teacher, it is famous for its rockery, a maze of grey limestone from Lake Tai, twisted into peaks, caves and tunnels, some of which are said to resemble lions. The artist Ni Zan, a celebrated painter of the period, is said to have helped with the design. The garden is part of the Suzhou group inscribed by UNESCO in 1997.

The rock maze is the main event. Paths wind through it, rising and falling, passing through tunnels and over little bridges, so that in a small area you can walk quite a distance and get pleasantly lost. Children love it. The best way to see it is without hurrying, pausing to notice the shapes. Seeing the lions depends on your imagination, and the guides will be glad to help.

The garden later passed into private hands, and in the twentieth century, it belonged to the family of the architect I. M. Pei, who was born in China and whose relatives owned the property for a time. It was given to the state in the 1950s and restored. Around it, the buildings are typical of the late imperial period, with whitewashed walls, dark tiles and carved wooden windows, and a pond with a pavilion and a small boat-shaped hall.

Suzhou is a large, prosperous city and its streets are busy. In China, motorcycle use is limited in city centres, and foreign riders face licensing and registration obstacles, so getting around by metro, taxi or on foot is much more practical, and the garden is a short distance from the centre. Fuel, food and rooms are all easy to find. Local specialities include squirrel-shaped mandarin fish and crab roe dumplings, and tea houses offer a quiet place to rest. Visit early on a weekday, in spring or autumn, and give yourself time to explore the rockery. Mist or light rain makes the stones look wonderful.
t.maisons la roche et jeanneret@48.9,2.3:
In the sixteenth arrondissement of Paris, tucked into a quiet cul-de-sac off the Square du Docteur-Blanche, stand two white houses that changed how people thought about living. The Maisons La Roche et Jeanneret were designed by Le Corbusier and his cousin Pierre Jeanneret in the mid 1920s, one for a Swiss banker and art collector, Raoul La Roche, and one for Jeanneret's brother, a musician. Today the building houses the Fondation Le Corbusier, and the interiors, with their ramps, flat roofs, ribbon windows and rather austere palette, are open to visitors on certain days, so check the schedule before you go.

The coordinates sit on the edge of the Bois de Boulogne side of the city, closer to Boulogne-Billancourt than the middle of Paris, which tells you something about how the day will go. This is urban riding at its most stop-and-go: Périphérique access, traffic lights, buses, delivery vans and scooters weaving in every direction. Any bike without an easy clutch will make you regret it by the second kilometre. Parking for motorcycles is better than for cars, with marked two-wheeler bays in much of the city, but the streets near the villa are narrow and residential, and I would not leave anything valuable strapped to the pillion.

You do not come to this place for the riding. You come for the architecture, and for the odd sense of a stage set from a hundred years ago that still looks modern. The quiet of the street, at least on a weekday morning, is a pleasant contrast to the busy avenues around. Auteuil, which surrounds it, is old Paris money, with art nouveau gems by Hector Guimard scattered through the neighbourhood, and the Roland-Garros tennis stadium is a few minutes away if you want to add some sport to your day.

For petrol, food and coffee you are well served in Boulogne-Billancourt, a big town of over a hundred thousand, and in the countless Paris cafés. The best advice is to arrive early before the traffic builds, take a long look at the white façade, and then leave Paris eastbound before the afternoon rush shuts every road in the city.
The Côte de Beaune and the Côte de Nuits are two ridges of gentle limestone, barely a hundred metres above the plain of the Saône, and they hold some of the most expensive agricultural land on earth. The phrase Les Climats du vignoble de Bourgogne refers to the small named vineyard plots, each with its own character of soil and exposure, that Burgundians have mapped and cultivated for centuries; the monks of Cluny and Cîteaux did much of the early work, noticing that wine from one plot tasted different from the next and writing it down. UNESCO recognised the whole system as a cultural landscape, and driving through it you can see why, because the walled vineyards, stone huts and village squares are all part of the same story.

Here, near Ladoix-Serrigny and Savigny-lès-Beaune, you are at the northern end of the Côte de Beaune, a few kilometres from the town of Beaune itself. The riding is the real draw. The D974, the old Route des Grands Crus, runs along the foot of the slope, and the smaller lanes weave up into the villages and between the vines. Nothing is steep, nothing is demanding; it is gentle, slow, and best taken at the speed of someone reading the labels on the wall plaques. Corners are soft, surfaces mostly good, and in September and October the harvest brings tractors and grape pickers onto every road, so you will be patient or you will be stuck.

There are no famous views in the Alpine sense, just the long green or golden stripe of vines on the slope, the red-tiled roofs of the villages and the occasional church spire. Spring brings the first bright green and sometimes frost fires among the vines, and autumn turns the whole hill to rust and copper. Summer is hot and bright; winter is quiet and grey.

Beaune, a town of about twenty-four thousand, has fuel, supermarkets and plenty of restaurants, and the Hospices de Beaune, with its glazed polychrome roof tiles, is one of the sights of eastern France and well worth an hour. The wine auction there each November is famous. The little villages you pass through have cellars that offer tastings, but remember that you are on a bike, and the only sensible approach is a single small glass or a bottle strapped on for later. Burgundy's food is rich and slow: boeuf bourguignon, gougères, poached eggs in red wine sauce, and the local snails.
t.cro de granville@45.0,1.0:
The Cro de Granville is a rock shelter in the Dordogne, near Rouffignac-Saint-Cernin, in the part of south-west France where the limestone plateaus are riddled with caves, shelters and overhangs and where early humans lived and painted for tens of thousands of years. I will be honest and say I do not know the details of this specific site, so I will not pretend to a guided tour, but the landscape around it I can describe from the road: this is the Périgord Noir, named for the dark oak and evergreen woods that cover the hills, and the Vézère valley a few kilometres to the south is the cradle of French prehistory, with Lascaux, Font-de-Gaume, Les Eyzies and the rest all within easy reach.

The nearest places you can count on are Rouffignac, a village of about fifteen hundred people, and Le Bugue, about eleven kilometres away, with a little under three thousand. Both have bakeries, a few cafés and basic supplies, but for proper fuel and supermarkets the larger town is Boulazac, near Périgueux, some twenty kilometres off. If the tank is low, fill it before you wander into the back lanes, because the plateau between the valleys is thinly settled and some of the pumps in the villages are automatic card-only machines.

The riding in this area is lovely in a way that sneaks up on you. The roads are narrow country departmentals, with gentle undulations, tight little bends through chestnut woods, and sudden open views over walnut orchards, maize fields and honey-coloured farmhouses. Surfaces vary, with patched tarmac and the occasional gravel patch on the smaller lanes, and farm vehicles are common, especially in late summer. The Vézère and Dordogne valleys are pretty roads in their own right, flat and fast along the river and busy with canoeists and caravans in July and August.

Food is a major part of the day here. This is duck, goose, walnut and truffle country, with foie gras, confit and cèpes on every menu, and the markets in the small towns are worth a detour on the right day. The Dordogne in high summer can be very crowded around the big cave sites, which often require timed tickets booked in advance, so check Lascaux IV and Rouffignac's own cave, which is visited by little electric train, before you commit to a schedule. May, June and September are the best months, when the light is warm and the roads are clear.
t.bajawa@-8.8,121.0:
Bajawa is a cool highland town in the middle of Flores, and the first thing the body notices is the temperature. You arrive from the sticky coast and climb to around eleven hundred metres, where evenings need a jacket and the air smells of woodsmoke and clove. The town sits in a bowl at the foot of Mount Inerie, a graceful volcano of over two thousand metres whose cone dominates the southern skyline, and its slopes are covered in coffee, vegetables and clove trees. This is the heartland of the Ngada people, whose villages of thatched houses, ancestral shrines and megalithic stones lie within an hour or two of the town.

The Trans-Flores Highway is the reason most people come by motorbike, and it is a great road, though not an easy one. It winds along the spine of the island through rainforest, rice terraces, volcanic craters and fishing villages, hair-pinning up and over ridge after ridge, and you rarely get more than a few hundred metres of straight tarmac. The surface can be broken by landslides, potholes and rain, trucks and buses come round blind corners well over the middle line, and the pace is rarely more than forty kilometres an hour, so a day's progress is shorter than the map suggests. Ride in daylight, as dusk comes fast and the roads are unlit, and expect afternoon rain, especially from November to March.

Bajawa itself is a real town, with petrol stations, markets, small hotels and warungs where you can get rice, grilled chicken and strong local coffee. Flores arabica is well regarded, and the beans are grown at just this kind of altitude. Fill up in town before heading east or west, because the long stretches between villages have only roadside bottles of petrol on sale from small stalls, which are best used only in emergency.

Close by lie traditional villages such as Bena and Luba, where rows of houses face a central yard of stones, with carved poles known as ngadhu and little thatched shrines called bhaga standing for male and female ancestors. They are lived-in places, not museums, so ask before photographing people and expect a small donation to be requested at the entrance. Portuguese traders and Dominican priests left a Catholic imprint, and you will see churches, crosses and rosaries in a country that is mostly Muslim.

Hot springs near Soa and the black-sand beaches of the south coast give good reasons to stay a night or two.
t.moret sur loing@48.4,2.8:
Moret-sur-Loing is what an impressionist painter would have ordered if asked for a small medieval town. It sits on a quiet bend of the river Loing, where an old stone bridge with a mill arches over the water, and the whole composition, with a church tower, reflections and drifting willow, is the one that Alfred Sisley painted again and again after settling here in the 1880s. He is buried in the local cemetery. The town was fortified in the Middle Ages, and two great gates, the Porte de Samois and the Porte de Bourgogne, still stand at the ends of the main street, which runs between them past old houses and tiny courtyards.

It also has a sweet claim to fame. Moret's sugar of the Sisters, a hard, golden barley sugar sold in little twisted sticks, was invented by nuns here in the seventeenth century, and you can still buy it in the town, in tins, with an old-fashioned label. A few hundred metres away at Saint-Mammès, the Loing meets the Seine, and barges laden with grain, sand and containers pass through the locks, so the water stop there is full of working boats rather than pleasure craft.

The surrounding countryside is particularly pleasing. Moret sits on the edge of the Forest of Fontainebleau, a huge royal hunting forest of oak and beech with sandstone boulders scattered through it, and the roads in and out are shady, with gentle bends and not much traffic during the week. The surface is generally good, though forestry lorries and cyclists share the lanes, and weekends are busier. Early morning, with mist on the river, is the best time. In spring the woods are fresh and green, and in autumn they turn copper.

For practicalities, a town with a few thousand inhabitants has bakeries, a supermarket and a couple of cafes beside the river, and the neighbouring Veneux-les-Sablons has fuel and bigger shops. There is a public tap and benches near the bridge, which makes it a convenient water stop. It is also a useful half-day escape from Paris, easily combined with a loop through the forest and the castle at Fontainebleau.
t.loire castle edge tour@49.1,1.1:
The Loire is nowhere near here. These coordinates put you in Normandy, on the plateau of the Eure department a few kilometres from Évreux, among villages such as Normanville, Aviron and Claville. This is a country of big arable fields, beech copses and long sightlines, with flint and half-timbered houses in the villages. In the late afternoon it has the soft, silvery light that painters followed here, and there is nearly always some weather moving through the sky.

Évreux, eleven kilometres away with nearly fifty-eight thousand people, is the place for fuel, supplies and a proper meal. It is a town that was badly bruised in the Second World War, so much of it is rebuilt, but the cathedral of Notre-Dame survived in good part and still shows the glass and stonework of centuries, and the fifteenth-century belfry that stands apart from it is a fine landmark. The little river Iton runs through town in channels, giving it unexpected quiet corners. A short ride away, the Château de Navarre, built for a duke in the seventeenth century, was later home to Empress Joséphine after her divorce from Napoleon.

The riding on this plateau is relaxed. Roads are mostly straight with gentle bends, sometimes a surprise dip into a wooded valley, and traffic is light on country roads. Normandy weather is changeable, so expect a shower even on a good day, and the tarmac can be slick on the farm roads where tractors carry mud. Agricultural traffic is heavy at harvest and in beet season. Cider and Calvados are the local drinks, and a decent bakery turns up in nearly every village, so a food stop is easy.

Keep an eye on the sky and the fields. Buzzards sit on fence posts, and in autumn mist lies in the hollows at first light. May to September is the best period, with long days and pleasant temperatures, though a morning ride in October, with red leaves and low sun, is a quiet pleasure of its own.
t.alpe d huez and oisans@45.6,4.6:
Alpe d'Huez is far away, a good two hours to the southeast, so put that label aside. This point is on the western edge of the Monts du Lyonnais, the rolling hill country that rises behind Lyon, near Saint-Martin-en-Haut, Saint-Didier-sous-Riverie and Larajasse, with Mornant as the nearest sizeable town at about seven kilometres. It is a landscape of orchards, pastures and small woods on hills of about seven or eight hundred metres, with farms scattered along the ridges and church spires poking out of every valley.

The Monts du Lyonnais are fruit country. Cherries ripen in early summer, apples and pears later, and the villages host fairs and markets through the season. It is also a place where Lyon goes for weekend walks and meals, so some of the village restaurants are better than you would expect. The hills catch the weather coming from the Massif Central, so they can be cool and misty when Lyon is warm and sunny, and in winter they sometimes carry a dusting of snow. To the south, the Pilat massif rises to over 1,400 metres, a darker line against the sky.

As a fuel gate, the logic is straightforward. Mornant has just over five thousand people and stations, and it is a sensible place to fill the tank before heading into the hills. Smaller villages such as Saint-Martin-en-Haut have a handful of shops and bars but cannot be relied on for fuel at all hours. Plan your top-up on the plain, and in the morning take coffee in a village bakery, where the first croissants are out by seven.

The riding is lovely and unpretentious. Roads are narrow, winding and well maintained, with mid-speed bends and short steep climbs, and traffic is light except on summer weekends when cyclists swarm over the hills. Watch for gravel at farm entrances and mud on the road after rain. Morning mist often fills the valleys, with the ridges sticking out of it like islands. May and June, when the orchards are in bloom or the cherries are red, and October, when the forests turn, are the loveliest seasons.
t.alpe d huez and oisans high point@45.6,4:
Chazelles-sur-Lyon is the place that gives this spot its flavour. The town was once the hat-making capital of France, and its hat museum tells the story of the factories that turned out felt hats for much of the world. The coordinates sit just outside it, in the rolling countryside of the Monts du Lyonnais, with Saint-Symphorien-sur-Coise and Aveizieux nearby, and Saint-Galmier a few kilometres to the west. Nothing about it is Alpine, and the label of a famous Alpe d'Huez climb is simply misleading.

Saint-Galmier is the town to remember. It is where Badoit sparkling water comes from, bottled here since the nineteenth century, and you can see the source and the factory. The mineral water of the Forez has been drunk for centuries, and the taste is slightly salty, with fine bubbles. The town also has an old centre with a handsome church and some pleasant cafés, and its size, with about five and a half thousand people, means it has fuel and shops. If you need a stop in the area, it is the best bet.

The terrain here is ridge and valley, with fields on the plateaus and woods in the clefts. The high point of the label is a modest rise, but on clear days you see the Forez mountains to the west, and in the east, over the Rhône valley, the line of the Alps with Mont Blanc occasionally visible in very clear winter air. The roads are narrow, curvy and quiet, and the best are the minor departmental ones that follow the contours between villages.

The weather can be changeable. Cool air comes off the hills in the evening, and fog lies in the valleys in autumn. Cyclists use these roads a lot, and in summer you will often be following a peloton around a bend. The surface is generally sound, though farm vehicles leave mud and straw. A good ride starts with fuel in Saint-Galmier or Chazelles, and ends with a long dinner in a village. Spring, with cherry blossom, and early autumn are the best.
t.alpe d huez and oisans scenic road@46.0,:
Between the broad valley of the Saône and the first ponds of the Dombes lies this stretch of flat farmland, with the villages of Chaleins, Francheleins and Villeneuve close by and Jassans-Riottier, almost a suburb of Villefranche-sur-Saône, a few kilometres south. The river is the dominating fact. The Saône is a slow, wide, green stream, one of the lazier rivers in France, and the country beside it is low and fertile, with poplars, hay meadows and the occasional heron standing in a ditch.

To the west, across the water, rise the hills of the Beaujolais, with vineyards, stone villages and a long wooded crest. Villefranche, the Beaujolais capital, has a long main street with houses hiding courtyards and passages called traboules, and wine bars where you can try the local Gamay. To the east, a plateau of mixed fields and woods leads up into the Dombes, a country of more than a thousand artificial ponds, built largely in the Middle Ages for fish farming. The ponds are still worked, with carp and tench raised and harvested in rotation, and they draw huge numbers of birds.

Fuel is simple. Jassans-Riottier, with nearly six thousand people, has stations, and Villefranche is larger and has everything. The coordinates themselves are in a rural area, so do not rely on anything close by. Food in the Saône valley is traditional, with frogs' legs from the Dombes, river fish and the sausages of Lyon. A lunch in a village inn costs a fair amount less than in the city and often tastes better.

On the road, the land is flat and the riding gentle, with long straights and plenty of tractor traffic. Wind is a consideration, and early morning mist can hang over the river and the ponds until nine or ten. In summer the heat reflects off the fields, and swarms of insects gather at dusk, so a visor is a good idea. For a more varied ride, cross the Saône at Villefranche and climb into the Beaujolais hills, where the roads are twistier and the views wider. Late May and September are best.
t.mont ventoux long south day@45.2,4.9:
Wine country starts here. The coordinates sit in the Rhône valley's northern Drôme, just inland from the river near Saint-Uze, Beausemblant and Saint-Barthélemy-de-Vals, with Tain-l'Hermitage the closest sizeable town at seventeen kilometres. Mont Ventoux, named in the label, is a hundred kilometres or more to the south, so this is a different corner altogether, a land of low hills and orchards, apricot trees and vineyards, with the Rhône's broad valley visible to the west.

Tain-l'Hermitage gives the area its reputation. Above the town, a steep terraced hill of granite, the Hermitage, produces some of the most prized Syrah wines in the world, named after a hermit who is said to have lived on the slope in the thirteenth century. The vineyards of Crozes-Hermitage spread around it, and are easier to find in a shop. Tain also houses a famous chocolate maker, whose factory has a visitor centre, so a break in the town is rewarded. Fuel and supermarkets are easy to find, and the town has some good bakeries.

A little inland from this point lies the Palais Idéal at Hauterives, one of the strangest buildings in France. It was built by a rural postman, Ferdinand Cheval, who began collecting stones on his rounds in 1879 and spent more than thirty years building a fantasy palace by hand. Its walls are covered in sculpted animals, grottoes, towers and inscriptions, and it was admired by Surrealists and later declared a national monument. It is an extraordinary thing to find in a quiet village, and a perfect reason to stop.

The roads here are quiet, narrow and well-surfaced, with gentle curves between orchards, and the hills around Saint-Uze have some modest climbs. The mistral blows down the Rhône valley from time to time, so wind can be strong on exposed stretches. Summer is hot, with temperatures reaching the mid-thirties in July, and the best seasons are April to June, when the blossom is out, and September, when the grape harvest begins and the air smells sweet.
t.paris ile de france escapes@49.5,2.3:
Beauvais, with its unfinished cathedral, is the real draw of this stretch of Picardy, about fifteen kilometres away, and the coordinates sit in the green valley of the Thérain river close to the villages of Bresles, Wavignies and Bailleul-sur-Thérain. The area is chalk plateau and river valley, with big fields of wheat and sugar beet on the heights and woods and meadows along the water. It lies about eighty kilometres north of Paris, and for people from the capital it is a quiet, flat place to ride out to for lunch.

The cathedral of Saint-Pierre in Beauvais is one of the strangest in France. The medieval builders wanted to make the tallest Gothic choir in the world, and reached almost forty-eight metres in the thirteenth century, but part of it collapsed in 1284 and had to be rebuilt. In 1573 the tall central tower fell as well, and the nave was never finished. The result is a soaring, lopsided building that is still astonishing from the outside, with an astronomical clock inside that is a marvel of nineteenth-century engineering. The town also has a tapestry manufactory, founded in the seventeenth century, that still produces work for the state.

The label here is swim, but I would not promise anything. Beauvais has lakes and the Thérain has some quiet stretches, but bathing places in this part of the Oise are limited, so ask locally. Fuel and supermarkets are easy to find in Saint-Just-en-Chaussée, about eleven kilometres away, and in Beauvais itself, with plenty of choice. Bresles is small and quiet, and has a few shops.

The riding is relaxed, with long straight roads and gentle bends, though the plateau can be windy and the farm traffic heavy at harvest. In autumn, mist fills the valleys and the sugar beet lorries leave mud on the road. A spring ride, with yellow rapeseed fields under a blue sky, is lovely, and so is a calm September morning. It is not a place for adrenaline, more a pleasant day with a good lunch and a church or two.
Gisors is the town to know, six kilometres from these coordinates, a place that has spent a thousand years guarding a frontier. The little river Epte, which flows nearby, was the boundary between the Kingdom of France and the Duchy of Normandy after the treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, which in 911 allowed the Viking chief Rollo to settle his followers in the lower Seine valley. The villages of Neaufles-Saint-Martin and Bézu-Saint-Éloi sit on the Norman side, and the rolling country is Vexin, a plateau of chalk and orchards with long views.

The castle of Gisors is a fine example of a Norman fortress, built in the twelfth century on an artificial mound, with a polygonal keep rising above the town. English and French kings fought for it, and it changed hands several times. A legend that Templar treasure was hidden under the castle drew treasure seekers in the twentieth century, and a man who dug beneath it in the 1940s claimed to have found chambers, a story that still gets repeated in the local bars. Neaufles-Saint-Martin has its own castle ruin, with a tall round keep that you can see from the road.

The label talks of the forest of Fontainebleau, which is far south of here, and the Loing, which is south as well. Ignore it. What you have is a quiet stretch of Normandy that is ideal for a food stop. Gisors, with over twelve thousand people, has bakeries, cafés and supermarkets, and fuel stations on the main roads. The area is known for apples and cider, and for dairy, so a lunch with a local cheese is easy to find.

The roads here are narrow and winding, with some pleasant bends where they dip into the Epte valley. The surface is generally good, and traffic is light except on summer weekends. Fog and mist are common in autumn, and the plateau can be windy. In spring the orchards bloom white and pink, and in September the apples are ripe. A slow morning ride, with a coffee in Gisors and a walk around the castle, is a good way to spend a day.
t.route napoleon weekend@46.1,4.5:
Far from the Alps, in the green hills of the Beaujolais north-west of Lyon, the little town of Lamure-sur-Azergues lies along a narrow valley with the river Azergues running through it. Grandris and Le Perréon are nearby villages, and the nearest town of any size, Gleizé, is nineteen kilometres away, so this is true backcountry. The label mentions the Route Napoléon, which lies far to the south-east, and has nothing to do with this district.

The hills here are steep and wooded, with chestnut, oak and Douglas fir on the slopes, and fields of cattle and small vineyards on the sunnier faces. Not far to the north-west rises the Mont Saint-Rigaud, the highest summit of the Rhône department at just over a thousand metres, a rounded forested peak with a lookout tower and long views over the Beaujolais and toward the Saône and the Alps. The roads that climb it are narrow and twisty, with a few steep hairpins and shady bends where leaves lie thick in autumn.

The Beaujolais is a wine region of the Gamay grape, and the southern half is famous for its fruity, light reds, drunk young. Every year on the third Thursday of November the new vintage, Beaujolais Nouveau, is released with a great deal of fuss. In the northern part, the villages of Fleurie, Juliénas and Moulin-à-Vent produce more serious wines that can age for years, and they are a good reason to bring a bag with a bit of spare room, if you are not too fussy about weight.

Fuel here is the issue, because small valley villages seldom have pumps that work at all hours. Gleizé and Villefranche-sur-Saône are the safe options, and Tarare to the west is another. Plan to fill up before the hills, and carry a little spare range. Food is hearty, in the Lyonnais tradition, with andouillette, quenelles, salads with bacon and pink pralines in the sweets. The cooking is generous and the portions large. In summer, the hills are warm and green, in October the vineyards turn red and gold, and in winter, snow occasionally closes the higher roads.
The Pilat regional park is the hill country south-west of Vienne, rising from the Rhône valley to a long ridge of nearly fourteen hundred metres, and these coordinates are on its eastern side, just above the river, close to Pélussin, Maclas and Chavanay. The Rhône itself, in its broad valley below, is visible from the heights, and on a clear day you can see the Alps, a white line far to the east. The landscape is steep and green, with chestnut woods, apricot orchards and terraced vineyards on the lower slopes.

The vineyards of the Rhône's northern bank produce some of France's great wines. At Condrieu, the Viognier grape gives a rich, perfumed white wine, and at Chavanay the Saint-Joseph appellation yields lively reds from Syrah. Farther north, the slopes of Côte-Rôtie are so steep that they must be worked by hand. Pélussin, a town of about three and a half thousand people, is the centre of the district, with a market, bakeries and a few restaurants, and it also has a station for fuel.

For a rider, the Pilat has some wonderful roads. The ascent from Pélussin towards the ridge, past the Crêt de l'Oeillon with its chapel and cross, is steep and twisty with fine views, and the high road along the ridge from the Col de l'Oeillon to the Col du Grand Bois offers long, flowing bends through woods and pastures. The highest point of the park, the Crêt de la Perdrix, at 1,432 metres, is a short walk from the road. The weather on the heights is often cool and windy, and fog can come in quickly, so carry a spare layer.

The people of the Pilat are famed for their produce, with chestnuts, cheeses, apricots and cured sausages, and the villages serve hearty food. The Rhône valley below is hot in summer and often hazy, and the climate on the hills is cooler. Spring brings blossom and fresh green, and autumn brings the chestnut harvest and the smell of woodsmoke. Winter can bring ice and snow to the heights, so check conditions before setting off. A morning on these roads is something you will remember.
t.annecy bauges loop@45.9,4.4:
Tarare is a town of about eleven thousand people four kilometres from this point, in the hills west of Lyon where the Beaujolais gives way to the Monts du Tarare, and the road here is the old and busy route that links Lyon with Roanne and the Loire. The label names Annecy and the Bauges, which are far to the east in Savoy, so forget them. What you have is a green, damp, rather unglamorous corner of the Rhône department, with fir plantations, pasture, textile towns and long grey roofs, and it is a very good place to fill a tank before riding off into the middle of France.

The town's history is cloth. Tarare grew rich on muslin, the fine light cotton fabric that was woven and embroidered here for the luxury trade, and its name became attached to the stuff in several languages. The big mills along the river are mostly quiet now, but the town still has the stately mill-owners' houses and a feeling of former fortune. Nearby Violay is a smaller place on the edge of the Forez, and its name will be familiar to anyone who has driven the autoroute between Lyon and Clermont-Ferrand, because the motorway disappears into a long tunnel under the hills there.

For riders, the old road is the point. Before the motorway, the climb west out of Tarare over the Col des Sauvages was a famous obstacle for lorries and holiday traffic alike, and its bends and long gradients are still enjoyable now that most of the traffic has gone underground. The surface is mostly good, and the road gets wet and misty in the hills.

Practical business here is simple. Tarare has stations, supermarkets and bakeries, and it is the best place for a proper stop. In the smaller villages the pump might be closed by early evening. Food is Lyonnais in spirit, so expect andouillette, pork in many shapes, and a pichet of local red. Weather on these hills can be cooler and wetter than in Lyon, so a waterproof layer belongs in the bag. Autumn mist and gold are lovely.
t.annecy bauges loop high point@45.9,4.1:
Balbigny lies on the Loire in the northern end of the Forez plain, six kilometres from this point, and the little river-valley towns round about, Neulise and Saint-Germain-Laval, are all part of the same broad, flat, farmed basin. The label claims a high point near Annecy, but Annecy is far away, and what you have here is rolling land between the Monts du Lyonnais on the east and the long dark wall of the Forez mountains on the west. Anything over four hundred and fifty metres looks like a summit in this country, and the views reach a long way.

The Loire is the great fact. Here it is still a young river, wide and grey-green with gravel banks, flowing north to curve around the Massif Central before it turns west to the Atlantic. Some twenty kilometres downstream it enters the gorges at Villerest, a chain of reservoirs and wooded cliffs. In the plain itself the water meadows are home to herons, kingfishers and, in winter, flocks of waders. A scatter of ponds across the Forez, many of them medieval, adds to the birdlife.

Feurs, sixteen kilometres away, has about eight thousand people and is the sensible town for fuel and a proper meal. It was a Roman town, Forum Segusiavorum, the market of the Segusiavi tribe, and it still has a small museum of its past. In between, Balbigny and Neulise are smaller but have bakeries and a bar, and a pump here or there for local farmers.

The riding is relaxed, with straight roads over fields and gentle bends along the river, and the feeling is of an open and uncrowded country. Wind from the north can be annoying, and in autumn thick fog sits on the plain until late morning. In winter the tops of the Monts du Lyonnais can be icy. On a clear day in spring, with the Forez hills still white on the tops and the plain green, it is a very beautiful place to roll along. Cattle and hay are the local business, and you will meet a few tractors.
t.bugey lakes and jura edge photo pull off:
Marcigny is three kilometres from here, a small town on the Loire at the heart of the Brionnais, the hilly cattle country of southern Burgundy. The label talks of the Bugey lakes and the Jura edge, which belong to a different part of France, so it helps to think of this as Charolais land: rolling green pastures, hedges, oak trees, and in nearly every field a herd of the big, creamy white cattle that give their name to the breed. There is something comfortable about the way they stand and watch you pass.

The Brionnais is also the Romanesque heartland of Burgundy, and the villages hide some of the finest twelfth-century churches in France. Semur-en-Brionnais, a short distance away, has a collegiate church with a superb octagonal tower and a hilltop castle where Saint Hugh of Cluny was born. Anzy-le-Duc has a carved porch and a pure interior, and the basilica of Paray-le-Monial, to the east, is a scaled-down version of the great abbey church of Cluny. Marcigny itself was the site of a priory founded in the eleventh century by Cluny for women, among them noblewomen who had left the world.

Fuel and food are simple matters. Marcigny has fuel, a few cafés and a bakery, and the larger town of Paray-le-Monial, about fifteen kilometres away, has plenty of everything. The Saturday and weekday markets, as in so many French country towns, are better than the restaurants. The local dish is beef, of course, usually grilled or in a sauce, with Burgundy wine to go with it. Close to the river, a small aerodrome at Saint-Yan hosts flying clubs and the odd noisy airshow.

The riding is leisurely. Roads wind through the hills in gentle bends, with few cars and plenty of farm gates, and the surface is generally sound. The Loire itself is broad and sandy, with willows along the banks, and on a warm day a quiet spot by the water makes a good place to rest the bike. Spring, when the meadows are full of flowers, and early autumn are lovely. In summer, thunderstorms can roll in quickly from the west, so keep an eye on the sky.
t.provins medieval ridge loop@49.2,3.6:
Fère-en-Tardenois is four kilometres from this point, the main village of the Tardenois, a rolling plateau of woods and fields in the south of the Aisne department. The label says Provins, a medieval town far to the south-west, but this is a different country entirely, a quiet one of cereal farms and beech woods about a hundred kilometres from Paris. For a food stop, the village is the right size, with bakeries, a small market and a few cafés, and it has the added benefit of a ruined castle that is one of the best surprises in the district.

The Château de Fère is a ruined fortress of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, but its most remarkable piece is a sixteenth-century stone viaduct, built by Constable Anne de Montmorency, which carries a gallery across the moat on tall arches. It stands in woods outside the village, and it is easy to walk to. The ruined keep and the arches have a rather romantic air, and the whole is surrounded by old trees. A hotel in the grounds makes use of the setting.

A few kilometres away, at Seringes-et-Nesles, lies the Oise-Aisne American Cemetery, where more than six thousand American soldiers of the First World War are buried in neat rows of white crosses on a gentle slope. It is beautifully kept and quietly moving, and visitors are welcome. The wheat fields and woods around it saw severe fighting in the summer of 1918 during the second battle of the Marne, and the contrast with the present calm is difficult to ignore.

The riding in the Tardenois is gentle, with long, quiet roads that wind through woods and fields and some pleasant dips into small valleys. Traffic is light, and the surface is usually sound, though winter frost can break the edges. Mist is common on autumn mornings, and in late spring the whole district smells of rape and hay. Fuel is easiest in Fère itself or in Fismes, thirteen kilometres to the east. A pleasant day here has no schedule at all.
t.vallee de l eure easy scenic@48.8,2.0:
The new town of Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines surrounds this point, a planned city of nearly forty thousand people in Montigny-le-Bretonneux alone, set up from the 1970s on the plateau south-west of Versailles. It is the opposite of a country hamlet, a place of roundabouts, offices, lakes and careful lawns, and the label of a gentle valley of the Eure is misleading, since that river runs thirty kilometres further south-west. A ride that begins here is a ride that begins in modern France, and the first job is to get out of it.

Fuel is no problem at all. Voisins-le-Bretonneux and Montigny have plenty of stations, supermarkets and cafés, and this is exactly the kind of place to start a day with a full tank and a decent breakfast. There is a national velodrome here, where Olympic cyclists train, and a large lake, the Étang de Saint-Quentin, which is a nature reserve with a good bird population. It is a surprising pocket of wild wetland in the middle of the suburbs.

Just south-east of the town, in the valley of the Chevreuse, lies the abbey of Port-Royal des Champs, now mostly ruins and a museum. It was the centre of Jansenism, a stern movement within French Catholicism, in the seventeenth century, and Blaise Pascal and Jean Racine were associated with it. Louis XIV had it destroyed in 1710, and the quiet meadows where it stood are now a place for walkers. Versailles itself, a short ride north, needs no introduction, and the park is lovely early in the day.

Once out of town, the riding opens up. The roads into the valley of the Chevreuse are narrow and wooded, with tight bends and old stone walls, and they lead through villages of thatched or tiled roofs. On weekends, they are busy with Parisians on bicycles and in sports cars, so a weekday is better. In winter the roads can be damp and slippery. Spring and autumn offer the best light, and a ride from here toward Rambouillet and its forest is a good long day.
t.vallee de l eure easy scenic@48.5,1.9:
Saint-Arnoult-en-Yvelines is five kilometres from this point, and with Sonchamp and Ablis it marks the south-western corner of the Yvelines, where the woods of the Rambouillet forest stop and the grain plain of the Beauce begins. The label talks of the Eure valley, which is further west, but this is the best part of the day anyway, a place to eat before the long open roads. Saint-Arnoult is a town of nearly six thousand people, enough to have bakeries, cafés and a petrol station, and it sits among oaks and chestnuts that were once royal hunting ground.

The Beauce is one of the great granaries of Europe, a plateau of deep silt soil that stretches south and west towards Chartres and Orléans, so flat and so open that the spire of a cathedral can be seen from thirty kilometres away. A little to the east lies the Hurepoix, a countryside of small woods and valleys. Ablis stands on the old road between Paris and Orléans, which carried coaches and mail for centuries, and a handful of old inns recall that time. The cooking around here is plain and good, with roast chicken, sausage and potatoes.

The forest of Rambouillet, to the north, is the real attraction for a rider. Its roads wind through oak and hornbeam, with few buildings, and in the early morning you may see deer crossing and hear woodpeckers. It was the favourite hunting forest of French kings, and the château at Rambouillet, where the presidents of the Republic sometimes host meetings, stands on its edge. A morning in the forest followed by lunch in a village makes a perfect rhythm.

Wind is the thing to watch in the Beauce. It blows freely across the flat fields and can lean a bike over on the straight roads, particularly in winter and spring, and in summer the heat shimmers on the tarmac. Surfaces are generally good. Fog in autumn can be thick, so slow down and use lights. May and June, when the wheat is green and the poppies come out along the verges, are the finest months, and a clear October morning is superb.
t.vallee de l eure easy scenic scenic road:
The Sénart forest begins a few kilometres north-west of this point, and the coordinates lie in the country of Nandy, Lieusaint and Moissy-Cramayel, on the plateau between the Seine and the Brie. It is a place that looks plain at first, a mixture of woods, fields and new housing, and it has been reshaped over the last fifty years by the new town of Sénart, which spread across the farmland. The label of the Eure valley is a long way off, but the district's real attractions are quiet ones, not much known to riders outside the area.

The forest of Sénart, about three thousand hectares of oak and hornbeam, is one of the surviving royal hunting forests of the Île-de-France. Its straight avenues and cross-roads were laid out for hunts, and in the forest are ponds, old lodges and the odd stone cross. A road through it on a weekday morning is a pleasure, with the light coming through the trees and a smell of leaf mould and damp bark. On weekends, the forest fills with cyclists, runners and families, and you have to take care.

Nandy, with nearly seven thousand people, is the local centre for fuel and a bite to eat, and the shopping area at Carré Sénart, a large retail park, has everything you could want, though it is not the kind of place you ride a motorbike to for pleasure. The Seine is about ten kilometres to the west, with Melun a little further south, and the chalky, rolling Brie to the east. The best minor roads are those that run through the villages and fields, between the main roads, where the traffic is light and the bends are gentle.

The weather is typical of the region, mild and changeable, with fog in the autumn and occasional frost in winter. Spring, when the forest turns fresh green and the verges are full of wild flowers, is a good time, and October gives a ride through red and gold leaves. A trip here is not about drama, but about the pleasure of escaping the capital in an hour and finding oaks, silence and long straight avenues of light.
t.ardeche gorge long day photo pull off@45:
Montbrison, nearly four kilometres from this point, was the capital of the old county of Forez and still has the quiet dignity of a place that once mattered. The coordinates lie just outside it, near Champdieu and Savigneux, in the broad plain of the Forez, with the long dark ridge of the Monts du Forez rising to the west. The label names the Ardèche Gorge, which is a good way south-east, so ignore it and enjoy a different landscape: a flat, farmed basin dotted with ponds, with a view of mountains that gets better as you look closer.

A photo stop here makes sense because of the contrast. The plain is green and level, with cattle, maize and lines of poplars, while behind it the mountains rise to the summit of Pierre-sur-Haute, at 1,634 metres, topped by a cluster of radio masts that glint in the sun. In winter the upper slopes are white and the plain is brown, and in spring the lower hills are green with beech and fir. The wind sings through the high pastures, called hautes chaumes, where flocks graze in summer.

Montbrison is known for its cheese, the Fourme de Montbrison, a mild blue cheese made with cow's milk, shaped like a tall cylinder, and protected by appellation. It is a good thing to try at a lunch table, with bread and the local wine, and it is sold in the weekly markets. The town has a handsome collegiate church, the Notre-Dame d'Espérance, and a lively Saturday market. Champdieu, just north, has a fortified priory church with a heavy tower.

Fuel and food are easy in Montbrison, with sixteen thousand people and every sort of shop. The roads into the mountains, climbing from the plain through forest to high pastures, are some of the best in central France, with bends, gradients and views, but the surface can be broken by winter. The high roads close for snow in winter, and fog can come in fast in autumn. For the best light, come in the late afternoon of a clear day, when the mountains glow and the plain falls into shadow.
t.ardeche gorge long day scenic road@45.3,:
Say it plainly: this is not a pretty stretch of road. These coordinates are on the Rhône's left bank, in the industrial belt south of Vienne, where Salaise-sur-Sanne, Sablons and Le Péage-de-Roussillon cluster around a large chemical and energy platform with its chimneys, pipes and tank farms. The label calls it scenic and talks of the Ardèche Gorge, which is far south, but the place has its own interest, and from it you are close to some of the finest riding in the district.

Across the river, the hills of the Ardèche and the Pilat rise in green steps, with vineyards on the terraces and villages tucked into valleys. The wines of the Rhône's northern bank come from here: Condrieu and Saint-Joseph, Côte-Rôtie and Cornas, grown on slopes so steep that the vines must be tied to stakes and tended by hand. A bridge or two crosses the river, and a road on the west bank winds north to Serrières, where a small museum tells the story of the Rhône boatmen who once towed barges up the river against the current.

A short way north is Vienne, one of the great Roman cities of Gaul, with a temple to Augustus and Livia that is almost intact, a large theatre cut into the hillside, and a cathedral of mixed styles. It is well worth a visit, and the town's jazz festival in July is famous. Fuel and supermarkets are no problem in the Péage-de-Roussillon area, which has nearly seven thousand people, and Vienne has everything.

Riding here is mostly about getting through. The valley road is busy with lorries, but a turn onto the minor roads of the east bank leads into the quiet hills of the Bonnevaux and the Valloire. The cycle route called ViaRhôna follows the river and gives the area a pleasant side. The light on the Rhône at sunset, with the factories glowing and the hills dark, has its own odd beauty, though it is not one for the faint of heart. Take the minor roads, and be ready for a bit of grit.
t.chartreuse forest passes high point@45.2:
Annonay, nine kilometres away, has a claim to a very particular piece of history. In June 1783 the brothers Joseph and Étienne Montgolfier, who ran a paper mill in the town, sent up the first public flight of a hot-air balloon from the market square, a paper-and-cloth bag that rose over a thousand metres and astonished the crowd. A few months later, at Versailles, the first living passengers, a sheep, a duck and a rooster, flew in a similar balloon. The town still has a paper tradition, and a museum, and a balloon appears on its coat of arms.

The coordinates lie just south of Annonay, near Sarras, Vernosc-lès-Annonay and Quintenas, in the northern Ardèche, on the edge of the Rhône valley. The label names the Chartreuse, which is a good way east, but the real scene is the green and hilly Vivarais, a country of chestnut woods, steep valleys and orchards, with stone houses and slate or tile roofs. To the north, the long ridge of the Pilat rises, and on clear days the Alps can be seen across the river.

Sarras is a Rhône river village, and the road along the river, the old N86, is busy but has some pleasant stretches with views over the water. For something quieter, the roads inland climb to a plateau of fields and small woods, with Annonay's viaducts visible in the valley. The surface is mixed, with good main roads and patchy minor ones, and the bends are tight in places. Wind can be cold on the heights, and rain is frequent in autumn and spring.

Fuel and shops are easy in Annonay, a town of eighteen thousand with plenty of cafés and bakeries. The Safari de Peaugres, a safari park a few kilometres south, is a curiosity, with lions and giraffes in the Ardèche. Food in the district includes chestnut specialities, charcuterie and cheeses made from goat's milk, and the local wine, from the Saint-Joseph and Saint-Péray appellations, is excellent. A stop in a village inn gives a sense of the region. Spring and early autumn are lovely, with the chestnut leaves turning gold in October.
Saint-Étienne is on the doorstep here, and this is a different kind of France from the one in the guidebooks. The coordinates lie in the suburbs just south-west of the city, at Roche-la-Molière, with Saint-Genest-Lerpt and Le Chambon-Feugerolles beside it. For more than two centuries this basin was a coal and steel country, with pits, forges, arms factories and ribbon mills, and the landscape still bears the marks, with spoil heaps now grown over with birch and gorse, old winding towers and rows of workers' houses climbing the slopes.

The label talks of the Chartreuse, far to the east, but a look at the map shows the real neighbour: the Pilat massif, rising to the south-east beyond Saint-Étienne. The city has also redefined itself. In 2010 it was named a UNESCO City of Design, and its museums include a large collection of modern art and a mining museum in the old Couriot pit, where visitors can go underground, in a sense, and learn what the work was like. The local football club, Saint-Étienne, with its green shirts, has a passionate following, and the Geoffroy-Guichard stadium is a landmark.

Fuel is no issue whatsoever. Roche-la-Molière has over ten thousand people, with stations, supermarkets and cafés, and the whole area is built up. What the label calls a pass is a modest rise on the ridge between valleys, a place to look at the sprawl and the hills behind. The riding starts when you leave the city, taking the Gier valley toward the Rhône or climbing the roads on the southern edge towards the Pilat, where the bends begin and the air gets cooler.

A word on timing. The roads around Saint-Étienne are busy during commuting hours, and the best moment to leave is mid-morning or early on a Sunday. In winter the hills above the city can be snowy while the valley is wet, and the temperature drop is considerable. The local food is hearty, with the potato pancake called the râpée, rich pork dishes and plenty of bread. If you want to understand a part of France that built things, this is the corner.
t.loire gorges and le puy photo pull off@4:
Noirétable lies eight and a half kilometres from this point, in the northern Monts du Forez, and the rest of the district, around Sail-sous-Couzan and Saint-Germain-Laval, is a country of wooded hills, pastures and small valleys on the western edge of the Loire department. The label talks of the Loire gorges and Le Puy, which are in fact well to the south, but the mountains here are real enough. Forests of fir and beech climb the slopes, and on clear days the view east across the Loire plain reaches the Monts du Lyonnais and even the Alps.

The most dramatic sight in the district is the castle of Couzan, a ruined medieval fortress that stands on a rocky spur above Sail-sous-Couzan, with its broken walls and tower high above the valley. It was the seat of the lords of Couzan, who controlled the road between the Loire and the Auvergne for centuries, and the ruins can be reached by a short climb. Sail-sous-Couzan itself is a small spa and mineral-water village, with a bottling plant on the edge of the village.

Further south-west rise the high mountains of the Forez, with Pierre-sur-Haute at 1,634 metres and pastures called hautes chaumes where cattle graze in summer. The roads that cross them include the Col du Béal, over thirteen hundred metres, which is closed in winter by snow and which has some of the loneliest and prettiest scenery in central France. At the top, the air is cool and the wind strong, and in summer the grass is full of wild flowers.

Fuel is a concern, because the nearest town of any size, Thiers, is twenty-six kilometres away, and the villages are small. Noirétable has a few shops and may have a pump, but a rider would be wise to fill the tank in the plain. The roads are narrow and twisty, with a good surface and little traffic, and the weather changes quickly. A fine morning can turn to fog and drizzle by noon, so carry a waterproof layer. Late spring and September are the best times to ride.
Anyone who has flown into Paris has seen this place from above, although the view from the ground is rather less appealing. These coordinates are north-east of the capital, a few kilometres from the runways of Roissy-Charles de Gaulle airport, on the farmland and logistics sprawl of the Goële plateau, near Mitry-Mory, Moussy-le-Vieux and Moussy-le-Neuf. The label talks of Vexin limestone and the Seine cliffs, which lie far to the west, so this is a very different place from the one the label describes.

The airport opened in 1974 and has since become one of the busiest in Europe, and the land around it has been transformed by warehouses, hotels, business parks and motorways. Mitry-Mory, a town of eighteen thousand people, is a working place with stations, supermarkets and cafés, and the whole area is well supplied. For a rider, it is an excellent place to start a long day, since the fuel is plentiful and the roads toward the north and east are open. The noise of aircraft overhead is constant, and a good deal of the traffic is lorries.

Beyond the built-up area, though, the land opens out. The plateau of the Goële is a country of big wheat and beet fields, with old farms and villages, and Dammartin-en-Goële and other small towns have medieval churches and a quiet air. To the north lie the forests of Ermenonville and Chantilly, with their sandy roads and old oaks, and within an hour you can be among the châteaux of the Oise, or at the Parc Astérix, which is a short way up the motorway.

The best approach is to get out early. On a weekday, the roads around the airport are clogged by seven, and a start at half past six gives you clear roads and soft light. Fog is common in autumn and winter, and ice is a hazard on the open plateau, where the wind has a clear run. The farm roads that cross the fields are narrow and sometimes muddy, with tractors a regular obstacle. Once you have escaped the warehouses, the day improves.
t.vexin limestone and seine cliffs photo p:
Étréchy lies two kilometres from this point, at the heart of the valley of the Juine, a small river that flows north through the limestone plateau of the Essonne to join the Seine. The coordinates are in the countryside near Auvers-Saint-Georges and Morigny-Champigny, with Étampes a few kilometres to the south. The label talks of the Vexin limestone and the Seine cliffs, which are in a different department, but the landscape here does have its own limestone and its own beauty, and a pull-off on the edge of the plateau gives a long view across the valley.

The Juine valley is known for watercress. The cressonnières of Méréville and Étampes, fed by springs and shallow streams, once supplied the markets of Paris, and a few growers still produce the peppery leaves that Parisians have long liked in their salads and soups. The hills on either side are covered with beech and oak, and sandstone boulders, a miniature version of those in Fontainebleau, stand in the woods. It is lovely to walk through them.

Étampes, the nearest town of any size, has an ancient centre with a medieval tower, the Tour de Guinette, which stands on a hill above the town and was once part of a royal castle. The Romanesque and Gothic churches of the town are numerous, and the narrow streets lead to markets and cafés. Further south, the park of Méréville, laid out in the eighteenth century with artificial rivers, temples and a tower, has been restored and is a charming spot for an hour's walk.

Étréchy has nearly six and a half thousand people, with stations and supermarkets and plenty of places to eat, and the whole valley is well supplied. The roads along the Juine are narrow and twisty, with some gradients as they climb the sides, and the surface is generally good. Traffic is moderate, heavier at weekends. Mist fills the valley on autumn mornings, and the light on the beech woods in October is superb. Take care on the bends where leaves and mud collect.
t.vexin limestone and seine cliffs high po:
Brie is not a hill country, and a point labelled high here means the highest of a flat region, a gentle rise in a plateau that sits only a little over a hundred metres above the sea. These coordinates lie among the villages of Ozouer-le-Voulgis, Solers and Soignolles-en-Brie, in the heart of Seine-et-Marne, and the nearest town of any size, Gretz-Armainvilliers, is eleven kilometres to the north. The label says Vexin, which is a long way west, but the landscape you have is a broad, quiet one with a character all its own.

The ground underfoot explains a great deal. The plateau is capped by a hard, creamy limestone, the calcaire de Brie, and under it lies a layer of clay that holds water, so the fields are rich and the ponds are many. In places the limestone contains a siliceous rock called meulière, a rough, honey-coloured stone that was used for houses, walls and millstones. The villages are built of it, with tiled roofs and big barns, and the churches have squat towers. Old fortified farms, with high walls and a gate, stand among the fields, a reminder of the days when the area was fought over by armies.

The big skies are the point of a stop here. On a clear day the horizon is wide, with the fields running out to a line of trees and the odd water tower, and the sunsets are good. The roads are straight and open, and in summer the heat shimmers over the wheat. Wind is the main factor, and in winter it can be bitter. Fuel is best found in the towns on the edge of the plateau, and the nearest villages offer a bakery and a bar at most.

If you want a short detour, the forest of Armainvilliers, to the north, offers cool shade and quiet roads, with oaks and hornbeams in rows. In autumn the roads are often covered with beet mud, and in spring the rape fields are bright yellow. A bright morning in June, with the barley turning silver, is as good as the Brie gets.
t.vexin limestone and seine cliffs scenic:
Disneyland Paris is the neighbour here, and it changes everything about this corner of Seine-et-Marne. The coordinates lie between Serris, Villeneuve-le-Comte and Bailly-Romainvilliers, in the eastern part of the new town of Marne-la-Vallée, with Bussy-Saint-Georges, a town of ten thousand people, six kilometres away. The resort opened in 1992, on beet fields, and drew in with it a district called Val d'Europe, a planned town of apartment blocks in pale stone and brick, with shopping streets, a lake and a station for the express train.

The label talks of Vexin limestone and the Seine cliffs, which are far to the west, but the best view you will find here is the contrast between the new and the old. Within a few minutes' ride of the glittering towers, you reach farm tracks, fields of wheat and rape, and old villages with church towers and walled farms. Villeneuve-le-Comte, in particular, keeps its rural air, with a village green and a church. It is a place where the Brie plateau shows through the suburbs.

One historic house is worth a stop. The château de Ferrières, a few kilometres to the west, was built by the banker James de Rothschild in the 1850s to a design by the English architect Joseph Paxton, who also designed the Crystal Palace, and it is a vast and sumptuous place, with a grand hall and a park. In September 1870, during the Franco-Prussian War, Bismarck met the French foreign minister Jules Favre there to discuss peace terms, and the talks failed. The château is open on some days, and the park has a forest of old trees.

As a finishing point, the area is practical. Bussy-Saint-Georges and the Val d'Europe have stations, supermarkets, cafés and restaurants, and a station for trains into Paris if you need one. Traffic around the resort is heavy at weekends, so the best time to ride is early on a weekday. The roads of the Brie plateau beyond it are quiet and gentle, with long views. Late afternoon light on the fields is lovely, and an autumn evening, with the sun low and the sky orange, is an excellent end to a ride.
t.provins medieval ridge loop@48.4,2.5:
Milly-la-Forêt is four hundred metres from this point, and it is one of those small French towns that is better than its size suggests. It lies on the edge of the Gâtinais, in the department of Essonne, at the foot of a sandstone and forest country that runs towards Fontainebleau, and it has been a centre for growing medicinal and aromatic herbs for centuries, supplying the pharmacies and perfumers of Paris. The label talks of Provins, which is far to the east, but Milly is a destination on its own account.

The covered market of Milly is a fifteenth-century timber hall, with a huge roof of tile supported by oak beams, standing in the middle of the town square. Nearby, the chapel of Saint-Blaise-des-Simples, a small medieval chapel in a garden of medicinal herbs, was decorated in 1959 by the poet and artist Jean Cocteau, who is buried there. The walls are covered in his light, wiry drawings of plants and figures, and the effect is quiet and strange. A few kilometres away, in the forest, stands the Cyclop, a gigantic mirrored head built by a group of artists led by Jean Tinguely, which visitors can enter on certain days.

As a fuel gate, Milly has nearly five thousand people, a few stations, bakeries and cafés, and it is the logical start for a ride into the forest. The roads around it wind through pine and oak, with sandstone boulders appearing among the trees, and the surface is generally good. The pale sandy soil gives the forest a different look from the plain, with heather and bracken under the trees, and in summer the smell of warm pine resin. Climbers love the boulders, and you may see them at weekends.

Weekends are busy with Parisians, so a weekday is better. Early mornings in autumn, with mist among the trees and the light coming sideways through the leaves, are the best moments, and in spring the forest floor is carpeted with flowers. In winter, ice on the shady bends can catch you out. Take a layer, because it gets cool among the trees, and stop for a coffee in the old square before you set off.
t.provins medieval ridge loop high point@4:
Nothing interrupts the sky on the Beauce. These coordinates lie in the open plateau of the Eure-et-Loir and Loiret border, near Toury, Janville and Outarville, a granary of such flatness that you can see church towers and silos for thirty kilometres in any direction. Pithiviers, the nearest town of any size, is twenty-five kilometres to the east, and Chartres, with its great cathedral, is about forty to the north-west. The label talks of Provins and a ridge, but the nearest ridge is a long way off, and a high point in the Beauce is a matter of a few metres.

The soil is deep, fertile silt, and the crops are wheat, barley, beet and rape, grown on a vast scale. In summer the plain is gold, and in spring it is green, and in winter it is bare brown, with a wind that can cut like a knife. Wind turbines now line the horizon, turning slowly, and they give a sense of scale. The villages are built of pale limestone and tile, clustered around churches and silos. Toury has a large sugar factory, whose chimney can be seen from a distance, and whose smell fills the air in the beet season in autumn.

Pithiviers is known for its almond pastry, a round cake of puff pastry filled with almond cream, with a swirl pattern on the top, and for its lark pâté, which was once a famous delicacy. The town has a small museum and a pleasant centre. For fuel in the Beauce, the small towns of Toury and Janville have stations, but opening hours can be limited, so a rider should fill the tank in a larger place and carry a reserve.

The riding is simple. Long, straight roads cross the plain, with the odd roundabout or village, and the surface is generally good. The wind is the main thing to reckon with, often strong and gusty, and it can add an hour to a day. Fog is thick in autumn and winter, and in summer the heat is considerable. For the best of the Beauce, ride on a clear day in May or June, when the fields are green and the sky is a huge blue bowl.
t.provins medieval ridge loop scenic road@:
Henri IV is the name to know here. On 14 March 1590 the Protestant king defeated the armies of the Catholic League at the battle of Ivry, on the plain beside the Eure, and the village that took part, Ivry-la-Bataille, has carried the mention in its name ever since. The legend says that before the charge he told his men to rally to his white plume, and a monument on the battlefield commemorates it. These coordinates lie a little to the south-east, near Oulins, Anet and Ivry, on the edge of the Eure valley, with Dreux sixteen kilometres away.

Anet, a town of under three thousand people, has one of the finest châteaux in France, though only part of it survives. It was built between about 1547 and 1552 for Diane de Poitiers, the mistress of Henri II, by the architect Philibert de l'Orme, and it was one of the first buildings in the country to show the full classical vocabulary of columns and pediments. Its great entrance gateway and the chapel remain, and the interior is open to visitors. Diane's initials, interwoven with the king's, appear in the decoration. The Revolution and later owners removed much of the rest, but what stands is impressive.

The label talks of Provins and a ridge, which are in a different part of the region altogether, and the road described as a pass is better thought of as a climb out of the valley onto the plateau. The surface is generally good, with a few bends and views over the meadows of the Eure. In spring the valley is green and the poplars are pale, and in autumn mist lies on the water. Traffic is light, apart from farm vehicles.

For fuel, Dreux has everything, with over thirty thousand people and a large shopping area. Anet and Ivry have a bakery and a few cafés, and there is a petrol station on the main road. The cooking here is Norman in character, with cream, apples and cider. A lunch in the old inn at Anet, if it is open, is a pleasant way to spend an hour. Visit on a weekday in May or September, when the valley is quiet and the light is gentle.
t.chantilly to ermenonville flow photo pul:
Dourdan is the real town of this district, nine kilometres from this point, and its castle is the thing to see. It was built around 1200 by Philip Augustus, the king who also built the Louvre as a fortress, and it stands in a moat in the middle of the town, with round corner towers and a great circular keep, one of the best-preserved royal castles of its age in the Paris region. The medieval market hall, in the main square, is a vast timber structure, and the town has a pleasant centre with bakeries and cafés. Dourdan was a royal town for centuries, and several queens held it as part of their dowry.

The coordinates themselves lie in the country to the west, near Corbreuse, Ablis and Aunay-sous-Auneau, in a landscape of woodland, meadow and the first fields of the Beauce. The forest of Dourdan, which covers hills of sand and clay just to the east, is a quiet place of oak and pine, with ponds and heath. The label talks of Chantilly and Ermenonville, which are far to the north-east, so ignore it. This is a southern, gentler country, and a pull-off here looks out over a wide patchwork of fields and woods.

Corbreuse is a small village among woods, and its nearby ponds are a peaceful spot for a rest. The roads in the area are narrow and winding through the woods, with tight bends and damp patches, and open and fast across the fields. Wild boar and deer live in the forests, and a rider on a misty morning may see one at the edge of the road, so slow down at dawn and dusk. The surface is generally good, with some patches broken by tree roots.

Fuel and food are easy in Dourdan, which has ten thousand people and several stations. Corbreuse and Ablis have small shops, and a bakery is open in most villages by seven. The weather here is mild and changeable, with fog in the autumn and frost in winter. In spring the woods are carpeted with bluebells and wood anemones, and the air smells of damp earth. A ride from here down to the châteaux of the Beauce, or west towards Chartres, is a good day.
t.milly forest roads and gatinais@49.5,2.9:
Ourscamp Abbey is the surprise of this corner of the Oise, and it stands at Chiry-Ourscamp, three kilometres from this point, on the bank of the river.
