It was founded in 1129 as a Cistercian house, and grew into one of the most powerful abbeys in northern France. The great church was destroyed after the Revolution, and only the ruins of its choir remain, but the medieval infirmary, a vast vaulted hall of the thirteenth century, survives and can be visited. Today it is a place of retreat, with a small community, and the grounds are lovely to walk in.

The coordinates lie near Dreslincourt and Cambronne-lès-Ribécourt, in the valley of the Oise between Compiègne and Noyon, with Thourotte, a town of five and a half thousand people, six kilometres away. The label talks of the forest of Milly and the Gâtinais, which are far to the south, but this is a different country, with the broad river, the canal beside it and wooded hills on the edges. The Oise here is wide and slow, and barges still use it.

Noyon, ten kilometres or so to the north-east, is the birthplace of the Protestant reformer John Calvin in 1509, and has a fine cathedral, one of the first Gothic cathedrals of the region, begun in the twelfth century. It was also where Charlemagne was crowned king of the Franks in 768 and where Hugh Capet was crowned in 987. The town has a museum devoted to Calvin and a pleasant centre with cafés and bakeries. A visit makes a good break from the road.

The area saw heavy fighting in the First World War, and in March 1918 the German spring offensive reached the valley of the Oise. Memorials stand among the villages. Fuel is available at Thourotte and Noyon, and the small villages have little. For food, the local specialities include the flamiche, a leek tart, and cheeses from the region. The roads are gentle, with long bends through woods and along the river, and traffic is light. Mist rises from the river in autumn, and the leaves along the canal turn gold. A quiet weekday ride is best.
t.chantilly to ermenonville flow@48.9,2.8:
Crécy-la-Chapelle is the pretty place nearby, and it earns the nickname that the tourist offices have given it, the Venice of the Brie. The little river Grand Morin splits into channels around the old town, with stone bridges, washhouses and gardens running down to the water, and the collegiate church rises over the roofs. It lies about eight kilometres from these coordinates, which sit among Serris, Magny-le-Hongre and Chessy, with Esbly, a town of five and a half thousand people, five kilometres away. This is the doorstep of Disneyland Paris, the first of many surprises on the ride.

The label talks of Chantilly and Ermenonville, which lie forty-five kilometres to the north, but this fuel gate is a departure point for a ride in either direction. Fuel is easy, as Chessy, Magny-le-Hongre and Serris have stations and supermarkets, and the new town of Marne-la-Vallée is well supplied with cafés and bakeries. Esbly, on the Marne, is an older town with a small centre and a station on the line to Paris.

The Marne here is a wide, slow river, with locks and canals and a towpath for cyclists. Further east, the valley passes through Meaux and the champagne country. The old villages of the Brie, with their stone houses and fortified farms, are a few minutes from the resort, and the contrast is a delight. Couilly-Pont-aux-Dames, a village on the Grand Morin, has an old abbey that later became a school for the daughters of the Legion of Honour.

For a rider, the best approach is to leave early and head into the quiet country east and north, where the roads run across the plateau between fields of wheat and rape. The surface is good, and the bends are gentle. Traffic around the resort is heavy at weekends and in school holidays, so avoid those times if you can. Spring and autumn bring soft light and quiet roads, and in summer, early starts are best, before the heat and the crowds arrive. A good breakfast at a village bakery sets up the day.
t.chantilly to ermenonville flow@49.3,2.9:
Morienval is the reason to stop here, and it has nothing to do with fast food. The village sits in the little valley of the Automne, on the edge of the great Compiègne woods, and its abbey church is one of those buildings that architecture students make pilgrimages to. Its Romanesque vaults, from the twelfth century, are counted among the earliest pointed ribbed vaults in France, a first rough draft of the idea that would later lift Gothic cathedrals toward the sky. Even if you know nothing about vaulting, the squat towers and the plain stone have a calm that suits a coffee break.

The land around is the Valois, a rolling plateau of wheat and beet cut by small wooded valleys. Crépy-en-Valois, six kilometres away and the proper town of the district, was once the seat of the counts of Valois, the family that eventually gave France a line of kings. For a rider the Valois is not dramatic, and I would rather say so than pretend otherwise. What it offers is quiet: narrow departmental roads, long sightlines over fields, villages built of pale limestone with steep tiled roofs, and very little traffic outside the hour when everyone drives to Paris or comes home from it.

Treat this as a food and rest stop. The villages here have a bakery and perhaps a café that opens at hours known only to its owner, so a sandwich from a boulangerie eaten on a wall in the sun is the realistic plan. Pass over the bigger shopping on the far side of the valley and use Crépy-en-Valois for fuel, since its fifteen thousand inhabitants support several stations while the hamlets do not.

On the bike the best moments come where the road dips into the Automne valley and the beech woods close over you. Dappled shade, damp leaves, a sudden cool smell of moss, then out again into open barley. Autumn is especially good, when the forest turns copper and the plateau fields are bare brown, though mornings can carry a fog that sits in the valley floor until ten. Watch for gravel dragged out of field entrances at harvest time, and for tractors that take the whole lane without apology.
t.chantilly to ermenonville flow high poin:
The ground rises quietly north of Verneuil-en-Halatte, and that gentle lift is the Forêt d'Halatte, a royal hunting wood that has been managed for deer and timber for something like a thousand years. Kings rode here with hounds long before anyone owned a motorbike. The high point is nothing like an Alpine pass, only a swell in the land where the trees thin and you get a view south over the Oise valley toward the roofs and chimneys of Creil. Still, in a flat region, a hundred metres of climbing has a way of feeling like a summit.

Creil, three kilometres down the hill, is an industrial town on the Oise with a past in faience. Its glazed earthenware tableware was once found on tables across France in the nineteenth century, and the old railway junction there made it a hub long before the motorway took over. It is not pretty, but it has big supermarkets and plenty of fuel, which is exactly what you want when the forest roads further on have none. Verneuil-en-Halatte, with its four thousand people, has what a village of that size has: a bakery, a few cafés, a pharmacy.

The riding in the forest is a series of broad, easy bends under tall oaks and beeches, with a few bumpy patches where roots have lifted the tarmac. The speed limits are low and enforced in places, and with good reason: deer cross at dawn and dusk, and so do cyclists, hikers and horse riders, who are very much at home in the Halatte. The surface is generally good but gets slick when leaves drop, and when rain wets the tar under the canopy it takes a long time to dry.

If you have time, leave the bike and walk a few minutes into the trees. The stone here is a pale limestone from the Paris basin, and old quarries and mossy boulders show up between the trunks. Late spring is the loveliest season, with new green light and bluebells in the clearings. In high summer the shade is a gift, and in winter the bare branches let you see how far the plateau really runs.
t.chantilly to ermenonville flow scenic ro:
This is the Seine just before it reaches the great bend that Parisians call the boucle de Chanteloup, and the water here is broad, brown and slow, pushed along by lock after lock. On the south bank sit Meulan-en-Yvelines and its neighbours Hardricourt and Mézy-sur-Seine, with the hills of the Vexin rising on the north side. Meulan has about nine thousand people and a small island in the river with an old quarter on it. Between the bridges and the church towers it is easy to forget you are only forty kilometres from the centre of Paris.

Riding here is about threading between river and plateau. Roads climb out of the valley on short hairpins through villages, then run along the shoulder of the hill with the Seine glinting below, then drop back to the water. The curves are tighter than in the open Vexin farmland, and with houses close to the road you cannot trust that corner exit to be empty. On a weekday morning it is a pleasure. On a sunny Sunday the valley roads fill with cyclists and day-trippers, and patience pays more than speed.

The history is quietly everywhere. The Seine valley downstream from here is Impressionist country, with Giverny and Auvers not far off, and the painters came for exactly this mix of river light and soft hills. The chalk and limestone slopes have been quarried for centuries, and many of the caves along the valley sides were used for mushrooms, a trade that once made the Paris region a big producer. You will see the signs of it in the pale stone walls and the odd cave mouth behind a garden.

For practical needs, Meulan is the answer. It has fuel, food, and a riverside where you can sit and watch barges push past, carrying gravel or grain. Hardricourt and Mézy have bakeries and little else. Go early on a clear day, when the Seine mist is still lifting off the water, and you will have the loops mostly to yourself.
t.milly la foret@48.4,2.5:
Milly-la-Forêt is a small town of just under five thousand people tucked at the western edge of the Fontainebleau sandstone country, at about seventy-five metres above the sea. The town's name tells you what it is: a settlement in a clearing of old forest, with the Gâtinais regional park around it. Its centre is built around a large wooden market hall dating back to the fifteenth century, with a vast timbered roof held on massive oak posts, and in the shade of this structure traders still sell vegetables and cheese. It is one of the finest surviving halles in the Île-de-France, and few visitors know it.

Milly has a long association with herbs. For centuries the surrounding sandy soils have been used to grow medicinal and aromatic plants, the so-called simples, and a fragrant landscape of mint, lavender and chamomile fields is part of the area's identity. The little chapel of Saint-Blaise-des-Simples, a mile or so from the centre, was decorated inside by the poet and artist Jean Cocteau in the early 1960s, and he is buried in the grounds. If you step inside you find delicate line drawings of herbs and flowers and a quiet that feels out of step with the busy world.

On the bike, Milly is a good place to wake up the day. The roads out of the town head into pine and oak forest, with the soft smell of resin on warm days and the odd grey boulder poking out of the heather. Tarmac is mostly smooth, bends are long and gentle, and traffic is light on weekdays but picks up on weekends, when climbers and walkers head for the forest. Not far away in the woods stands the Cyclop, a giant mirrored sculpture by Jean Tinguely and friends, which will make you think you have lost your mind if you come across it by accident.

For coffee and a croissant, the cafés on the market square are the natural choice, and the bakeries around it open early. Fuel is available in the town, so it makes a good place to fill up before going on. Take a seat under the old roof timbers, order a coffee, and look up. It is the kind of ceiling that reminds you how much skill went into everyday buildings before anyone worried about speed.
t.milly forest roads and gatinais@48.6,2.7:
I would not call Moisenay a destination. It is a small village on the Brie plateau east of Melun, among cereal fields, and the nearest bigger centres are Vaux-le-Pénil, with nearly twelve thousand people and an ample supply of petrol stations, and the sprawl of Melun beyond it. As a fuel gate it does exactly what it promises: a convenient place to top up on the way out of the Paris region before the ride proper begins.

What makes this corner worth knowing is what lies three kilometres to the south-west, in Maincy: the château of Vaux-le-Vicomte, built in the 1650s for Nicolas Fouquet, Louis XIV's finance minister. Fouquet hired three men who would later work together at Versailles, the architect Louis Le Vau, the painter Charles Le Brun and the gardener André Le Nôtre, and in August 1661 he gave a party so splendid that the young king, watching, decided the man was too rich and too ambitious. Fouquet was arrested within weeks and spent the rest of his life in prison. The king took the artists, the ideas and even some of the orange trees. It is one of the great stories of French power, and you can ride past the end of the avenue without noticing if you are not looking.

The riding here is gentle. The Brie is a plateau of fertile loess, ploughed in long fields, and the roads are straight or lightly curved with shallow dips where small streams cut through. Hedgerows are rare, which gives a sense of space and also of exposure on windy days. In spring, rapeseed turns the horizon yellow, and in autumn the black soil after ploughing makes a handsome contrast with the pale roads. Brie cheese takes its name from this country, and the soft cow's milk wheels of Brie de Melun are a local relative of the more famous Meaux.

A tip for early starts: the Brie in October mornings is often fogbound, and the plateau holds the cold. A few kilometres of damp air at dawn will clear by ten, so layer up, tank up at Vaux-le-Pénil, and wait for the sun to burn through before you push on.
t.milly forest roads and gatinais high poi:
This is the Beauce edge, and the high point is a gentle swell in a country that rarely bothers to rise. North of Pithiviers and Malesherbes the plateau spreads out in enormous fields of wheat, barley and sugar beet, with a few wind turbines turning in the distance and the occasional line of poplars marking a stream. The nearest villages are Sermaises, with about seventeen hundred people, and the two small towns of Malesherbes and Pithiviers, both a short ride away. If you are looking for a viewpoint, this is the kind where the view is mostly sky.

Pithiviers gave its name to a pastry. The pithivier is a round puff pastry pie filled with almond cream, scored on top in curving lines like the spokes of a wheel, and it has been made in the town for a couple of centuries. You can still buy a good one in the local bakeries, and I would suggest buying a small one to eat on the spot. The Gâtinais around here was also once famous for saffron, grown in the sandy fields, and the trade has been revived by a few local growers in recent years.

Riding across the plateau is a pleasure of a particular, meditative sort. Straight roads cut the fields into huge rectangles, and the long gradual rises are so subtle that your bike barely notices. The danger is the wind, which can be fierce and unrelenting when a westerly settles in, and in winter the crosswinds are accompanied by icy patches where the shade of a hedge lies on the road. In summer you will smell the dry straw and diesel from the combine harvesters.

For fuel, Malesherbes is the logical choice at eleven kilometres, and Pithiviers is about the same. Both have bakeries, cafés and small supermarkets. In between, villages like Sermaises are tidy and quiet, with a church, a bar and little else, so fill the tank before you leave the larger towns. If you have time, climb a grain silo or a farm gate for a minute and look back. The horizon is a perfect line and the sky does the rest.
t.milly forest roads and gatinais scenic r:
The roads between Ablis and Auneau cross the northern reaches of the Beauce, where the plateau tilts imperceptibly toward the Rambouillet forest, and this is a landscape that rewards a certain kind of patience. Fields run to the horizon in every direction, the soil is a rich ochre, and every few kilometres a village appears with a church spire and a cluster of barns. Ablis, about two thousand eight hundred people, once stood on the great road from Paris to Orléans and Bordeaux, and the long main street shows it. Auneau, with four thousand, is a little larger and has a castle site and a river, the Voise.

As a scenic road it is more about openness than curves. On a clear day the sky is huge and the cloud shadows slide across the wheat like slow ships. In June, when the fields are green turning gold, the effect is of a vast tilted sea, and the wind turbines that stand on the plateau add to the impression. Far off to the south-west the cathedral of Chartres, forty kilometres away, can sometimes be spotted as a faint spike on the horizon if the air is clean. It was the pilgrims' beacon for centuries and it still does the job for those on the open plain.

The surface here is generally good, because agricultural traffic demands it, though the margins can be rough where heavy trailers have chewed the edges. Crosswinds are the main hazard, and in winter a sharp frost can last late into the morning on shaded stretches. Because this is working farmland, the roads can be muddy near field entrances after harvest or rain, and a tractor in front of you will rarely pull over. Be calm about it. There is nowhere to hurry to.

If you need fuel, Saint-Arnoult-en-Yvelines, about eleven kilometres away and with just under six thousand people, has several stations and shops, and Auneau is also an option. For coffee, the villages along the way mostly offer one bar and one bakery, so pick whichever has the open door and the cars outside.
t.lac du bourget balcony ride@45.7,4.5:
Saint-Martin-en-Haut sits high in the Monts du Lyonnais, the rounded hills that rise west of Lyon and separate the Rhône valley from the Loire basin. At around seven hundred metres or so, the air is distinctly cooler than in the city, and the town has the feel of a hill market centre, with about three and a half thousand people, a handsome church and plenty of small shops. Lyon is only thirty kilometres away, but the pace here is slower, and the landscape is a patchwork of pasture, orchards and woods.

The label mentions Lac du Bourget, but that lake is much further east in Savoie. The ground under your wheels here is the Lyonnais upland, and what it does well is steady, flowing riding. Roads run along ridges and drop into little valleys, with plenty of medium-radius bends and short climbs through villages like Aveize and Larajasse. Traffic is light apart from commuters near the town, and the surface is generally decent, although winter frost can linger on north-facing slopes and the occasional pothole opens after the thaw. Tractors and cattle trucks are part of the scene.

This is an area of fruit growing, with apples, pears, cherries and especially raspberries and redcurrants, which are sold in the markets and used in the pastries of local bakeries. A tarte aux framboises from a baker here is a very good reason to stop. Saint-Martin-en-Haut has fuel and a handful of cafés, and Mornant, eleven kilometres away, is bigger if you need more choice. In the hills beyond, services are patchy, so make sure the tank is full.

From a clear viewpoint on a ridge, you can see west across the hills toward the Forez and, on a very good day, glimpse the white line of the Alps far to the east. The best time to ride is late spring, with blossom on the orchards, or early autumn, when mornings are crisp and the hillsides turn gold. Winter brings snow to this altitude, sometimes for days, so be careful if you come between December and March.
t.lac du bourget balcony ride@45.4,4.4:
Saint-Étienne is the city that makes people raise an eyebrow, because few riders think of it as a destination, yet it has a story worth hearing. It grew up on coal, which lay under the hills of the Forez, and on the factories that coal powered: steel, arms, ribbons and, later, bicycles and the famous mail-order catalogue of Manufrance. By the early twentieth century it was one of France's great industrial cities. The mines are now closed, but the city has reinvented itself around design, and in 2010 UNESCO named it a City of Design, an unexpected honour for a place known for slag heaps.

With about a hundred and seventy-six thousand people, Saint-Étienne has every service imaginable, from fuel stations on every approach to restaurants of all kinds. Its football club, AS Saint-Étienne, known as Les Verts, won ten French championships and reached a European Cup final in 1976, and the green of the shirts is visible all over town, especially on match days at the Geoffroy-Guichard stadium. The old industrial buildings of the Manufacture d'Armes have been transformed into the Cité du Design, where you can walk around exhibition spaces and a pleasant café.

For a rider the city is a food and rest stop rather than a scenic highlight. The streets are steep, with tramlines and traffic, and the centre has its share of one-way systems that can confuse. Aim for the edges of the town, where the hills of the Pilat Regional Park rise to the south-east, and good riding begins within a few minutes. Parking a motorbike in the centre is easy, as the city is generally relaxed about two-wheelers.

If you want a meal, look for a local bouchon-style place serving Lyonnais or Forézien dishes such as sausage and potatoes, tripe, or a local cheese like the fresh rigotte. The mixture of grit and warmth in the city is genuine, and it gives a good contrast to the cleaner mountain villages. Allow some extra time to cross the city at rush hour, when the ring roads fill.
t.vanoise gateway overnight scenic road@45:
Tarare is the gate of the Monts du Lyonnais and the Beaujolais hills, a town of about ten thousand people crammed into a steep valley west of Lyon, and the road from here to Amplepuis is one of the best short bends of tarmac in the region. Tarare grew rich on textiles, especially muslin, the fine cotton cloth that was woven here in the nineteenth century and exported across Europe, and the old factories still line the valley. The town is not pretty, but it is real, with a market, bakeries and fuel stations, and it feels like a place where people actually work.

From Tarare the road climbs steeply through forest to a col on the ridge, and then descends toward Amplepuis, a smaller town of over five thousand people that also made its living from weaving. The hills here are covered with dark Douglas fir, planted in the twentieth century for timber, and the air smells of resin on warm days. The road twists through the trees with tight bends and short straights, climbing and falling with the contours, and the surface, while often patchy, is generally decent. Look out for gravel on the corners and damp patches in the shade.

This is a quieter part of the Beaujolais than the famous wine hills to the east, a land of dairy farms, forest and small villages, with high ground that stays cool in summer and cold in winter. Violay, eight kilometres from Amplepuis, is a modest village on the border with the Loire department and the next place for a break. In bad weather the hills disappear into cloud, and frost and snow can make the road tricky between December and March, so check conditions before setting out.

The ridge gives views across to the Monts du Forez in the west and, on a very clear day, the distant Alps to the east. Stop at the col if you can, and breathe the cold pine-scented air, which will be a welcome contrast to the heat of the valley. The sharp climb from Tarare is a good test of an engine, and the descent a good test of the brakes.
t.vanoise gateway overnight photo pull off:
This corner of the Loire département is a meeting place of two worlds, the coal-mining basin of Saint-Étienne and the quiet green uplands of the Pilat regional park. La Ricamarie and Saint-Étienne lie to the north-east, an industrial landscape of old pitheads and workers' housing, while Saint-Genest-Malifaux, a village of nearly three thousand people about a thousand metres up, is already in the high country. The change takes only a few kilometres, and in that short distance the air becomes cooler, the woods thicker and the roads more interesting.

The Pilat is a rounded massif of old granite and gneiss, standing between the Rhône and the Loire, and its highest summit, the Crêt de la Perdrix, reaches about fourteen hundred and thirty metres. The slopes are covered with beech and fir forest, with pastures and small farms in clearings, and the whole range is protected as a regional park. Near here is the Col du Grand Bois, a well-known road pass at around eleven hundred metres that climbs from Saint-Étienne in a series of hairpins and offers excellent views. It is a favourite of local riders on weekends, so expect company in summer.

As a photo spot, the point gives a view over the industrial basin toward the hills of the Forez, and on a clear day the contrast between the green slopes and the grey city is striking. The light is best in late afternoon or early morning, when the haze lifts and the colours deepen. The ride here ends, so you might well find it a quiet place to reflect on the miles behind you, with the engine ticking as it cools.

For practical needs, Saint-Étienne has everything, and Saint-Genest-Malifaux has fuel, a bakery and a few cafés. La Ricamarie, a town of nearly eight thousand people six kilometres away, is another option. The Pilat is known for its cheeses, particularly a small goat's milk round called Rigotte de Condrieu, and for its chestnut and bilberry tarts, which make good rewards at the end of a ride. In winter snow is common above a thousand metres, so plan accordingly.
t.jura wine roads and cascades@46.2,4.8:
The Saône is the slowest river in France, so slow that Julius Caesar is said to have remarked that it was hard to tell which way it flowed, and this stretch near Thoissey shows why. The water is broad and brown, moving with great calm between low banks of willows and poplars, and the flat land on either side is dotted with farms and meadows. You are on the Ain side of the river, in the southern Bresse, and the old Burgundy hills of the Mâconnais rise on the opposite bank, covered with vines. It is a classic piece of French river country, soft and unhurried.

Thoissey, Saint-Didier-sur-Chalaronne and Grièges are small villages of one to three thousand people, each with a church, a bakery and a handful of houses in warm local stone. Mâcon, twelve kilometres away with about thirty-five thousand inhabitants, is the main town on this reach of the Saône and has all the services you could need, including fuel, restaurants and a riverside promenade. It was the birthplace of the poet and statesman Alphonse de Lamartine in 1790, whose romantic verse about the lakes and hills of this country is still taught in French schools.

The label mentions the Jura, and the mountains do appear on the eastern horizon on a clear day, but here the riding is gentle and flat. Roads follow the river and cross the plain, with wide bends and long straights, and a bridge now and then to cross the water. The main hazards are farm vehicles and, in autumn, the mist that gathers over the river and can reduce visibility to a few metres until midmorning. In summer the afternoon sun is strong and the shade of the riverside trees is welcome.

This is wine country too, though the great names lie on the other side of the river. Pouilly-Fuissé and the other white Burgundies of the Mâconnais are made from chardonnay grown on limestone slopes just a short ride away, and a restaurant in Mâcon will happily pour you a glass. Go for a plain local menu with a river fish, such as pike-perch in cream sauce, and you will not go far wrong.
t.jura wine roads and cascades high point@:
Montmerle-sur-Saône is a small town of about three thousand people on the east bank of the river, with a bridge across to Belleville on the other side, and the label calls it a high point, which is generous. This is the flat floodplain of the Saône, and there is barely a rise anywhere. The real interest is the view west across the river, where the hills of the Beaujolais rise in a soft green wall covered with vineyards, and the ten famous crus, from Brouilly to Saint-Amour, are produced on their slopes.

Belleville, on the far bank with just over six thousand people, is the local centre, with fuel stations, shops, cafés and a fine twelfth-century abbey church, and it sits at the foot of the Beaujolais hills, which makes it the natural gateway to wine country. Francheleins and Guéreins, on the Ain side, are small villages with a church and a few houses, and the countryside around is flat and agricultural, with maize, poplars and the occasional pond. The Saône floods in winter and spring, and the meadows beside the river can be under water for days.

For a rider, the interest here is the contrast between the plain and the hills. On the east bank, the roads are straight and quick and the traffic light, but cross the bridge and head west, and within minutes you are climbing through vineyard lanes with sharp bends, narrow roads and beautiful views. The surface in the vineyards is often rough, with patches of gravel and mud from vehicles carrying grapes at harvest, and the roads are shared with tractors and cyclists. Autumn, when the vines turn red and gold, is the most beautiful time, though the harvest brings extra traffic.

In Montmerle itself there is a riverside walk and a couple of cafés where you can watch the barges and the fishermen. The Beaujolais wines are best enjoyed with a plate of charcuterie and a bit of bread, and the local bouchons offer simple dishes at fair prices. Fill the tank before you cross into the hills, because the villages up there have few stations.
t.lyon rhone alpes rides@46.4,4.8:
You are in the Mâconnais, the southern end of Burgundy, where chardonnay vines cover the limestone hills and the villages are built of honey-coloured stone. Hurigny, La Roche-Vineuse and Sancé are small places within a few kilometres of each other, each with a church and a bakery, and Charnay-lès-Mâcon, with about seven thousand people, offers fuel and a supermarket. Mâcon itself lies a short way to the east on the Saône. The label calls this a swim stop, which is optimistic, but the countryside is lovely for a quiet pause.

The great landmark of the district is the Rock of Solutré, a limestone crag topping out at nearly five hundred metres above sea level that rises abruptly from the vineyards a few kilometres to the south-west, with its neighbour the Rock of Vergisson. At Solutré, archaeologists found a huge prehistoric site where hunters, tens of thousands of years ago, are thought to have driven wild horses over the cliff, and the bones of thousands of animals have been found at the base. The rock gives its name to a whole prehistoric culture, the Solutrean, and is among the best known sites of the Stone Age in Europe. A walk to the top takes about half an hour and offers a vast view.

North-west of here, about twenty-five kilometres off, lies Cluny, where in the Middle Ages the greatest monastery in Christendom stood. Its abbey was the head of a network of over a thousand monasteries across Europe, and its church was the largest in the world until St Peter's in Rome was rebuilt. Only fragments remain, but they are impressive. The wines of the Mâconnais, especially Pouilly-Fuissé and Saint-Véran, are the white wines that pair so well with the local goat's cheeses, which come in small cylinders and are sold in every market.

The roads here are made for gentle touring, with rolling hills, vineyard lanes and farm tracks, and the surface is generally good. In September and October the harvest brings tractors and lorries, but also a lovely atmosphere. Spring and autumn are best.
t.pilat ridge and rhone view@46.1,4.3:
Chandon, Saint-Denis-de-Cabanne and Cours-la-Ville are small places at the edge of the Beaujolais hills, where the green slopes of the Monts du Beaujolais drop toward the plain of the Loire and the old textile town of Roanne. Cours-la-Ville, with about four and a half thousand people, was a centre of weaving and cloth finishing, and its streets still carry the memory of the mills that once made it prosperous. The villages are a mix of stone farms and modest houses, and the countryside is a patchwork of meadows and woods.

This is cattle country, and you may see the white Charolais cows in the pastures, a breed famous for its beef and known across the world. The Roannais lies on the edge of the Charolais-Brionnais, where the cattle are bred, and the butchers and restaurants of the region serve some of the best beef in France. A grilled steak or a slow-cooked stew of beef in red wine is the obvious order at a roadside restaurant, and a dessert of local cheese or a tart is a fine finish.

Roads here wind through the hills in a pleasant way, with bends of medium radius and short climbs, and the surface is mostly good. The traffic is light, and in summer the hills are green and cool compared to the plain. The air is fresher, and the nights can be cold even in July. In winter, snow and ice can cover the higher roads, so be careful from December to March, and expect fog in the valleys in autumn.

For fuel, the nearest place of any size is Mably, eighteen kilometres off, and Roanne is not far beyond it, so top up before you head into the hills. Small cafés and bakeries in the villages will provide coffee and a sandwich, and a local boulangerie will often sell a slice of fruit tart that is worth the stop. It is a quiet, lived-in landscape, far from tourist routes, and its modesty is part of its charm.
t.fontainebleau forest road@48.4,2.7:
Fontainebleau is a small town that holds a very big place in French history, and the forest around it is one of the finest woods in Europe. The château was a royal residence for eight centuries, from medieval kings to Napoleon III, and each ruler added something, so that the building is a glorious jumble of styles. It was here, in the courtyard known as the Cour des Adieux, that Napoleon said goodbye to his guard in April 1814 before leaving for exile on Elba. The town of nearly twenty thousand people sits at about ninety metres above the sea, and it has every service, including several fuel stations.

The forest covers some twenty-five thousand hectares, and its sandstone boulders, heathland and tall trees make it unlike any other woodland near Paris. The rocks are the remains of ancient dunes, and some of them are the size of houses. In the nineteenth century, painters of the Barbizon school came to work here, leaving the studios of Paris to paint the trees and light directly, and their work helped lead to Impressionism. Today climbers come from around the world to scale the boulders, in a sport that was practised here long before it had a name, and the climbing area is known simply as Bleau.

The forest roads are a joy to ride. They run through beech and oak, with long gentle bends and flickering light, and the tarmac is usually in good shape. However, the speed limit is low, and police and cameras are active, so stay within it. Wild boar and deer cross the road, especially at dawn and dusk, and cyclists and walkers are everywhere on sunny weekends. On wet days, the leaves and pine needles make corners treacherous, so take care.

Spend a little time in the town if you can. The streets around the château have cafés and restaurants, and pastry shops where a slice of something sweet makes a fair reward. A walk in the palace gardens, with their carp pond and formal parterres, is a gentle way to rest between rides.
t.anse@45.9,4.7:
Anse is a small town of just over five thousand people on the Saône, at the point where the little river Azergues joins it, and it is the gateway to the Pierres Dorées, the Golden Stone country of the southern Beaujolais. The villages of this district are built of a soft, honey-coloured limestone that glows in the evening light, and the vineyards that cover the hills produce the lighter Beaujolais wines. As a fuel gate and start and finish of the ride, Anse is a convenient place, with fuel stations, a supermarket, bakeries and cafés, and it is easy to reach from Lyon, about twenty-five kilometres to the south.

The town has a long past. In Roman times it was a staging post called Asa Paulini on the road from Lyon to the north, and its position on the Saône made it a trading centre in the Middle Ages. The Château des Tours, on the edge of town, dates from the thirteenth century and was a residence of the archbishops of Lyon, who held much of the surrounding land. It is a solid fortified building with towers and a moat, and today it hosts events and exhibitions.

Leaving Anse, the road quickly climbs into the hills, with vineyards on the slopes and villages perched on ridges. The bends are gentle to medium, the surface is mostly good, and the views open across the Saône valley to the Dombes plateau and, on a clear day, the Alps. This is a classic day-trip landscape for Lyonnais riders, which means that weekends, especially sunny ones, can be busy, and cyclists share the roads. A weekday ride is calmer.

For a final or first meal, the local restaurants serve the food of Lyon and the Beaujolais, with sausages, andouillette, cervelle de canut, a herb and cream cheese spread, and the local wine, light and fruity and best served slightly cool. Fill the tank before the climb, because the hill villages have few stations, and enjoy a cup of coffee on the terrace before setting off.
t.seine loops and roche guyon@49.3,2.4:
The Thérain is a quiet river that rises near Beauvais and flows south-east through the Oise to join the Oise near Creil, and the valley between Balagny-sur-Thérain and Mouy is a gentle landscape of meadows, poplars and small villages. Bury, Cires-lès-Mello and Mouy, towns of three to five and a half thousand people, each have a bakery, a café and a few shops, and Mouy has fuel. The valley sides are limestone, and the pale stone from quarries in this region was used to build churches and houses across the Oise and as far as Paris.

The stone has left its mark on the landscape. Old quarry faces show white among the trees, and many villages have houses built of the same cream-coloured stone, with steep tiled roofs and walls topped with moss. The nearby Oise valley at Saint-Leu-d'Esserent has medieval quarries that supplied building stone for the great Gothic cathedrals of northern France, including Notre-Dame de Paris, and the churches here are some of the best examples of the style. If you have time, a stop at a village church to look at the stonework is worthwhile.

As a food stop, this is a modest place, but a bakery sandwich on a bench by the river is a fine lunch. Mouy is the best bet for fuel and a larger choice of cafés. The riding along the Thérain valley is relaxed, with gentle bends, a smooth surface and light traffic, and the climbs to the plateau on either side are short and easy. In spring, the meadows are bright with buttercups, and in autumn, the mist rises from the river and softens the light.

If you are riding on to the Seine, the route climbs onto the Vexin plateau, where the roads run straight and fast across open fields, and the valley behind you shrinks to a green line of trees. Remember that these are working landscapes, and farm vehicles use the roads at all hours. Treat the quiet as part of the pleasure.
t.seine loops and roche guyon high point@4:
The Pays de Thelle is a plateau of limestone and clay that lies between the valleys of the Oise and the Thérain, north of Paris, and it has a character quite its own. Crouy-en-Thelle and Le Mesnil-en-Thelle are small villages of one to two thousand people, set among fields of wheat and beet, with woods on the slopes and wide views to the horizon. The high point on the label is a gentle rise on the plateau, where the road crests and the land falls away toward the Oise valley, with the town of Persan and the river below.

Persan, six kilometres away with over nine thousand people, is the nearest town of any size, and it has fuel stations and shops. Boran-sur-Oise, on the river itself, was once a ferry crossing, and the valley here is a mixture of industry and green space, with railway lines running along the bank and poplar groves between the factories. A few kilometres south is the Forêt de Carnelle, a large wood of oak and beech that is popular with walkers and offers cool shade on hot days.

The ride up from the valley is pleasantly twisty, with a few tight bends through woods, and then the plateau roads are open and fast. The surface is good, apart from patches near farm entrances, and traffic is light except around Persan and Beaumont-sur-Oise. The wind can be strong on the plateau, so take care in gusts, and in winter mist can hang on the high ground for hours. In autumn the beech woods turn to copper and gold, and the fields are bare and brown.

It is easy to underrate this kind of country. It has no famous monument and no dramatic scenery, but it has a quiet, lived-in beauty, with villages of pale stone, church towers on the skyline and small woods in every fold of the land. The Thelle plateau gives you a feeling for the ordinary landscape of northern France, shaped by centuries of farming, and it is a pleasure to ride through.
t.fontainebleau forest and loing sweep hig:
This is the Seine at its most rural, a river curving through meadows and poplar groves between Melun and the northern fringe of the Fontainebleau forest, with the villages of La Rochette, Livry-sur-Seine and Chartrettes strung along its banks. Each has fewer than three thousand people, a church, a bakery and a riverside path, and they have the feel of places that have long lived by and from the water. Barges still push slowly past, carrying gravel and grain, and in summer rowing crews and anglers share the water.

Chartrettes in particular has a pleasant riverside, with a long promenade and a lock, and the opposite bank is covered with the green edge of the forest. Vaux-le-Pénil, three kilometres away with nearly twelve thousand people, has the nearest fuel stations and supermarkets, so fill the tank there before heading into the quieter lanes. The high point of the label is a rise of land above the river, where the road climbs to a plateau and the view opens across the valley to the woods beyond.

The riding here is relaxed and varied. The roads follow the river for a while with gentle bends, then climb onto the plateau for a faster stretch through fields, and then drop back into the valley through a village. The surface is mostly good, but the climbs through the woods can be damp and covered in leaf litter, and in places the road is narrow, with high walls on either side. Traffic is light on weekday mornings and heavier at weekends, when cyclists and families take to the riverside.

The history of the valley is long. The Seine was the great highway of medieval France, carrying wine, grain and stone to Paris, and the villages along its banks owed their living to it. Today the river is quieter, but the sense of an old working landscape remains. Early morning, when the mist lies on the water and the first light touches the poplars, is the best time to see it.
t.fontainebleau forest and loing sweep sce:
Melun is an old town on the Seine with a surprisingly deep history, and a ride that ends here finishes in a place with real character. The oldest part of the city stands on an island in the river, where a Gallic settlement known to the Romans once stood, and the church of Notre-Dame on the island dates back to the eleventh century. In the twelfth century the philosopher Peter Abelard taught at Melun, drawing students from across the country, and the town was a favourite of the early Capetian kings, who held court here. With nearly thirty-nine thousand people, it is the prefecture of the Seine-et-Marne department, and it has every service a rider needs.

Fuel stations, cafés and restaurants are plentiful, and the riverside quays offer a pleasant place to sit and watch the barges go by. The town is also known for its Brie de Melun, a cheese with a stronger, more rustic flavour than its cousin from Meaux, and a good cheese shop will let you taste both. Voisenon, two kilometres from the road and with about twelve hundred people, was the home of an eighteenth-century writer and priest, the Abbé de Voisenon, a witty man who wrote plays and verses for the salons of Paris. His château still stands.

The scenic road leading to Melun runs through the quiet country south-east of Paris, across the Brie plateau and down toward the Seine, with gentle bends and small villages. Rubelles and Maincy are near neighbours, and Maincy is close to the great château of Vaux-le-Vicomte, which makes a fine excursion for another day. The surface is good and the traffic is light outside the town, but Melun itself has the usual urban congestion at rush hour, so allow a little time for the last few kilometres.

As the end of the day, it is a satisfying place to arrive. The light on the river in the evening is soft, the old streets are calm and a glass of wine on the quay is a fine reward for the miles behind you. Park the bike in a central car park, take off your helmet, and walk the old town before dinner.
t.mantes la jolie@49.0,1.7:
Mantes-la-Jolie carries its pretty name with a straight face, though the town of forty-four thousand is mostly practical rather than pretty, a Seine-side workhorse about fifty kilometres downstream from Paris. Tradition says Henri IV gave it the nickname, and the one thing that truly justifies it is the collegiate church of Notre-Dame, a Gothic building of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries whose façade and proportions echo the cathedral in Paris so closely that architects call it a rehearsal for it. Walk in and the light through the nave is worth five minutes even if you are in leathers.

For a rider, Mantes is the natural place to gather yourself at either end of a day. Fuel is easy, since a town this size has stations all around the ring roads, as well as supermarkets, bakeries and a station with trains to Paris Saint-Lazare if you need to bail out. Across the river lies Limay, with an old humpbacked bridge and a church on the slope, and the cluster of Mantes-la-Ville beside it. The two bridges over the Seine are bottlenecks at rush hour, so a finish here at six in the evening can cost you twenty minutes in a queue.

What makes the area good for riding is what lies on either side. North of the river the Vexin plateau rolls away in wheat and rapeseed, cut by small valleys and strung with villages of pale limestone, while downstream the Seine swings through long loops under white chalk cliffs. The roads that drop to the water tend to be narrow, with blind bends and walls, and they are at their best early on a weekday when the river mist has not yet lifted. Surface quality is generally fine, though farm traffic leaves mud on the corners at harvest and in wet weather.

If you have time at the end of the ride, sit by the Seine and watch the barges. Commercial traffic still moves grain, sand and containers along this stretch, and the slow rhythm of the water is a good way to let the engine cool and the day settle. The cobbled lanes of the old centre are worth a slow walk, with the bike parked near the church.
t.auvers sur oise@49.1,2.2:
Few villages have as much weight on their shoulders as Auvers-sur-Oise. Vincent van Gogh came here in May 1890, lodged in a small room above an inn, and in the seventy days he stayed painted around seventy canvases, among them the church, the wheat fields and the town hall bedecked with flags, before he died of a gunshot wound in July. He and his brother Theo lie side by side in the little cemetery above the fields, under a blanket of ivy. The room he rented at the Auberge Ravoux is preserved almost bare, and it is more moving for being so small.

He was not alone in loving this valley. Daubigny settled here before him and painted from a floating studio on the Oise, and Pissarro, Cézanne and Corot all worked in and around the village. At roughly seventy metres above sea level, the Oise here runs wide and slow between poplars, with low chalk hills behind, and you can understand why painters liked the light. The village has about seven thousand people, enough for a couple of bakeries, restaurants and cafés, which in season fill with day trippers who come to follow the painter's footsteps.

For a rider it is a food stop, and a good one if you arrive before the coach parties or after they leave. The roads in are pleasant, running along the river and climbing a short way to the plateau, with bends that call for attention rather than speed. Traffic can be heavy at weekends in summer, with cars searching for parking, and the lanes around the church are narrow and cobbled in places. Leave the bike on the edge and walk up.

Climb to the church and the cemetery behind it, and the wheat fields that Van Gogh painted stretch out beyond the wall. In June they are green and gold, and the crows that wheel above them are a quiet allusion to his last great painting. Take an hour if you can. The village sells postcards and prints, but the best souvenir is the view from the top of the hill, with the valley and a distant line of trees on a clear afternoon.
t.saint etienne@45.4,4.4:
Saint-Étienne wears its history in layers of coal, iron and cloth, and from the ring roads on the north side you can see how a city spread across a series of ridges, with the hills of the Pilat to the south and the mining basin of the Gier to the east. This is the second time the rides use it as a base, and it makes sense: with nearly a hundred and seventy-six thousand people, it has fuel on every approach, early bakeries and a tram that runs through the centre. The suburbs of Saint-Genest-Lerpt and Saint-Priest-en-Jarez, each with about six thousand people, climb the hills on the north side and make the quickest exit onto quieter roads.

The city's industrial story is still visible, not least in the preserved Puits Couriot, a former pithead with a tall headframe that now forms part of a mining museum. Nearby in Firminy, about ten kilometres west, stands the largest ensemble of buildings designed by Le Corbusier in Europe, including a housing block, a stadium and a church whose concrete cone rises against the sky. These are the places to see if you have a free hour or an interest in modern architecture, and they are no distance from the route.

As a ride start, Saint-Étienne offers an easy exit to the hills. In twenty minutes you can be climbing among beech and fir toward the Pilat, with the ridge road and its views opening out over the Rhône valley, and in an hour you can be in the high country, the air noticeably thinner and cooler. The same roads bring you back at the end of the day, usually in the lower light of evening, with the glow of the city below you and the smell of woodsmoke on the air.

Coming back in the dark, take care at the junctions near the ring road, where trams, buses and delivery vans share narrow streets. The city can be damp and foggy in autumn and winter, while in summer the heat in the valley is a pleasant contrast to the hills. A plate of local sausage with potatoes in a simple restaurant is the right way to end it.
t.mont ventoux long south day@45.7,4.4:
Forty-odd kilometres west of Lyon, in the Monts du Lyonnais, the land is a patchwork of small fields, orchards and woods, divided by hedges and stone walls, with scattered farms and villages on every hill. Haute-Rivoire, Saint-Laurent-de-Chamousset and Sainte-Foy-l'Argentière are all within a few kilometres of each other, and none has more than two thousand people, but each has a bakery and a bar and the usual run of French small-town services. It is an ordinary landscape, and that makes it charming. Lyonnais families come here at weekends for walks, picnics and lunch at a farm inn.

The ride is called the Mont Ventoux Long South Day, and the mountain itself is far away, at the other end of a long day's riding. Ventoux, at 1,912 metres, stands alone in Provence, a bald white cone of limestone that can be seen from a hundred kilometres around, and its summit is often swept by the mistral. Cyclists know it for the Tour de France climbs and a memorial to the British rider Tom Simpson, who died near the top in 1967. A rider heading there from here has a long way to go, down the Rhône valley, so the early start and full tank are not optional.

Stations around the Monts du Lyonnais are modest. The bigger fuel stops are on the main roads and near the motorway, and on Sundays many of the small ones are closed, so fill up at a supermarket station on the way in, where prices are lower anyway. At seven or eight in the morning the lanes are almost empty, and the mist often lies in the valleys, while the hills stand clear in the first sun.

A good way to begin is to take the small roads over the hills toward the Rhône, rather than the motorway. They are narrow, winding and well kept, with a pleasant mix of climbs and descents, and they let you warm up gradually. The air smells of cut grass in summer and of woodsmoke in autumn. Spring is lovely, with orchards in bloom.
t.mont ventoux long south day high point@4:
The plain of the Forez is a quiet, open piece of France that few visitors see. It lies in the upper valley of the Loire, between the Monts du Lyonnais on the east and the higher Monts du Forez on the west, and it is flat and green, with fields of grain and pasture, ponds and small villages of stone and brick. Feurs, the main town here, with about eight thousand people, was a Roman settlement, with a forum, and the straight streets still reflect that origin. Montrond-les-Bains, a few kilometres south, is a small spa town with a ruined castle above it and a reputation for its mineral waters. The famous sparkling water Badoit comes from Saint-Galmier, close by.

It is not a high point in the way that name suggests, since the plain lies at about four hundred metres. But the label points to a lookout, a rise in the land where the plain opens before you, with the Forez mountains blue and low on the western horizon. On a clear day in spring, when snow remains on the highest ridges, the view is beautiful. The Loire itself runs through the plain in broad loops, bordered by poplars and willows, and in autumn the mist that forms over the river in the early morning can linger until ten.

For a rider, it is easy riding. The roads are straight and well surfaced, with gentle curves and occasional villages, and a good place to settle into a rhythm. Traffic is moderate on the main routes and light on the minor ones, though the market days in Feurs bring a bustle to the centre. The wind can blow hard along the valley, and in winter it can be cold and foggy.

For fuel and food, Feurs is the best choice, with supermarkets, bakeries and cafés on the main street, and Montrond-les-Bains has a few good restaurants. Local dishes include sausage, river fish and cheeses from the Forez hills, along with fruit from the orchards in season. The nearest large city is Saint-Étienne, about forty kilometres to the south-east, and Lyon is an hour away. A good time to visit is late spring, when the meadows are bright with flowers, or September, when the light is clear and the roads are quiet.
Coupvray has a small but real claim to fame. In 1809 a boy named Louis Braille was born here, the son of a saddler, and a few years later an accident in his father's workshop blinded him. At fifteen he invented the system of raised dots that is still used by blind readers around the world. The family house, now a small museum, stands in the village, and his grave is in the churchyard. It is a quiet place, a short ride from Disneyland Paris and the commuter belt of Marne-la-Vallée, and it is surprising how rural it still feels.

The fuel gate lies a few kilometres away, near Esbly and Chalifert, in the valley of the Marne, east of the capital. The river runs here in wide, slow bends between low hills, with a canal alongside, and the towns are practical ones, with stations, bakeries and a railway line that carries commuters to Paris. For a ride that heads south to the Fontainebleau forest, this is a convenient starting point, since it avoids the worst of the city traffic and gets you onto the quieter roads quickly. Be sure to leave early on weekdays, because the morning traffic on the main roads can be heavy.

This is the Brie, a country of broad plateaux, wheat fields and small woods, which gives its name to the famous soft cheese. The Brie de Meaux, made in the town a few kilometres to the north, is one of the best-known cheeses in France, and you can buy it in the local markets. The roads that cross the plateau are straight and fast, with long views, and the wind can be strong in open ground.

As the ride continues south, the landscape changes. After Melun the land becomes more wooded, and then the great forest of Fontainebleau appears, with its sandstone boulders, oaks and pines, and the old royal château in the middle. It is one of the most loved forests in France and a favourite of Parisian cyclists and climbers, and the roads through it are smooth and winding, with a speed limit that is often enforced. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, when the air is cool and the light is soft.
West of Lyon, the Monts du Lyonnais rise in a series of green, rounded hills, and here, around Mornant, Saint-Andéol-le-Château and Saint-Maurice-sur-Dargoire, they are at their most agreeable. This is orchard and vineyard country, with cherries and apples on the slopes, and the vines of the Coteaux du Lyonnais, which produce light, fruity wines, mostly from the Gamay grape. Villages of golden stone, with church towers and small squares, sit on the ridges, and the lanes between them wind among hedges and walnut trees.

The history of the area is remarkable. In Roman times the city of Lugdunum, now Lyon, was supplied with water by a long aqueduct that brought it from the valley of the Gier, and its remains can still be seen in this region, in the form of arches, bridges and sections of channel, some of them partly buried in the fields. The most visible stretches lie around Chaponost and Mornant, where tall arches rise above the trees. The aqueduct ran over thirty kilometres, and some of its engineering, including the inverted siphons that carried the water across valleys, is quite sophisticated.

The label says swim, and the area has a number of small lakes and pools, but I would treat it with caution. Swimming here means local ponds and municipal pools, not a great wild river. The land is hilly, with plenty of curves and short climbs, and the riding is a pleasure, in a gentle sort of way, with views across the Rhône valley to the Alps on clear days. Roads are narrow and often shaded, so watch for damp patches and leaves, particularly in autumn, and for cyclists, since the hills are popular with Lyon's racing clubs.

Mornant, with just over five thousand people, is a lively market town, with fuel, shops and cafés, and a good choice of bakeries. Pastry shops sell a local tart made with cream and sugar, and the restaurants serve the cooking of Lyon, rich with sausage, offal and cream. In summer the lanes are busy at weekends. Late spring, when the cherries are in flower, and October, with its colours, are the best times.
t.dombes lakes easy scenic@46.0,4.6:
This is the Haut-Beaujolais, the hilly, upper end of France's famous wine country, and it is a good deal wilder than the postcards suggest. Le Perréon, Lamure-sur-Azergues and Grandris lie in the valley of the Azergues, a small river that runs between steep wooded slopes, with vineyards on the sunny faces and pastures and forests above. Each village has about a thousand people, a church, a bakery and a bar, and the stone houses, the colour of old honey in the south, here turn grey and brown. It is quiet, rural country, with few tourists.

The grape is Gamay, grown on granite soils, and produces light, fruity red wines that are drunk young and slightly cool. The famous Beaujolais Nouveau, released on the third Thursday of November, is only the beginning, and the better wines of the villages and crus can age well. In Lyon, wine is served in a thick-bottomed bottle called a pot, and the local restaurants, known as bouchons, serve hearty plates of sausage, tripe sausage, pork, cheese and a salad with bacon and egg.

As a place for lunch, the area is perfect. A small restaurant in one of the villages, with a plate of charcuterie, a stew or a roast, a piece of local cheese and a glass of the local red, takes up an hour or two, and costs less than in the city. Tables fill quickly at weekends, so book if you can. Many restaurants close one or two days a week, and often on Sunday evenings, so check before you go.

The riding in the Azergues valley is excellent. The roads climb and drop through vines and forest, with tight bends and viewpoints over the valley, and there are quiet back roads that link the villages. Traffic is light except at harvest time, in September and early October, when tractors and grape trucks fill the lanes. Fuel is available in the larger villages, but not at every one, so fill up at the town before you enter the hills. Late spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.dombes lakes easy scenic high point@46.0:
Villefranche-sur-Saône is the capital of the Beaujolais, and a more practical place than the label suggests. It lies on the right bank of the Saône, where the hills end and the plain begins, and it has about thirty-three thousand people, and a long main street, the Rue Nationale, lined with shops and old houses, which follows the line of the medieval town, founded in the early thirteenth century. Gleizé and Limas, its immediate neighbours, merge into it, and the whole area has the feel of a prosperous provincial town, with supermarkets, car dealers and fuel stations at every roundabout.

The label says swim. There are municipal pools and a few lakes in the area, but the Saône itself is a slow, wide, muddy river, and not a place for swimming. The Dombes, on the opposite bank, is the landscape the ride is named for: a flat country of a thousand ponds, created in the Middle Ages for fish farming and still drained and refilled in a regular cycle. The fish, carp and pike, are a speciality of local restaurants, along with frogs' legs, and the ponds are a major stop for migratory birds in spring and autumn.

The high point is the rise of the hills to the west, the first slopes of the Beaujolais, where vines begin within minutes of the town centre. The golden-stone villages of the Pierres Dorées, to the south, take their colour from the local limestone, which glows orange in the evening sun. The roads are narrow and winding, through vineyards and orchards, with views across to the Saône plain and, on clear days, to the Alps.

For riders, Villefranche is an excellent base for services, and the place to fill up before heading into the hills or across the plain. Traffic is heavy at rush hour and on market days, and the ring road can be slow, so aim to arrive outside those times. The Saône valley is prone to mist in autumn and winter, which can be thick and slow in the morning. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons for riding here, and a coffee on the Rue Nationale, with the world going by, is a good way to take a break.
t.loire castle edge tour@49.3,2.3:
Mouy lies in the Oise, in the chalk country that rolls gently between Beauvais and the Paris basin, and it is the sort of town that most people only see from the car. A few thousand people live there and in the neighbouring villages of Angy and Bury, in an area of farms, woods and quiet lanes called the Pays de Thelle, where the soil is white and flinty and the fields are large. It is not a beautiful landscape in the way the Alps are, but there is an honest charm in the small stone churches, the hedged lanes and the long skyline of the plateau.

The reason to know it is that it makes a practical start for a day that heads south and west. Mouy has fuel stations, supermarkets and bakeries, and the roads out are easy, lightly trafficked and fast, so you can cover the first stretch of the day without trouble. Beauvais, a short way to the north-west, has a cathedral whose Gothic choir is the highest in the world, rising to nearly forty-eight metres, and it was never completed, because the vault collapsed in the thirteenth century and a tower fell in the sixteenth. The unfinished building has a certain romance, and the astronomical clock inside is worth a look.

To the south lies the forest of Chantilly, where the roads wind in long curves through oak and beech, and the great château with its stables and racecourse stands among lakes. Beyond that comes the Île-de-France and the long drive toward the Loire. If the ride is heading for the châteaux of the Loire valley, you have a long way ahead, so an early start is important.

Weather matters here more than you might think. The plateau is exposed, and a cold north wind can sweep across it for days in winter, while in summer the heat shimmers off the fields. Fog is common in autumn and early winter, particularly in the river valleys. Late spring, when the rape fields blaze yellow, and September are the best times to ride, and the traffic on the main roads is lighter on weekday mornings.
t.route napoleon weekend high point@46.1,4:
Roanne is not on many riders' lists, but it is on every gourmet's. The town, with about forty thousand people, stands on the upper Loire where the river leaves the hills and begins to slow, and it has a handsome port on the Canal de Roanne à Digoin, a riverside promenade and a lively market. What put it on the map, though, is a restaurant, the Maison Troisgros, which has held three Michelin stars since 1968, and has made this working town an unlikely place of pilgrimage for people who care about food. You do not need to eat there to feel the effect: the bakeries and bistros of Roanne are very good.

The hills around the town are the real reason to be here. To the west rise the Monts de la Madeleine, wooded and cool, with narrow roads that wind through beech and fir, and to the south-east the Monts de Tarare and the first heights of the Beaujolais. The label high point suggests one of these ridges, and that is a fair reading: from Perreux and Le Coteau, the villages on the river just outside town, the land lifts quickly into pastures and forest, and a short climb gives you a view back over the Loire plain.

The ride is named for the Route Napoléon, which is far away to the south-east in the Alps, so this stretch is part of the long approach, and a very good one. The roads are quiet and well surfaced, with moderate curves and few cars, and the landscape changes from river plain to hill country in a matter of minutes. Spring is excellent, with fresh green meadows, and autumn brings gold to the beeches. In winter the higher roads can be icy, and in July and August afternoon storms are common.

For services, Roanne has all you could want, with fuel at the supermarkets and the main roads, plenty of hotels and restaurants, and secure parking near the centre. Le Coteau and Perreux, across the river, are quieter. Lunch in a local bistro is a good idea, since the cooking is serious, with Charolais beef, river fish and local cheeses, and prices are lower than in Lyon.
t.morvan southbound weekend photo pull off:
Upstream of Paris, the Seine flows through a wide, tree-lined valley of old industry, new housing and surprisingly green corners, and this stretch near Corbeil-Essonnes is a typical mix. Corbeil is a town of forty thousand people, with the huge Grands Moulins, the flour mills on the riverbank that have been a landmark since the nineteenth century and once supplied much of Paris with flour. The old mills stand like cathedrals of brick and concrete, and are now partly converted. Nearby, Saintry-sur-Seine and Le Coudray-Montceaux are quieter, with riverside paths and woods.

The photo pull-off in the name is a modest place, a spot along the river where you can stop to look at the water, the willows and the barges. The Seine is a working waterway, and long, low barges pass slowly, loaded with sand, grain and containers. In the morning mist hangs over the water and the light is soft, which is the best time to take pictures. It is also a good place to say goodbye to Paris before heading south.

The ride goes toward the Morvan, a region of granite hills, forests and lakes in the middle of Burgundy, whose wooded summits reach around nine hundred metres, with narrow roads and plenty of curves. It is a long day to get there, and this is a good place to start it, since the roads south run quickly toward Fontainebleau, past the great forest, and then on toward the Yonne valley. Leave early to avoid the traffic out of Paris, which is heavy on Friday afternoons, and consider the motorway for the first stretch.

Corbeil has fuel stations and supermarkets, and the smaller villages have bakeries. It is a useful place to take on supplies, since the countryside to the south is thinner in services. In autumn the forest around Fontainebleau turns gold and red, and in spring the bluebells flower beneath the beeches. On a quiet weekday morning, with the barges moving slowly on the water, it is a gentle start to a long journey.
t.morvan southbound weekend scenic road@48:
Paris-Saclay is the name of the plateau that rises south-west of the capital, and it has become a kind of French Silicon Valley, with universities, research institutes and laboratories among its fields. Orsay has a large university campus and a particle accelerator, Bures-sur-Yvette is home to the Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques, a small, elite centre for mathematics and physics, and Les Ulis, the biggest of the three towns with about twenty-six thousand people, is a modern town built mostly in the 1960s and 1970s. It is a surprising place to think about scenic roads, and yet the valley of the Yvette, which cuts through it, is attractive, with wooded slopes, small meadows and old stone mills.

The river runs west toward the Chevreuse valley, and on the way the landscape becomes much greener. The regional park of the Haute Vallée de Chevreuse, which begins just beyond, is a popular weekend destination for Parisians, with castles, abbeys and half-timbered villages. The roads there are narrow and winding, with plenty of curves and short climbs through beech woods, and on a fine morning in spring or autumn they make a lovely ride. The best time to go is early on a weekday, because on Sunday afternoons the lanes are crowded with cyclists and cars.

A point worth knowing is that the Paris region has many speed cameras, and the limits on small roads are often fifty or seventy, which are enforced. It is also a place where police checks are frequent near the suburbs. Surfaces are generally good, but in autumn the leaf litter and the shade can make for slippery bends.

The ride is named for the Morvan, in Burgundy, far to the south, and the road here is the connection between the capital and the countryside. The suburbs of Orsay and Bures have fuel stations, cafés and supermarkets, so it is a practical place to stop before you leave the city region behind. A coffee near the river in Bures, with the plane trees overhead, is a pleasant way to pass a quarter of an hour. Avoid the rush hours, when the roads around Les Ulis and the N118 are jammed, and plan to be on your way before seven or after nine.
t.morvan southbound weekend@49.1,2.1:
The Vexin is the plateau that lies between Paris and Normandy, north-west of the capital, a country of big open fields and low wooded ridges that has remained surprisingly rural for being so close to the city. Part of it is a regional nature park, created in the 1990s to protect the villages and the farmland from the spread of suburbs. Marines and Ennery are small, and Osny, with sixteen thousand people, is on the edge of Cergy-Pontoise, one of the new towns built around Paris from the 1960s, a place of tall housing, ponds and modern design.

That contrast is part of the story. Within a few kilometres you can pass from a tower block to a field of wheat with a ruined windmill, and the roads that connect them are good for easy riding, with gentle curves, big skies and light traffic. The soil is rich and the farms are large, and at harvest time in July the golden fields stretch to the horizon. In spring the rape is bright yellow, and the poppies bloom on the verges.

A few kilometres to the east, the village of Auvers-sur-Oise is famous as the place where Vincent van Gogh spent the last ten weeks of his life in 1890. He painted more than seventy canvases there, including the church and the wheat fields, and he is buried in the village cemetery beside his brother Theo. The place is a gentle pilgrimage and it is easy to see why the painters liked it, with the light on the river and the old stone houses.

As a food stop, the area offers the plain, good cooking of the Île-de-France, with a few farm shops selling cheese, honey and vegetables, and restaurants in the small towns. The cheeses of the Brie and the cream of Normandy are not far away. Fuel is plentiful in Osny and in Cergy, at the supermarkets, and this is a good place to fill up for the long ride south. Weekday lunches are quiet, and restaurants often close on Mondays. Take a layer, because the plateau is breezy, and the wind can be sharp in spring.
A bend in the Oise, some thirty kilometres north-west of Paris, shelters a group of villages that were once the haunt of painters. Valmondois, Butry-sur-Oise and Mériel stand along the river, with the forest of L'Isle-Adam rising behind them, and the whole stretch has the soft, green, slightly sleepy air of the Île-de-France before the suburbs arrived. The caricaturist Honoré Daumier spent his last years in Valmondois, in a small house lent to him by his friend the painter Corot, and he died there in 1879. His grave was later moved to Père Lachaise in Paris, but the village keeps his memory with a small museum.

The high point is a gentle one, a rise on the plateau above the valley from which you can look down on the river and the roofs of the villages. In the morning mist often fills the valley and the church towers stand out like islands. The road along the ridge is quiet and offers wide views, with a few bends and a good surface, and it is a pleasant ride at the start of the day. The forest on the other side of the river has long straight avenues and some fine old oaks.

The ride is named for the Morvan, the granite hills of Burgundy, a long way to the south-east, and from here it starts with the broad plateaux of the Vexin and the Île-de-France. If you are heading there, make an early start to avoid the traffic, especially on Friday evenings and on Sunday afternoons, when the roads around the Oise valley are crowded with weekenders.

The villages have small centres with bakeries and cafés, and Mériel, the largest of the three, has about four thousand people, and a station with a fast train to Paris. For fuel, the best choice is the roadside stations on the main road, or the supermarkets in Pontoise and L'Isle-Adam. In summer the river bank is a place for walks and fishing, and in autumn the leaves turn red and gold. The air has a faint smell of woodsmoke and wet leaves in the evening.
t.bugey lakes and jura edge@45.3,4.9:
Valloire is the name of the broad, flat valley that lies between the Rhône and the hills of the Bas-Dauphiné, and the villages of Épinouze, Saint-Sorlin-en-Valloire and Sonnay sit in it among fields of walnut trees, maize and orchards. It is quiet and open, an agricultural plain, with big farms and long straight roads, and it is a good place for a start because it is so uncomplicated. Everything is a little further apart than you expect, and the skies are large.

The old farms here are of a kind you will find across the Dauphiné, built of pisé, rammed earth, which was pressed in wooden moulds between boards and then covered with a coat of lime plaster. It is a very ancient technique, and the thick walls keep the house cool in summer and warm in winter. Some of the buildings are very large, with courtyards and barns, and the earth colour of the walls gives the villages a soft, warm look in the evening light.

The ride goes toward the Bugey, a southern spur of the Jura mountains, and its lakes, rivers and cliffs, which lie to the north-east. The first stretch crosses the Rhône valley and then climbs into the hills, with a mix of gentle roads and a few more challenging ones. Early morning is the best time, when the air is still and cool and the mist lies on the fields. In summer it can already be hot by ten.

For services, the villages are small, and Épinouze and Saint-Sorlin, each with about a thousand or fifteen hundred people, offer a bakery, a bar and a few shops. Fuel is more reliable in the larger towns, such as Saint-Rambert-d'Albon, and the stations along the main road, so make sure you start with a full tank. The walnuts are harvested in autumn, and at that season the roads have a few slow tractors and trailers. A walnut tart or a bag of fresh nuts from a farm stall is a good souvenir, and it is a tasty reminder of the region.
Riotord, Dunières and Montfaucon-en-Velay lie in the Haute-Loire, on the high plateau of the Velay, at between eight hundred and a thousand metres, in a country of cold, windswept pasture, fir woods and small farms. The landscape is austere and open, with long views, lonely farmhouses and a sky that changes quickly, and the winters are hard, with snow lying for weeks. It is part of the eastern edge of the Massif Central, the old volcanic country, and the rounded hills and rocky summits of the Velay, with its dark basalt outcrops, are a sign of that history.

The label says swim, which is optimistic. The area has a few small lakes and ponds, and in summer local people swim in them, but the water is cold, even in August, and the facilities are modest. A better reason to come is the riding. The roads over the plateau are quiet and sweeping, with open curves, good views and little traffic, and they pass through villages of grey stone with steep roofs. In late spring the meadows are covered in wild flowers, including narcissus, which bloom in white sheets in May and June, and in autumn the larches turn gold.

Dunières, the largest of the three, has about three thousand people, and in the nineteenth century it was a centre for silk ribbon and the weaving of cloth. The old mills along the river are still visible. Montfaucon-en-Velay has a medieval keep on a hill, and Riotord, a small village with about twelve hundred inhabitants, is the quietest.

The ride is named for the Bugey, a long way to the north-east, and this is part of the long cross-country route. Weather can change fast on the plateau, and cold, wet or foggy conditions are possible at any time of year, so bring waterproofs and warm layers.
